'This is where people can come and ease the load, have a few bets and chill' - government wants change but London's betting shop customers definitely don't
![Betfred have settled an investigation held by the Gambling Commission](https://www.racingpost.com/_next/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fs3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com%2Fprod-media-racingpost%2Fprod%2Fimages%2F169_1008%2Faf877e0440ea-gettyimages-2264874448.jpg&w=3840&q=75)
Click here to add us to your Google preferred sources or find out more here
The more things change, the more they stay the same. As ever-increasing legislative pressures threaten the very existence of retail spaces for the gambling industry, the shops themselves remain constant.
That is why many normal people from all walks of life, who share the joy of having an opinion strong enough to feel it is worth having something at stake, will miss them when they’re gone.
Saturday started with Fred Done, the UK’s highest taxpayer and the man behind Betfred, making an apocalyptic prediction in the Financial Times. Done said if chancellor John Healey follows through with the reported plan to raise machine gaming duty from 20 to 40 per cent it would result in the death of the high-street betting shop by 2030. That’s just over four years away. An entire, nationwide, regulated and taxed industry wiped from the British landscape.
![Fred Done is still vigorously driving his betting shop empire at the age of 76](https://www.racingpost.com/_next/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fs3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com%2Fprod-media-racingpost%2Fprod%2Fimages%2F169_1008%2F1fb2c48100e7-73042.jpg&w=3840&q=75)
And yet, if you wander into either of Done's two shops within a well-struck five iron of Waterloo station in the centre of London, and you would have no idea the big boss had suggested the bricks-and-mortar betting experience was at grave risk.
That is the beauty of these spaces – they never seem to change. If only everything in life could be as constant as the betting shop.
To walk into one is to be reminded of every previous visit. The print on the wall may have turned to screens in some of the fancier ones, but a mass extinction event is unlikely to wipe out betting shop regulars. An older guy sat quietly, nose in the Post, looking over form he’s already studied, experiencing great joy at the late surge of 11-2 shot Bells Grove in the 1.42 at Navan. Someone in the corner filled out a football coupon, while an occasional expletive could be heard from the FOBT player.
The machines may be the focus of the Exchequer but Done revealed, despite the £2 limit introduced in 2019, they account for half a shop's profit. Double the tax on them and Done predicted 495 of his 1,094 shops, 2,575 jobs and £67 million in taxes would evaporate immediately, with the rest of the retail estate wrapped up by 2030.
Those are worrying words for anyone in the industry or working in a sport that relies heavily on the levying of bookmaker profits, but when you're the human consequence of political decisions, they hit that bit harder.
![Betting shop closures - includng those of Betfred - have been in the news this summer](https://www.racingpost.com/_next/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fs3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com%2Fprod-media-racingpost%2Fprod%2Fimages%2F169_1008%2F3046cd439311-6211432.jpg&w=3840&q=75)
Raj Ashutosh has worked for Betfred for almost seven years and manages the shop on The Cut, less than a mile from the Houses of Parliament where decisions will be made that affect his life with little to no thought given to the impact they will have on him. He is, potentially, the human cost of the government's targeting of the gambling industry.
"It's going to be a tough time if this tax goes up," Ashutosh said. "We've already lost a lot of business – as you can see the shop is almost empty."
He added: "It will only make it more difficult. There have already been many shops shut down. At four staff per shop, ten shops, that's 40 jobs, 100 shops, that's 400 people losing their job. Further closures would make us very nervous.
"The central London shops have not been too affected so far. We've only had a few close, so I hadn't been that worried, but I know other colleagues who have had their shops close or are having a really difficult time. Until now it has been okay, but if they close down more it'd be very worrying – it's very difficult for people to get jobs at the moment."
Coker, in his 70s, and Bigs, 59, are two punters enjoying the afternoon's racing in Betfred's other Waterloo shop on Lower Marsh and they too would lose out if their local shop was to shut.
![The government is set to give local councils more powers over betting shops opening](https://www.racingpost.com/_next/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fs3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com%2Fprod-media-racingpost%2Fprod%2Fimages%2F169_1008%2F23cb3914e581-andy-and-bookmakers2.jpg&w=3840&q=75)
"It wouldn't be great, not at all," said Bigs – who was indeed big. "This is where people can come and ease the load, have a few bets and chill.
"Why do they want to change that, cleaning up the high street? Look at what opens when shops close. All around it's takeaways or vape shops. That's no better.
"You can come here and have a laugh and a few bets. If you win, you win, and if you lose, you lose."
Around the time of Tottenham's disallowed equaliser in their match against Aston Villa, numbers in the shop swell to a dizzy six – which the manager revealed was at the busier end of the flow of the day.
Forcing shops to shut would not stop Coker betting. "I'm a regular," he said. "You can come in here and sit down, have a chat, have some bets, I don't see what the problem is?
"If they stop the shops I would keep betting. This is the nearest shop to where I live, so I come here, but if they closed I would go to the other shop down the road, or bet somewhere else."
The government may want things to change, but for those who use their local betting shop, all they want is for things to stay the same.

summary: Betfred founder Fred Done has warned that a reported government plan to raise machine gaming duty from 20 to 40 per cent could lead to the extinction of high-street betting shops by 2030. While officials target the gambling industry, local London customers and shop staff value these retail spaces as places to socialise and relax. Many regulars and employees worry about potential job losses and the negative impact that closures would have on local communities.
key_points: Fred Done predicted that doubling the machine gaming duty to 40 per cent would cause the death of high-street betting shops by 2030.
Central London betting shops like those near Waterloo currently remain a constant, unchanging space for customers to socialise and bet.
Shop managers and staff are anxious about potential job losses and further business closures resulting from government tax increases.
Regular customers view betting shops as community hubs where people can relax, rather than being replaced by vape shops and takeaways.

title: Healey’s mansion tax raid to hit 270,000 families
author: Sabrina Miller
content:
![John Healey leaves No 10](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/19/TELEMMGLPICT000501635813_17898291681260_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwVVuduJKBIVmdsWxwOVYZQY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![John Healey leaves No 10](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/19/TELEMMGLPICT000501635813_17898291681260_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwVVuduJKBIVmdsWxwOVYZQY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
John Healey’s planned changes to the mansion tax mean more than a quarter of a million families will be hit with the levy.
Some 270,000 homes will have to pay the fee if the Chancellor goes ahead with proposals to lower the starting threshold to £1.5m.
The tax was first announced by Rachel Reeves at the Budget last November as an annual charge on properties worth more than £2m. Properties above this valuation would pay a £2,500 annual charge and the scheme is due to start in April 2028.
Properties worth £2.5m to £3.5m are to be hit with a £3,500 fee, rising to £5,000 for £3.5m to £5m homes. The upper threshold is a £7,500 charge for houses worth more than £5m. This fee is applied on top of council tax.
At the time, it was estimated to be levied on around 134,000 homes and to raise about £400m each year by 2029-30.
The Chancellor is now reportedly set to lower the starting threshold to properties worth £1.5m, plunging another 150,000 homes into the affected tax bracket, according to The Times.
Analysis by Dan Neidle, the founder of Tax Policy Associates, has shown that the proposed alterations could raise around £800m per year.
To reach this figure, he has assumed that the £2,500 charge would be lowered to affect houses worth £1.5m-£2m and that the sliding scale would continue as previously outlined until houses costing more than £5m are charged an annual £10,000 fee.
Mr Neidle has warned that making these changes could have a “serious downside”, as adjusting a tax after it has been announced but before it has been implemented undermines perceptions that Britain has a stable tax system.
‘Disproportionate burden’ on London residents
Analysis shows that around half of the newly caught homes would be in London and a further 25 per cent would be in Surrey and Oxfordshire.
Only a small number of affected buildings will be in the North, a region that Prime Minister Andy Burnham has a strong connection with.
Four London councils – Wandsworth, Kensington and Chelsea, Westminster and Richmond – wrote to Mr Healey urging him to ditch the “unfair” tax that they said placed “a disproportionate burden on London residents”.
Opponents of the mansion tax have warned that it would negatively affect Britain’s property market as people would deliberately undervalue their homes to avoid the fee.
Kirstie Allsopp, the presenter of TV property show Location, Location, Location told Times Radio: “It’s going to stop people adding value. It’s going to stop people doing basic maintenance, because everyone is going to be terrified of sending their property, which is worth £1.3 or £1.4m, over the £1.5m threshold.”
Data show that since the mansion tax was announced last year, the number of homes valued at more than £2m has fallen by 6.5 per cent.
The speculation comes as Mr Healey scrambles to fill a £15bn defence spending black hole before the delivery of the Budget on Oct 28.
His fiscal headroom has been cut from £23bn to around £5bn as a result of Donald Trump’s war in Iran, which has significantly increased the cost of government borrowing.
A Treasury spokesman told The Telegraph: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”
summary: Chancellor John Healey is reportedly planning to lower the starting threshold of the upcoming mansion tax from £2m to £1.5m to help fill a defence spending gap ahead of the October 28 Budget. This proposed adjustment would increase the number of affected families from 134,000 to approximately 270,000 and raise annual revenues to an estimated £800m. Critics and local councils warn that the levy places a disproportionate burden on London and South East residents and could damage the UK property market.
key_points: Lowering the mansion tax threshold to £1.5m will bring an additional 150,000 homes into the tax bracket, totaling 270,000 affected families.
About half of the newly captured homes are located in London, with another 25 percent in Surrey and Oxfordshire.
Tax experts and TV presenter Kirstie Allsopp warned that the tax could discourage property maintenance and penalize homeowners attempting to add value.
The speculation arises as the Chancellor seeks to address a £15bn defence spending shortfall ahead of the Budget on October 28.

title: Supermarkets cash in on ‘protein-maxxing’ boom
author: Tom Haynes
content:
Step into a supermarket and you could be forgiven for thinking you had wandered into a gym bro’s fever dream.
Protein is everywhere. It has been added to yogurt, ice cream, tortillas, wraps, porridge, pasta, cheese, ready meals and even bottled water.
Morrisons has launched a range of 53 products with Applied Nutrition, including high-protein bread, cheese, pasta, ice cream and pizza. Sainsbury’s has introduced “High Protein” and “Small but Mighty” ranges, while Marks & Spencer is selling a 20-product “Nutrient Dense” line.
Even Ocado has launched a virtual “weight management” aisle featuring smaller portions, high-protein meals, fibre-rich products and supplements. Waitrose is opening physical “Wellbeing Bays” across its shops.
Across social media, influencers have embraced a trend for “protein-maxxing” diets. According to NIQ figures, 57pc of UK shoppers are following a high-protein diet to some extent. A Consumer Trends survey found that an estimated 65pc of Gen Z and millennials are “actively trying to get more protein” into their diets.
But the rush into protein is being driven by more than enthusiasm for fitness culture. Britain’s weight-loss drug boom is changing the way people eat. Supermarkets are scrambling to keep up.
Demand for weight-loss and anti-obesity drugs is soaring. People who take so-called GLP-1 inhibitors that suppress the appetite, such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, are given advice to prioritise protein to help preserve muscle mass while they lose weight.
summary: Supermarkets are increasingly stocking high-protein foods and launching specialized health ranges to capitalize on the "protein-maxxing" trend driven by fitness culture and social media influencers. This retail shift is also fueled by the UK's weight-loss drug boom, as users of appetite-suppressing medications like Wegovy and Mounjaro seek high-protein diets to preserve muscle mass. Major grocery chains including Morrisons, Sainsbury's, Marks & Spencer, Ocado, and Waitrose have all introduced new products or dedicated sections to meet this surging demand.
key_points: Supermarkets are adding protein to a wide variety of everyday foods, from yogurt and ice cream to bread and bottled water.
Major UK retailers like Morrisons, Sainsbury's, Marks & Spencer, Ocado, and Waitrose have introduced new high-protein ranges and wellness sections.
An estimated 57% of UK shoppers follow a high-protein diet, with 65% of Gen Z and millennials actively trying to consume more protein.
The demand for high-protein products is significantly driven by the rise of weight-loss and anti-obesity drugs like Wegovy and Mounjaro.
Users of GLP-1 inhibitors prioritize protein consumption to help preserve muscle mass while losing weight.

title: Retail sales bounce back in Great Britain amid brighter signs for economy
author: Mark Sweney
content:
Retail sales across Great Britain unexpectedly rose last month, the latest economic indicator to defy gloomy forecasts as the chancellor, John Healey, prepares to present next month’s budget.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold rose 0.5% month on month in August, defying analyst expectations of a 0.2% fall.
It marks a significant bounce back in consumer spending after a 0.5% month-on-month fall in July.
The summer heatwaves fuelled increased sales of items including fans, air-conditioning units, sports merchandise and clothing in the three months to August.
The unexpected sales boost is the latest positive update on the state of the economy for the government, after a surprise 0.4% increase in gross domestic product in July that was reported by the ONS last week.
“August’s warm weather delayed the usual shift towards autumn purchases, but retailers successfully kept consumers spending,” said Sandra Prince, the head of corporate consumer at Lloyds. “The late bank holiday weekend and back-to-school shopping are also likely to have supported demand, with online sales among the areas seeing the biggest boost.”
Across the three-month summer period sales rose 2.4% year on year, again significantly above forecasts of a 1.9% rise.
Among the strongest performers were department stores, which recorded a sales rise of 1.8% month on month in August – a bounce back after a fall in July, which the ONS attributed to stock availability problems.
Non-store retailing, primarily online shopping, rose by 1.7% month on month, a major bounce back after sales fell 3.7% the previous month due to heavy promotional activity driving June sales.
Overall, non-store retailers enjoyed a strong summer with a 5.4% sales rise across the three-month period.
Retailers selling alcohol and beverages performed well across all three months to August 2026, the ONS reported, which they attributed to promotions, the hot weather and the men’s football World Cup.
after newsletter promotion
Fuel sales dropped again, down by 1.3% in August and 2.5% across the three-month period as motorists cut back on non-essential journeys after big increases in the price of petrol and diesel since the start of the Iran war in February.
UK petrol prices have hit the highest level in four years as the conflict in the Middle East intensifies.
On Thursday the Bank of England monetary policy committee voted to hold the base rate at 3.75%. However, it indicated that the latest rise in energy prices because of the conflict was likely to result in a rates increase to keep inflation in check. Inflation rose to 3.1% in August, from 2.9% in July.
“There are some challenging headwinds for consumers to navigate as we head into autumn,” said Andy Carlisle, the consumer goods and retail lead at Accenture.
“Higher energy bills, food, fuel and transport prices continue to weigh on purse strings. We’re beginning to see consumers preparing for these pressures, prioritising everyday needs while showing greater caution around discretionary and bigger-ticket purchases.”
summary: Retail sales in Great Britain unexpectedly rose by 0.5% in August, recovering from a 0.5% decline in July as summer heatwaves and online shopping boosted demand. This positive economic indicator comes ahead of the upcoming budget presented by chancellor John Healey. However, challenges remain as inflation rose to 3.1% in August and high fuel and energy prices continue to weigh on consumers.
key_points: Retail sales volumes grew 0.5% month on month in August, beating analyst forecasts of a 0.2% fall.
Summer heatwaves, online shopping, and back-to-school demand helped drive sales, particularly in department stores and non-store retailing.
Fuel sales dropped 1.3% in August as motorists cut back due to surging petrol and diesel prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
Inflation increased to 3.1% in August, and the Bank of England indicated that rising energy prices could lead to higher interest rates.

title: Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman
author: AP; Reuters
content:
![Warren Buffet](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/2011101162254258734_20.jpeg?resize=570%2C380&quality=80)
Warren Buffett is stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway in the next step of the transition at the top of the $1 trillion conglomerate he led for more than six decades.
Buffett, 96, will become chairman emeritus and will take on his new role immediately, nine months after handing the CEO reins to longtime lieutenant Greg Abel, the company said Friday.
