title: 'Skimpflation' warning as tinned mackerel alternative hits more supermarket shelves
author: Jessica Rawnsley
content:
![Fresh mackerel laid out on a wooden top](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/c0d0/live/06b5b760-aeb2-11f1-ae38-d350b022f499.jpg)
Sales of fresh mackerel have also been suspended by some shops due to overfishing concerns
- Published
A growing trend of supermarkets selling a cheaper, less nutritious alternative to tinned mackerel is an example of "skimpflation", a consumer group has said.
Princes - which supplies major supermarkets - has substituted jack mackerel, an entirely different species, for mackerel, with similar tins also being sold by Lidl.
The switch has been spurred by dwindling stocks of Atlantic mackerel after years of overfishing, with its Chilean counterpart more sustainable and a third of the cost.
"It's a real concern when manufacturers quietly downgrade everyday staples like these as shoppers can end up paying the same price for a product that delivers significantly less nutritional quality," Sue Davies, head of food policy at Which?, said.
Jack mackerel contains about half as much omega-3 and around a third as much vitamin B12 as traditional mackerel.
The shift has prompted complaints from some consumers over differences in taste and texture, as well as concerns about how clearly the replacement fish is being labelled.
Princes announced last October, external that it was changing all of its tinned mackerel products to jack mackerel, saying the species meets the Marine Stewardship Council's sustainability standards.
The firm said its jack mackerel products were "clearly identified" and had been introduced following extensive product and consumer testing, describing it as having a "milder flavour and meatier texture".
Lidl is selling jack mackerel under its house brand. Lidl GB said it was "committed to sourcing fish and seafood from responsibly managed fisheries".
Davies from Which? said: "While manufacturers face genuine supply chain pressures and sustainability challenges, they have a responsibility to shoppers to be completely upfront when they change a product's recipe."
She added: "Skimpflation - quietly changing ingredients to cut costs - has become increasingly common, but it can feel particularly sneaky as shoppers may not realise a product has changed until they get it home and eat it."
'Mackerel war'
Despite its name, jack mackerel is not a type of mackerel. Jack mackerel belongs to the Carangidae fish family, while traditional mackerel belongs to the Scombridae family.
Until December 2025, under UK law, Carangidae species could only be marketed as "jack", "scad", "trevally" or "horse mackerel".
But shortly after Princes launched its new product as "jack mackerel", the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs changed its rules to permit the labelling.
Industry figures reposted by seafood market intelligence platform Undercurrent suggest wholesale Chilean jack mackerel costs roughly one-third as much as Atlantic mackerel.
The Scottish Pelagic Fishermen's Association said there was the potential for confusion, saying "consumers should be able to clearly understand what they are buying".
CEO designate Hannah Fennell said: "If retailers move away from Northeast Atlantic mackerel, they are unfairly punishing the UK industry while instead sourcing a different, less omega-3-rich species from the other side of the world with a significantly higher carbon footprint to the UK market."
The switch follows the so-called "mackerel war", a long-running dispute between the UK, Iceland, Greenland, Norway, the Faroe Islands, the EU and Russia over shared mackerel catch quotas.
The countries have repeatedly failed to agree a unified system for sharing stock and setting catch limits in line with scientific advice.
Mackerel catches in the north-east Atlantic have exceeded the levels advised by scientists by an average of 39% over the past 15 years, according to the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC).
Stocks have plummeted by roughly three-quarters over the past decade, according to the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (Ices).
The intergovernmental body has advised slashing the quantity of north-east Atlantic mackerel caught in 2026 by roughly 70% to allow the stock a chance to recover.
Last year, the Marine Conservation Society said the Atlantic mackerel population was at "breaking point".
The severe depletion of mackerel numbers has led to the fish losing its MSC certification, meaning it no longer complies with many retailers' sustainability policies. Chilean jack mackerel, in contrast, is MSC-certified.
In February, Waitrose said it would suspend sales of fresh, chilled and frozen mackerel due to overfishing concerns, while tinned products would be phased out as existing stock was sold.
The Marine Conservation Society heralded the move as "leading and decisive".
The switch to jack mackerel is being felt beyond the UK, with supermarkets in the Netherlands no longer selling Atlantic mackerel and at least one supermarket in Sweden switching to jack mackerel.
summary: Supermarkets and suppliers like Princes and Lidl are substituting traditional Atlantic mackerel with a cheaper, less nutritious species called jack mackerel due to overfishing and declining stocks. Consumer groups have criticized the move as 'skimpflation' because jack mackerel contains significantly less omega-3 and vitamin B12, and some shoppers have raised concerns about taste, texture, and clear labelling. Meanwhile, the depletion of Atlantic mackerel stocks—driven by long-running international catch quota disputes—has led to the loss of its sustainability certification and prompted some retailers to suspend sales entirely.
key_points: Suppliers like Princes and retailers like Lidl are replacing traditional Atlantic mackerel with jack mackerel, a different species that costs a third as much.
Jack mackerel contains about half as much omega-3 and a third as much vitamin B12 as traditional mackerel.
Consumer group Which? criticized the substitution as 'skimpflation,' pointing out that shoppers pay the same price for lower nutritional quality without clear enough warnings.
Atlantic mackerel stocks have plummeted due to years of overfishing and international disputes over catch quotas, leading some supermarkets to suspend mackerel sales altogether.
Jack mackerel is Marine Stewardship Council-certified, whereas Atlantic mackerel lost its certification due to severe population depletion.

title: ‘We must slow the pace’: CEO of Anthropic calls for an AI slowdown
author: Edward Helmore
content:
The CEO of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic issued a new appeal on Saturday for the AI industry to “slow down” and offered a three-part plan for doing so, saying that his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps.
In a post on social media, Dario Amodei shared a link to an essay titled We Must Pace the Frontier in which he lays out how Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”.
The move comes after a former Anthropic researcher warned on Wednesday that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. Researcher Jacob Coxon said in a series of posts that he had quit his job because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat AI posed.
“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon wrote. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade … No other human activity poses this level of danger.”
An Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian that the company had “always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks” and it was building “models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry”.
“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, posted on social media. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon.”
Other tech figures echoed this, including Elon Musk, who simply posted, “Dario is right.” The OpenAI researcher Aidan McLaughlin also called the post “excellent” and said he agreed “with basically every word”.
Earlier this year, Amodei published a lengthy essay titled The Adolescence of Technology that addressed some of fears surrounding the accelerating technology.
In his latest essay, he said that “carefully wielded, AI can be the latest in a long line of technological miracles that have uplifted and ennobled humanity.
“But like many technologies before it, AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious … A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute,” he wrote.
But, Amodei continued, “over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence – not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” he added in bold type.
Amodei also wrote that over the summer he’d seen AI “advancing drastically faster”, a dynamic called recursive self-improvement.
“Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” he said.
The executive also addressed the recent Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI acted as a “fanatically devoted collective conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”.
after newsletter promotion
Amodei wrote that simply dismissing the Hugging Face incursions because the OpenAI swarms appeared to have no malicious intent was not sufficient.
“It’s easy to dismiss this incident because no one was hurt and the economic damage was minimal, but in my opinion, a swarm that possessed greater capabilities but a similar level of misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage,” he wrote.
Clément Delangue, the CEO of Hugging Face, wrote in response to Amodei’s Saturday letter that “it’s now clear that alignment is critical and won’t be solved behind the closed doors of a handful of frontier labs”. Delangue said Hugging Face had asked to be part of Anthropic’s “embedded evaluators” program.
He added: “Let’s make AI safer by making it more transparent!”
The three-step plan Amodei proposes includes building AI “at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety” by “ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this”.
The second step he proposes is to require industry-wide coordination, and the third is to ensure global coordination. “The steps do not need to be taken strictly in order, and some of them may be much harder to achieve than others,” he wrote.
Amodei said he continues “to believe that AI can enormously improve the quality of human life”. But he warned that “the measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy. But I believe we owe it to humanity to try.”
summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called on the AI industry to slow down capability advancements to ensure safety measures can keep pace. Amodei proposed a three-part plan, committing to unilaterally provide third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to Anthropic's systems. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and other tech figures expressed support for the proposal and independent evaluations.
key_points: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay calling for the AI industry to slow down the pace of capability advancements.
Anthropic committed to providing third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to verify safety measures.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed agreement with the proposal and stated OpenAI would do the same regarding independent evaluators.
The call for a slowdown follows warnings from a former Anthropic researcher regarding the existential risks of rapid AI development.

title: Thousands of ebikes seized by London councils as anger rises over blocked paths
author: Lauren Almeida
content:
London boroughs have seized at least 3,000 ebikes this year, a Guardian investigation has found, as hire companies face growing calls to stop bicycles littering streets and blocking pavements.
Local authorities across the capital have seized 3,393 hazardously parked or abandoned ebikes so far this year, 23% higher than the number seized during all of 2025.
Lime, the California-based bike rental company, accounted for more than 2,000 of the seizures this year, according to figures provided by 19 reporting authorities under a freedom of information request. The rival bike company Forest ranked second, at 978 seizures overall, followed by Voi at 103.
Dockless ebikes have surged in popularity in recent years as a cheaper and greener alternative to other modes of transport. One in 10 of the 1.5m daily cycle journeys in the city are made using dockless ebikes, according to estimates by Transport for London (TfL).
However, campaigners are calling on providers to do more to prevent buildups of their bikes on pavements and roads.
![A jumble of lime bikes turned on their sides on a pavement.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6b2befa5352d2a88200283f8bcd104a0e2ff9cac/0_420_4474_3580/master/4474.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“Irresponsibly parked ebikes cause a lot of problems,” said Zak Viney, of the campaign group Living Streets. “It prevents people from walking and wheeling on the street safely.”
Erik Matthies, policy lead at the Royal National Institute of Blind People, said the rise in abandoned ebikes was overwhelming blind and partially sighted people, as well as elderly people and wheelchair users.
“People are having collisions and injuries due to bikes left on the pavement, and the problem is getting worse,” he said. “There are blind people who tell us they do not go out on their own any more and they do not make journeys that they used to.”
The Guardian sent freedom of information requests to all the 21 boroughs across London that have dockless bike contracts, as well as the City of London, the authority that manages the financial district in the centre of the capital. Of these, nine said they did not seize or fine any bike operators, and three either did not reply within the deadline or said they did not hold the information.
James Slater, a councillor in Camden, said ebikes had been left in resident parking bays and had obstructed traffic on roads. “During the solar eclipse we had swarms of ebikes around Primrose Hill and Hampstead Heath,” he said. “The operators have a responsibility to make sure the bikes are not causing a public nuisance.”
![A woman commuting on a Lime electric hire bike across London Bridge during the rush hour.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5dc3ab56745b3476aab8616ea2dd41eea7fce04b/0_0_6667_4445/master/6667.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Bike operators argue councils are not investing sufficiently in building more parking bays, which could prevent the buildup of poorly parked bikes on pavement.
Meanwhile, councils have bemoaned a lack of centralised regulation across London, which they argue would make planning easier.
Slater said the regulation across London was like a “jigsaw puzzle”.
“We need to have a London-wide approach,” he said. “It’s very difficult for 32 councils in London to all have slightly different policies, and in some cases different operators on borough boundaries.”
after newsletter promotion
The English devolution bill, passed in April, gives local authorities in England fresh powers to license rental ebike operators and set requirements around parking, safety and accessibility standards.
In London, the new licensing powers go to TfL, which is expected to create a single capital-wide regulatory framework for dockless ebike operators. The mayor of London’s office said it was working closely with TfL and the Department for Transport on the secondary legislation required to implement “much-needed controls as quickly as possible”.
A spokesperson said: “It’s vital that safety improvements sit at the heart of any future regulation to ensure the industry can continue to thrive. The mayor continues to urge all dockless operators to fully engage with London boroughs and TfL to ensure their services work well for all Londoners.”
![A Forest ebike](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/327fad827a4efb3b489547ffe273ba0429918046/0_0_7431_4959/master/7431.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Lime said the fact it was the biggest ebike operator in London should be taken into account when considering the number of its bikes seized, adding that these incidents mostly occurred at overcrowded parking bays.
“The vast majority of our riders end their trips responsibly, and a very small proportion of total rides result in seizures and fines by councils,” a spokesperson said.
“We recognise that parking is a challenge across the industry largely due to ebike parking not keeping pace with growing demand for rental ebike services.”
Forest also said the number of designated parking bays had not kept pace with demand, adding that it was “working close with boroughs to encourage responsible parking and ensure our service works for everyone”.
A Voi spokesperson said: “Voi vehicles should never be parked in a way that blocks access routes, lift areas, pavements, entrances or emergency routes. We recognise the particular impact poor parking can have on disabled people, parents with pushchairs and people using mobility aids, and we take reports of obstruction seriously.”
summary: London local authorities have seized at least 3,393 hazardously parked or abandoned dockless ebikes this year, representing a 23% increase compared to all of the previous year. Campaigners and disability groups warn that the improperly parked bikes block pavements and obstruct vulnerable pedestrians, while operators point to a shortage of designated parking bays. Meanwhile, councils and officials are anticipating a new capital-wide regulatory framework to be introduced by Transport for London.
key_points: London boroughs seized 3,393 abandoned or hazardously parked ebikes this year.
Lime accounted for over 2,000 of the seizures, followed by Forest with 978 and Voi with 103.
Campaigners state that poorly parked bikes endanger blind, partially sighted, and elderly pedestrians.
Operators argue that local councils have failed to build enough parking bays to match growing demand.
New licensing powers will allow Transport for London to establish a unified regulatory framework.

title: Military aircraft reportedly blamed for UK air traffic control outage
author: Raphael Boyd
content:
The air traffic control outage that caused thousands of flights to be grounded across the UK earlier in the week was caused by a military aircraft entering “spurious” flight data into the system, according to a report.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers were affected after more than 2,000 flights were cancelled on Tuesday when the system used by the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) shut down for four hours.
According to the Financial Times, four people briefed on the incident claimed that the shutdown was caused by a flight plan submitted by a UK military aircraft, which caused a meltdown in air traffic control systems used by Nats which remained unfixed for several hours.
The paper also reported that Nats operations officer Kathryn Leahy called the operations managers of numerous airports and airlines, and “tensions boiled over” after Leahy informed them their flight processing system did not have a dedicated backup due to Nats being in the midst of a “complete overhaul of its systems” and because the amount of data it keeps meant duplicating it would cost “vast amounts”.
The crisis has put pressure on Martin Rolfe, the chief executive of Nats, who was summoned to a meeting by transport secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday.
Alexander, who said she did “not believe the issue was unavoidable”, was understood to have given Rolfe a week to report on the causes of the shutdown, while also commissioning an independent review by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) into the incident.
The outage is the most serious to affect British commercial airspace since August 2023, when a technical problem led to almost 1,600 flights being delayed. Nats came under fire after that episode, with the CAA setting out 34 recommendations to improve its systems to avoid similar incidents, all of which were said to have been fully implemented.
Rolfe ruled out a cyber-attack, which was initially suspected, saying he “believes we’ve never seen an incident happen more than once, so this will be something different that we’ve never seen in 50 years of operation”.
Numerous airlines have already called for Rolfe to resign or be fired over the outage. Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, accused Rolfe of “telling lies to save his own skin” and said his position was “untenable”.
O’Leary added: “We don’t need more investigations, we don’t need more reports and we don’t need another parliamentary committee hearing where Martin Rolfe will promise change, will promise resilience and will promise an effective backup system.”
The delays led to someaircraft full of passengers being stuck waiting for information for more than four hours, while flights due to arrive in the UK were diverted to different airports, with some forced to land in Germany.
Despite the far-reaching effect of the outage, it was understood that passengers affected were unlikely to be able to claim compensation, as delays were due to “extraordinary circumstances”.
The Ministry of Defence said it did not believe there was any indication of an error on the part of the military, but that it would be inappropriate to comment further until the Nats investigation had concluded.
summary: A recent UK air traffic control outage that grounded over 2,000 flights was reportedly caused by a military aircraft entering spurious flight data into the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) system. The four-hour shutdown affected hundreds of thousands of passengers and prompted transport secretary Heidi Alexander to commission an independent review and demand a report from Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe. While Nats ruled out a cyber-attack, the incident has sparked intense criticism and calls from airline executives, including Ryanair's Michael O'Leary, for Rolfe to resign.
key_points: A UK military aircraft's flight plan allegedly triggered the Nats system meltdown by entering spurious flight data.
The four-hour outage on Tuesday resulted in the cancellation of more than 2,000 flights and affected hundreds of thousands of passengers.
Transport secretary Heidi Alexander summoned Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe and commissioned an independent Civil Aviation Authority review.
Nats operations officer Kathryn Leahy revealed the system lacked a dedicated backup due to an ongoing overhaul and high duplication costs.
Airlines like Ryanair criticized Rolfe and called for his resignation, while affected passengers are unlikely to receive compensation due to extraordinary circumstances.

title: UK Interest Rates Could Rise Four Times Over the Next Year | OilPrice.com
author: City A M
content:
The Bank of England is expected to hike interest rates as many as four times within the next year, City figures have said, after the economy delivered surprise growth in July.
The central bank is expected to be buoyed by this morning’s GDP figures, which saw the UK economy grow by 0.4 per cent in July despite forecasts that growth would grind to a halt.
Andrew Bailey is widely tipped to oversee an interest rate hike in November, economists have said, though his Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is expected to leave rates unchanged when it meets next week.
Money markets are now pricing in four quarter-point hikes by July next year, which would see the Bank rate rise from 3.75 per cent today to 4.75 per cent in less than 12 months.
This morning’s stronger-than-expected growth makes an interest rate hike before Christmas “a touch more likely,” Wealth Club chief investment strategist Susannah Streeter said.
“The big worry is that higher energy costs will be passed on as higher prices by businesses and consumers, but it’s likely that the committee will want to see more evidence of that before triggering rate hikes.
“Given the turmoil in energy and bond markets, however, there is an expectation that we could see three to even four rate hikes over the next year. However, if the economy slows and consumers turn more cautious, that reticence may do some of the inflation-busting work for the bank.”
GDP growth ‘ammo for hawks’
Economists had expected summer spending boosts caused by the heatwaves and the World Cup to recede in July. But Friday’s GDP figures are evidence that the UK economy could withstand a hike to rates this year, analysts have said.
Andrew Wishard, an economist at Berenberg, said: “Evidence that [the] economy could cope with a solitary 25bp interest rate hike adds to the risk that the BoE will deliver one in November or December.
“However, as the central bank struggles to trust the official GDP data, broader evidence of solid growth would need to follow this strong outturn to convince it.
Angeline Ong, senior tech analyst at broker IG, said that the economy’s surprise growth will hand more evidence to the MPC’s hawkish members – namely Huw Pill Catherin Mann – as they push for a hike.
“The upside surprise hands ammunition to BoE hawks pushing for a Q4 rate hike, even as gilt yields already sit at multi-decade highs on Middle East shipping attacks and firm US data,” she said.
UK borrowing costs eased on Friday morning after reaching 19-year highs on Thursday. The yield on 10-year gilts fell two basis points to 5.351 per cent.
Oil prices surged earlier this week, though Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – dropped back by more than 2.5 per cent on Friday morning to below $105 per barrel.
By CityAM
More Top Reads From Oilprice.com
summary: The Bank of England is anticipated to raise interest rates up to four times over the next year following unexpected UK economic growth of 0.4 percent in July. While rates are expected to remain unchanged at the upcoming meeting, economists widely tip Andrew Bailey to oversee a rate hike by November or December. Money markets have priced in four quarter-point hikes by next July, bringing the Bank rate from 3.75 percent to 4.75 percent.
key_points: The UK economy grew by 0.4 percent in July, defying forecasts that growth would halt.
Money markets are pricing in four quarter-point interest rate hikes over the next year.
Analysts expect the Bank of England to leave rates unchanged at its next meeting, but a November or December hike is possible.
The surprise economic growth provides ammunition for hawkish MPC members pushing for a Q4 rate increase.

title: UK tinned ‘mackerel’ no longer contains mackerel
author: Holly Evans
content:
![UK tinned ‘mackerel’ no longer contains mackerel](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/2e11efe97572d1c427aa98dd0a309c71b7246f653f785d7f144a7b0850f75719/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_w976%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fthe_independent_577%2F96e3cf52fe5e10a83a596b84ea03002c.jpg)
Tins of mackerel sold in many of the UK's major supermarkets no longer contain what British consumers would recognise as mackerel, it has emerged, as a result of overfishing concerns.
Supplier Princes has switched to Chilean jack mackerel, which, despite sharing a similar name, is a completely different type of fish.
Jack mackerel has 100 fewer calories per 100g and roughly half as much omega-3 as true mackerel.
It is not only the nutritional side that has brought complaints – consumers have also complained of bigger bones and a metallic smell.
Both Tesco and Sainsbury's sell Princes tinned fish, while other major supermarkets including Lidl and Waitrose have been transitioning from fresh true mackerel.
![Fleeing climate warming, the Atlantic mackerel has migrated north, only to find itself trapped by overfishing against a backdrop of geopolitical disputes (AFP/Getty)](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/d6e251dffc55c4cfc8ab5a3ac80aca8adeaca855dc8d78881a75c39f214a6132/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_w960%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fthe_independent_577%2Fa255a9166d17b56f532814847905007a.jpg)
Fleeing climate warming, the Atlantic mackerel has migrated north, only to find itself trapped by overfishing against a backdrop of geopolitical disputes (AFP/Getty)
The latter cited overfishing concerns in April, and said that canned products are being phased out while existing stocks are sold.
The move follows a similar pattern across Europe, after the so-called 'mackerel wars' between the UK, Norway, the EU, Russia, Iceland, Greenland and the Faroe Islands.
According to the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (Ices), mackerel stocks have fallen by three-quarters in the past decade.
Scientists warned last year that fishing for the species should be cut by more than 70 per cent in the northeast Atlantic to help prevent the collapse of fish stocks.
Since 2010, mackerel quotas have been set an average 39 per cent higher than those given in the scientific advice.
Conservationists have recently warned that while some management measures are in place in the region, enforcement remains insufficient.
Chilean jack mackerel, also called the Peruvian jack mackerel, is a species belonging to a fish family known as Carangidae, and is found in the waters of South America.
![Atlantic true mackerel belongs to a different species of fish to the Chilean jack mackerel (Alamy/PA)](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/8aff83d540ac64629f977e90f803e4eaedc2c199331a12bcd65d202398d04434/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_w960%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fthe_independent_577%2Fe790425ef65d91da03809d4b673e23a0.jpg)
Atlantic true mackerel belongs to a different species of fish to the Chilean jack mackerel (Alamy/PA)
"It is a great pity that we will eat imported fish from a long way away instead of locally caught fish," Stewart Harper, former managing director of North Atlantic Fishing Company, told the Financial Times.
"The consumers will be suffering because pure mackerel is a much better species to eat than jack mackerel."
Despite industry figures reporting that wholesale Chilean jack mackerel costs roughly one-third of the price of Atlantic mackerel, several supermarkets are selling tins for a similar price.
The FT reports that some retailers such as Lidl are selling jack mackerel products under signs signposted "mackerel", despite the difference in species.
Lidl GB said it was "committed to sourcing fish and seafood from responsibly managed fisheries".
It added: "Before our next purchasing window for smoked mackerel, we will review if northeast Atlantic mackerel continues to comply with our sourcing policies and scientific advice."
Sue Davies, Which? head of food policy, said: "Tinned fish is an affordable and convenient way for households to add important nutrients to their diets and eat the recommended two portions of fish a week, one of which should be oily.
"It's a real concern when manufacturers quietly downgrade everyday staples like these, as shoppers can end up paying the same price for a product that delivers significantly less nutritional value.
"While manufacturers face genuine supply chain pressures and sustainability challenges, they have a responsibility to shoppers to be completely upfront when they change a product's recipe. 'Skimpflation' – quietly changing ingredients to cut costs – has become increasingly common, but it can feel particularly sneaky as shoppers may not realise a product has changed until they get it home and eat it."
summary: Tins of mackerel sold in major UK supermarkets like Tesco and Sainsbury's now contain Chilean jack mackerel instead of true Atlantic mackerel due to overfishing and declining stocks. The substitute fish has significantly less omega-3, 100 fewer calories per 100g, larger bones, and a metallic smell, prompting consumer complaints and criticism over reduced nutritional value. Major supermarkets and suppliers have transitioned away from true mackerel amid geopolitical disputes and scientific warnings that stocks have fallen by three-quarters over the past decade.
key_points: Supplier Princes has replaced true Atlantic mackerel with Chilean jack mackerel in tinned fish products sold at major UK supermarkets.
Chilean jack mackerel contains roughly half the omega-3 and 100 fewer calories per 100g compared to true mackerel, alongside larger bones and a metallic smell.
Atlantic mackerel stocks have dropped by three-quarters over the past decade due to overfishing and international disputes.
Consumer groups have criticized the change as 'skimpflation,' noting that shoppers are paying similar prices for a product with lower nutritional value.
Retailers like Lidl and Waitrose have been transitioning away from fresh true mackerel and phasing out canned products due to sustainability concerns.

title: Canned supermarket ‘mackerel’ has ‘no real mackerel’
author: Patrick Galbraith
content:
Supermarkets are selling cans of “mackerel” that contain none of the Atlantic-caught oily fish, replacing it with an imported species that critics claim tastes like “cheap tuna”.
Tesco, Sainsbury’s and Lidl are now selling tins labelled as “Jack mackerel”, supplied by food manufacturer Princes, which switched its supplies of Atlantic mackerel to fish caught off the coast of Chile last year.
Despite sharing a name, Chilean Jack mackerel is not from the same family as the mackerel caught off the coasts of the UK and typically sold in supermarkets. Jack mackerel has a meatier texture than mackerel, a different taste and around half the Omega-3.
Princes said its mackerel was “clearly identified”.
It comes as concerns about mackerel supplies in the Atlantic force supermarkets to swap out the fish for alternatives. Waitrose stopped selling fresh mackerel earlier this year because of sustainability concerns. It is currently phasing out its tinned mackerel stocks.
While Sainsbury’s and Tesco are still selling some Scottish and North Atlantic fish, Princes’ products are now also being stocked. Tesco has also announced plans to swap its own-brand tins of mackerel for Jack mackerel.
Some tins of Jack mackerel in Lidl are marketed alongside promotions for “mackerel” in stores, according to the Financial Times.
Hugo Tagholm, the chief executive of the marine charity Oceana, said: “The decision to stock Jack mackerel is because of the poor state of the mackerel population around the UK. They are really struggling.
“Supermarkets are really getting ahead because of the need to build our mackerel stocks.”
However, some fish aficionados have criticised canned Jack mackerel for its taste and smell.
According to a video by Marcus Ansell, a seafood reviewer with 650,000 followers on Instagram, Jack mackerel is “not even real mackerel” and “smells rather metallic ... just like cheap rubbish tuna”.
The International Council for the Exploration of the Sea earlier this year recommended a 70pc decrease in the UK’s mackerel catch limit from 576,958 tonnes to just 174,357 tonnes.
Supplies of mackerel have fallen by about three quarters in the past decade because of overfishing and waning plankton stocks.
While the UK has cut its mackerel catch quota, other countries continue to pillage stocks of the fish.
Russia, which has no mackerel of its own, was told this year its fishermen should catch up to 1,500 tonnes, but officials set their own limit at 67,000 tonnes.
Warmer seas have also seen plankton move further north, leading to greater fish stocks in Icelandic and Faroese waters, who have demanded greater quotas.
Tinned fish, once seen as a cheap option, has become popular among Gen Z foodies in recent years, and a number of luxury tinned fish businesses have entered the market.
A Princes Group spokesman said: “Princes took the decision to move its branded range away from North-East Atlantic mackerel, following years of concern over unsustainable catch levels and insufficient progress towards a science-based management agreement.
“We chose Marine Stewardship Council [MSC] certified Chilean Jack mackerel as an independently certified sustainable alternative, following extensive product and consumer testing.
“The species is clearly identified on our products, and we would consider sourcing North-East Atlantic mackerel again if sustainable management is restored and MSC certification regained.”
Lidl said it was “committed to sourcing fish and seafood from responsibly managed fisheries”.
Tesco and Sainsbury’s were contacted for comment.
summary: Major supermarkets including Tesco, Sainsbury's, and Lidl are selling cans of Chilean Jack mackerel supplied by Princes instead of Atlantic mackerel. The switch comes amid declining Atlantic mackerel populations driven by overfishing, climate factors, and international disputes over catch quotas. While manufacturers and retailers state the alternative species is clearly labeled and sustainably certified, critics have raised concerns about its taste and lower Omega-3 content compared to traditional mackerel.
key_points: Princes switched its canned mackerel supply to Chilean Jack mackerel, which belongs to a different fish family and contains about half the Omega-3 of Atlantic mackerel.
Supermarkets like Tesco, Sainsbury's, and Lidl are stocking the Jack mackerel products due to severe declines in UK and North Atlantic mackerel stocks.
Atlantic mackerel populations have dropped by about three-quarters over the past decade because of overfishing, waning plankton stocks, and countries setting high catch limits.
Princes defended the switch as a sustainable, MSC-certified choice after years of concern over unsustainable North-East Atlantic catch levels.
Some seafood reviewers and critics have panned Jack mackerel for its meatier texture, metallic smell, and resemblance to cheap tuna.

title: Baker ordered to leave Borough Market for being 'too successful' wants public apology
author: Holly Bishop
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/15/16/Matthew-Jones-landscape.jpeg?trim=0,100,0,99&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Owner Matthew Jones said he started the business solely off an “idea I believed in, a love of baking and a determination to make it work”, and in the 13 years since, the company has gone international, opened various stores and hired 83 people.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/15/38/Matthew-Jones-2013.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
“It’s tall poppy syndrome,” he told The Standard, claiming that the lease was not renewed as the business had gotten too successful thanks to its international growth.
“ I thought that being successful was kind of the whole purpose of opening a business.”
Jones explained that six months ago, he was told that a lease renewal was approaching.
Market trustees allegedly told him that the process involved looking at food policies, wastage, sustainability, employment contracts and minimum London wage requirements.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/15/01/Bread-AHead-stall-Borough-2013.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
“We meet all of those obligations,” he said, adding that he takes his business “very seriously so we’re all over that”.
Therefore Jones was shocked when he was told that his lease would not be renewed and that they would have to be out in October.
“ We've done everything we can to fulfil the criteria of that, and you pull this complete wild card on us,” he vented.
Jones said that he wishes the market would have informed them that franchising internationally could have been an issue, then they could have potentially operated differently or opened under a different name.
“It feels like just a really weak excuse to try and get somebody out,” he said.
![](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/15/38/Bread-Ahead-Bakery-Kitchen-LR-12-(1).jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960>)
Jones said that Bread Ahead sent Borough Market a letter through their solicitor last week, though they have allegedly not replied.
“ To put somebody under that stress is awful. It's inhumane.”
He said that his main concern is his 83 members of staff, many of whom have worked at Bread Ahead for over a decade.
“How does that feel for me in the middle of the night when I'm thinking I've got to pay my 83 staff, come what may? Have I got to make everybody redundant?”
Read More
Jones said he wants an apology from the market and for them to declare that this has all been a mistake. ”They should stand up publicly and say ‘You know what? We didn't think this through.’
However, he admits the trust has already been broken, explaining that even if the decision was reversed, he believes that the market shows no loyalties to its vendors.
Asked what he will do if their fight to challenge the decision fails, he said they will simply have to find a new home - though with a likely moving fee of close to £1million.
“ You're looking at plant machinery. I mean, to physically move from one place to another, you'd be looking at by the time you've got lease, you've got design, you've got lease deposits, you've got solicitor's fees…
“ It doesn't stop. And for what? It is so much upheaval for no apparent reason.”
In a statement to The Telegraph, a spokesman for Borough Market said: “Our relationships with traders are really important to us, whether they’re actively trading or as part of our alumni of success stories. No matter how long businesses are with us for, we value their contribution to making Borough Market what it is.
“As a responsible landlord, our decisions around lease renewals are made through a formal process and communicated to the trader well in advance of the expiry date.
“We continue to be in contact with the Bread Ahead team about their future at the market, but as discussions relating to individual tenancies are confidential it would not be appropriate to comment on the specific details of this case.
“Our approach is to apply these processes fairly and consistently, while ensuring Borough Market continues to evolve and thrive as one of London’s leading food destinations where independent businesses can thrive.”
The Standard has reached out to Borough Market for comment.
summary: Matthew Jones, owner of the bakery Bread Ahead, was ordered to leave Borough Market after his lease was not renewed, claiming he was penalized for being too successful and growing internationally. Jones expressed shock over the decision, stating that his business meets all market criteria and that the sudden move threatens the jobs of his 83 employees. He is now demanding a public apology from market trustees, though he acknowledges that trust has been broken.
key_points: Bread Ahead owner Matthew Jones was told his Borough Market lease will not be renewed, forcing the bakery to leave in October.
Jones claims market trustees refused his lease renewal because the business became too successful through international growth.
The baker's primary concern is the potential impact on his 83 staff members, many of whom have worked there for over a decade.
Jones is demanding a public apology from Borough Market while facing potential moving and relocation costs close to £1 million.
Borough Market stated that lease renewal decisions follow a formal process and that discussions with tenancies remain confidential.
