title: North Sea gasfield decision likely delayed until after Holborn and St Pancras byelection
author: Rowena Mason; Kiran Stacey
content:
A decision on approving the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea is to be delayed until later this autumn, with the Greens accusing Labour of hiding their position before the crucial Holborn and St Pancras byelection.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation to approve the Jackdaw field off the coast of Aberdeen next week.
However, multiple Whitehall sources say the decision is not expected to be made in the remaining few days before the House of Commons goes into recess on Tuesday for party conference season.
The delay means the announcement is unlikely to come before Holborn and St Pancras constituents vote in a high-profile byelection on 8 October, in which the Green party leader Zack Polanski is the candidate vying against Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali in Keir Starmer’s former seat.
Polanski has criticised the government over signals that it will press ahead with Jackdaw despite the hottest ever summer caused by the climate crisis.
After his selection, Polanski said Labour has “started the campaign with an act of dishonesty and betrayal”.
“They are clearly going to allow new drilling in the North Sea but want to keep it under wraps during a byelection where they know the public want tougher action on climate, not backsliding.
“Labour talks about change, but this is change for the worse. We have a climate crisis but Labour is taking the side of fossil fuel corporations, and the voters have a clear choice in this byelection between action on climate change or shortsighted rowing backwards.”
The delay also means Andy Burnham could avoid controversy over Jackdaw at the Labour party conference in Liverpool at the end of the month.
Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said delays in approving Jackdaw would mean it takes longer to increase UK domestic production in the North Sea.
In a letter to the prime minister published on social media, Bowie asked Burnham to confirm “suggestions that you are about to delay the decision on the Jackdaw gasfield until after the conference recess and Holborn and St Pancras byelection”.
He added: “If this is the case, it would be nothing short of you placing the interests of the Labour party before the interests of Great Britain.”
A separate decision is also pending on the Rosebank oilfield project.
Environmental campaigners have called for both projects to be abandoned, while the US president, Donald Trump, has urged the prime minister to open them.
after newsletter promotion
Labour’s manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, but the companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank are seeking environmental approval for existing licences.
Last week, a spokesperson for the energy department said: “The North Sea remains a vital national asset, supporting jobs, growth and the UK’s energy security. We are clear that oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come, alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.”
The companies resubmitted their applications for environmental approval earlier this year. Granting those permits would not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment not to issue new oil or gas licences, but many of the party’s MPs are opposed to the projects entirely.
Under the process, the energy secretary gives her recommendation to the North Sea Transition Authority, which then later issues a formal approval.
Consultations on Jackdaw and Rosebank, which the industry says will provide 10% of the UK’s oil and gas output at their peak, closed last month, and Fahnbulleh has since been considering her response.
Campaigners say the fields would produce as much as £336bn worth of damage to the economy as a result of the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced.
Both fields have licences to operate, but environmental approval was rescinded after a judge ruled the companies running them – Shell and the Norwegian firm Equinor – needed to account for the carbon emissions that would be created by burning the oil and gas they produce.
summary: The decision on approving the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea has been delayed until later in the autumn, avoiding the upcoming Holborn and St Pancras byelection and the Labour party conference. The Greens accused Labour of hiding their position on the fossil fuel project to avoid political fallout, while the Conservatives argued the delay harms the UK's domestic energy production. Companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank are seeking environmental approval for existing licences following a court ruling requiring them to account for downstream carbon emissions.
key_points: A decision on the Jackdaw gasfield is delayed until later this autumn, pushing it past the Holborn and St Pancras byelection and party conference season.
Green party leader Zack Polanski accused Labour of dishonesty and hiding plans to allow new drilling during the byelection.
Shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie criticized the delay as placing Labour party interests ahead of Great Britain.
Environmental approval was previously rescinded because operators must account for carbon emissions from burning the produced oil and gas.
Granting the permits for existing licences would not violate Labour's manifesto commitment against issuing new drilling licences.

title: Speed up electricity grid upgrade or else face higher bills, warns UK watchdog
author: Alex Daniel
content:
Consumers will pay higher energy bills unless the UK government speeds up work on a vast programme of upgrades to the electricity grid to enable the switch to renewables, the public spending watchdog has warned.
The National Audit Office (NAO) said that without faster action the extra costs associated with managing the ageing power network, which are ultimately passed on to the public, could reach £7.8bn a year by 2030.
A £70bn programme is under way to modernise Great Britain’s network of pylons, overhead lines and substations so that more power can be carried from wind and solar farms and other clean energy sources to homes.
Labour has said its plan to decarbonise the grid by 2030 will keep consumer bills lower than they would otherwise be, but the NAO said that if the planned upgrades did not happen fast enough then bills could rise instead.
Of the 80 projects it said were needed to meet the target, just 16 are finished and most are in their early stages.
Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said the planned upgrades would “test systems not designed for activity at this pace or scale”.
He added “Value for money now depends on delivery. Failure to implement these necessary grid upgrades will hamper economic growth as well as increase consumer bills.”
When the grid cannot carry enough electricity from where it is generated to where it is needed, the system operator pays windfarms to switch off and gas plants to switch on elsewhere to meet the demand. These so-called constraint costs are added to bills, and reached £1.9bn in 2025-26. Without faster upgrades, the NAO said, they could climb as high as £7.8bn by 2030.
Meanwhile, the £70bn investment will require transmission owners – the private companies that build and manage the network – to more than quadruple their annual spending on upgrades, from £2.5bn in 2025-26 to more than £11bn by 2027-28.
Ofgem, the industry regulator, believes households would be about £30 a year better off if the upgrades happen at the required pace because of the reduced curtailment costs. But the NAO said meeting that schedule would be “very challenging”.
It said some of the projects were already forecast to run beyond 2030, meaning “some new generation” was likely to connect before necessary grid upgrades were completed.
“It is important to minimise this gap, as delays will increase project and constraint costs and postpone the benefit of achieving clean power,” the NAO said.
It added that neither Ofgem, the National Energy System Operator (Neso), which balances the grid, nor the government publishes enough data on the cost and progress of projects, and called for more transparency.
Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the chair of parliament’s spending watchdog, the public accounts committee, said: “Renewables now generate the majority of the UK’s electricity, but the grid has failed to keep pace and is in dire need of upgrading to support the transition to clean energy.
after newsletter promotion
“As one of our most important pieces of infrastructure, the grid must be capable of meeting rising demand whether that is from new homes or datacentres.
“[The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero], Ofgem and Neso must deliver critical projects on time and provide transparent reporting so parliament and the public can hold them to account.”
Ofgem welcomed the recommendations, adding that the planned upgrades would “reduce costly constraints on the system and help shield consumers from volatile international gas prices”.
“Protecting consumers and driving down costs remains our priority,” a spokesperson said. “Funding is released in stages, costs are rigorously scrutinised and companies face financial penalties if they fail to deliver.”
The energy minister Michael Shanks said: “This report is another stark reminder of the cost of years of historic underinvestment in the grid … Our once-in-a-generation reforms are finally building the infrastructure we need: reducing our dependence on the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price spikes and helping lower people’s bills for good.”
Neso also welcomed the NAO findings. A spokesperson said: “We are doing everything within our control to keep balancing costs down while maintaining security of supply and will continue working with government, Ofgem and network companies on the strategic planning needed to support delivery across the system.”
summary: The National Audit Office has warned that UK consumers face higher energy bills unless the government accelerates a £70bn programme to upgrade the electricity grid for renewable energy. Without faster modernization, costs associated with managing the ageing network could reach £7.8bn annually by 2030 due to constraints. Out of 80 required projects, only 16 are completed, and meeting the necessary delivery schedule remains a very challenging task.
key_points: Consumer energy bills could rise if grid upgrades do not keep pace with the transition to renewables.
Management costs for the ageing power network could reach £7.8bn a year by 2030 without faster modernization.
Only 16 out of the 80 necessary grid projects have been completed.
Private transmission companies must more than quadruple annual spending on upgrades to meet targets.
The NAO called for greater transparency and more data reporting on the cost and progress of projects.

title: Burnham delays crucial North Sea drilling decision
author: Jonathan Leake
content:
![Andy Burnham](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/11/TELEMMGLPICT000501825537_17891172403210_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq5yQLQqeH37t50SCyM4-zeGcv5yZLmao6LolmWYJrXns.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Andy Burnham](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/11/TELEMMGLPICT000501825537_17891172403210_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq5yQLQqeH37t50SCyM4-zeGcv5yZLmao6LolmWYJrXns.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Andy Burnham is set to delay approving plans for the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea until after a crucial by-election battle between Labour and the Green Party.
The major project had been expected to be approved as soon as Monday, but Whitehall sources said it had now been delayed until the late autumn.
It means the announcement is now expected after the Oct 8 contest to replace Sir Keir Starmer as the MP for Holborn and St Pancras. It is expected to be a two-horse race between Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, and Sagal Abdi-Wali, the Labour candidate.
The delay comes despite warnings of looming gas shortages facing Britain this winter. Jackdaw bosses have previously said the field could be needed to avert a “gas supply emergency”.
Pushing back the plans would allow Mr Burnham to avoid awkward confrontations at the looming Labour Party conference in Liverpool at the end of September.
Approval for Jackdaw and its sister project, the Rosebank oil field off Shetland, is bitterly opposed by a significant number of Left-wing Labour MPs.
However Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said delays in approving Jackdaw would push the offshore work needed to get gas flowing deeper into winter, when bad weather would increase the risks to offshore workers.
In a letter to Mr Burnham, seen by The Telegraph, Mr Bowie asked him to confirm “suggestions that you are about to delay the decision on the Jackdaw gas field until after the conference recess and Holborn and St Pancras by-election”.
He added: “If this is the case, it would be nothing short of you placing the interests of the Labour Party before the interests of Great Britain.”
Mr Bowie has also tabled a set of parliamentary questions designed to bring Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, or Michael Shanks, her junior energy minister, to the Commons before Parliament goes into recess next Tuesday.
The decisions on Jackdaw and Rosebank formally lie with Ms Fahnbulleh. A Department of Energy Security and Net Zero spokesman refuted suggestions of a delay, saying there was no agreed timing for a decision on Jackdaw.
Mr Polanski, speaking after he was confirmed as a by-election candidate on Friday, said: “Labour are running scared, and have started the campaign with an act of dishonesty and betrayal.
“They are clearly going to allow new drilling in the North Sea but want to keep it under wraps during a by-election where they know the public want tougher action on climate, not backsliding.”
The Jackdaw gas field is the UK’s largest untapped known gas reservoir, capable of boosting UK output by around 6pc.
Most of the preliminary works have been completed, meaning its gas could enter the UK grid within a couple of months of being approved.
This could support the UK during what is expected to be a winter dominated by surging prices and tight supplies, linked to the Strait of Hormuz crisis.
UK gas prices climbed to a four-year high on Thursday as oil jumped to almost $110 (£81).
However, completing the final works will still take some weeks, meaning any political hold-up in approval will push that work deeper into the winter bad weather.
A spokesman for Adura, the joint venture between Equinor and Shell, said: “Jackdaw and Rosebank represent a major opportunity for the UK Government. Together, they will contribute more than £28 billion to the economy and support over 3,500 jobs at peak construction.
“Following the closure of public consultation of Jackdaw and Rosebank last month, we now await a government decision on consent to allow the two projects to move forward to production.
“The Jackdaw platform is installed in the North Sea and, subject to receiving consent, could be supplying gas to British homes and businesses within weeks.”
summary: Andy Burnham is reportedly set to delay approving plans for the Jackdaw North Sea gas field until after the October 8 by-election in Holborn and St Pancras and the upcoming Labour Party conference. The postponement aims to avoid political confrontations with Left-wing Labour MPs and Green Party opponents. Critics, including shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie, warn that the delay prioritizes party interests over national energy security and pushes crucial offshore work into hazardous winter weather.
key_points: The decision on the Jackdaw gas field has reportedly been delayed until late autumn, following a by-election and the Labour Party conference.
The delay aims to avoid political conflict over fossil fuel drilling and opposition from Left-wing Labour MPs and the Green Party.
Critics argue that delaying the approval risks pushing offshore work into winter weather and places party interests ahead of national energy security.
Jackdaw is the UK's largest untapped known gas reservoir and could supply gas to the UK grid within weeks of approval to help offset expected winter shortages.

title: UK economy defies forecasts with surprise 0.4% growth in July
author: Heather Stewart
content:
The UK economy grew in July despite the fallout from the Iran war, in welcome news for John Healey ahead of next month’s budget.
Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed a 0.4% increase in gross domestic product (GDP), compared with 0.3% growth in June.
City economists had forecast zero growth.
With conflict in the Middle East continuing to rattle the global economy, the news comes as the UK government’s borrowing costs have surged to the highest level in almost two decades.
Economists warn the rise in the global oil price- to well above $100 a barrel – is likely to stoke higher inflation worldwide.
Britain recorded the strongest growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026 despite the onset of the conflict.
Economists have warned the chancellor could be forced to increase taxes or cut spending at his first budget on 28 October in response to rising interest rates after the war in Iran triggered turmoil in global bond markets.
More details to follow …
summary: The UK economy grew by a better-than-expected 0.4% in July, outperforming economists' forecasts of zero growth. This positive news comes despite ongoing global economic fallout from the conflict in the Iran war and rising government borrowing costs. However, economists warn that soaring global oil prices and interest rates could force the chancellor to raise taxes or cut spending in the upcoming October budget.
key_points: UK gross domestic product increased by 0.4% in July, following 0.3% growth in June.
City economists had forecast zero growth for July.
Britain recorded the strongest growth in the G7 during the first half of 2026.
Rising global oil prices above $100 a barrel threaten to increase worldwide inflation.
The chancellor may face pressure to increase taxes or cut spending in the 28 October budget.

title: More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils as Musk terms fears a ‘psyop’
author: Johana Bhuiyan
content:
A day after a former researcher at Anthropic made an apocalyptic declaration about artificial intelligence, more researchers and staff members at the AI startup publicly agreed with him and posted their own dire warnings.
In response, Elon Musk and other conservative figures on X, formerly Twitter, called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”.
The Anthropic insiders fear the technology they are building could become so advanced and dangerous as to cause human extinction within the decade, and they assert many of their colleagues feel the same but haven’t said so publicly.
These researchers and staff are posting in response to a now-viral thread from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who said on Wednesday he was resigning from the company because neither Anthropic nor its competitor OpenAI, also his former employer, were building AI models responsibly and are “gambling with our lives”.
Anna Wang, who works on Artificial General Intelligence Safety at Anthropic and previously worked at Google’s DeepMind, said Thursday that many people at Anthropic want to slow down development to come up with a plan to mitigate the risks that could come with these AI models.
“There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI,” Wang wrote on X.
Drake Thomas, another Anthropic employee, said that he respected Coxon’s choice to abstain from building these models if he worries they could pose planet-scale risks.
“Things are moving way too fast, we don’t have anywhere near the degree of assurance we’ll want for ASI [artificial superintelligence],” Thomas said.
Musk took a more adversarial stance. “Seems like a setup,” he wrote.
Coxon replied to the world’s richest man with a selfie, writing, “I’m real and these are my real beliefs. You could ask your xAI researchers about me if you hadn’t fired them.”
In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said.
Musk and others with a more positive view of AI have started to spread theories that Coxon’s post and the resulting fallout are part of a “psyop” to negatively influence the public’s feelings about AI.
“I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time,” Musk posted on X. “This was just the match that lit the fire.”
Musk was responding to a post by Parker Thayer, a researcher at conservativethinktank Capital Research, in which he floated a theory with little evidence that Coxon’s post was the start of a “VERY sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion”. Other notable figures took notice.
after newsletter promotion
Bill Ackman, the billionaire CEO of the hedge fund Pershing Square, also quoted Thayer’s post, simply saying “Interesting.”
Other Anthropic employees had posted their agreement with Coxon shortly after he declared his resignation on Wednesday.
“AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Samuel Marks, who works on safety research at Anthropic. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.”
Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said Coxon was “correct” and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential.
“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.
It’s not exactly clear how Coxon and others expect AI models to usher in the demise of humanity. Some experts doubt that the technology will become so intelligent as to cause the apocalypse. Gary Marcus, a scientist and leading voice in AI, said that it’s time to boycott AI, but because it’s already causing harm.
More than extinction, Marcus said he worried about the “risk of catastrophe” from “from AI-generated pathogens, from wars started or escalated by AI-generated disinformation, from hacks that destroy critical infrastructure, and so on. Nothing I have seen gives any indication that any of that is under control”.
The same day, Anthropic released a report documenting how the company dismantled an operation attempting to build a biological weapon using its AI models.
summary: Following a former researcher's resignation over irresponsible AI development, several current Anthropic employees have publicly warned that advanced artificial intelligence could pose extinction-level risks to humanity within the decade. While these insiders argue that development is moving too fast without adequate scientific safety plans, figures like Elon Musk and other conservative commentators have dismissed the warnings as a "psyop" or setup. Meanwhile, Anthropic defended its strategy, stating it builds models with industry-strong safeguards, and scientists like Gary Marcus highlighted near-term risks such as AI-generated pathogens and disinformation.
key_points: Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, warning that companies like Anthropic and OpenAI are gambling with human lives by not building AI responsibly.
Multiple Anthropic employees publicly agreed with Coxon, expressing fears that artificial superintelligence could cause human extinction within the next decade.
Elon Musk and other conservative figures dismissed the researchers' warnings as a "psyop" and a coordinated PR operation to promote AI regulation.
An Anthropic spokesperson defended the company's approach, highlighting its commitment to transparency and strong industry safeguards.
Scientist Gary Marcus raised concerns about more immediate catastrophic risks, including AI-generated pathogens, disinformation wars, and infrastructure hacks.

title: Borrowing costs surge to 1998 levels on fresh bonds sell-off
author: Tim Wallace
content:
![Bank of England](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000359970369_17890574959510_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Bank of England](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000359970369_17890574959510_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Government borrowing costs have surged to levels not seen in decades after a jump in the price of oil reignited a bond market sell-off.
The Treasury’s 10-year interest rate rose above 5.3pc on Thursday, a level not seen since 2007. Its 20-year borrowing costs rose above 5.8pc, the most expensive since 1998.
The rise in borrowing costs threatens to wipe around £10bn from John Healey’s fiscal headroom before his first Budget next month, according to economists at the Item Club.
The jump in borrowing costs came in response to fears of a fresh wave of inflation after oil climbed by more than 6pc to trade above $107 per barrel. It followed advances by Houthi rebels in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern entrance point of the Red Sea and one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
The US Treasury sold $22bn (£16bn)-worth of 30-year bonds at the highest interest rate since 2001 in another sign of the pressure the Iran war is putting on government finances around the world.
Earlier this week the UK also agreed to pay the highest interest rate in more than a quarter of a century on newly issued bonds.
The European Central Bank (ECB) raised interest rates from 2.25pc to 2.5pc on Thursday, amid mounting pressure on central banks to take further action to curb price rises.
Christine Lagarde, the president of the ECB, said raising borrowing costs in the eurozone was a “no brainer”.
She said: “The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period.
“The energy shock could intensify further and its effects on other prices and wages could be stronger than currently expected.”
The ECB president added: “Gas prices, in particular, could increase in the event of further supply disruptions or an unusually cold winter coinciding with low storage levels.
“The longer energy prices stay high, the more likely they are to drive up broader inflation through indirect and second-round effects.”
![Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/10/TELEMMGLPICT000502030556_17890486741880_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Goldman Sachs raised its forecasts for European natural gas prices by one-third in response to the persistence of the conflict in the Middle East. The investment bank expects gas to reach €70 per megawatt-hour in the final quarter of the year, up from €53 in previous forecasts.
Pressure is mounting on the Bank of England to raise rates in response to the wave of energy-led inflation sweeping the world.
Traders in financial markets now expect four increases over the next year, taking interest rates to 4.75pc.
It is affecting the interest paid on the Government’s near-£3tn debt, and the rate charged on mortgages to home buyers and remortgaging owners.
Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s Governor, has so far resisted pressure to raise borrowing costs. This week, he noted that rates were higher in the UK than in the eurozone.
The Bank is expected to keep the UK’s base rate on hold at 3.75pc at next week’s meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).
However, holding rates is becoming increasingly difficult with inflation set to rise back above 3pc and as the US Federal Reserve is expected to join the ECB in raising rates.
However, Huw Pill, the Bank of England’s chief economist, has argued in favour of higher rates. At July’s MPC meeting he was one of three to vote to increase the base rate to 4pc.
Mr Pill has warned that waiting too long to see the full effect of the price shock from the war risks allowing inflation to become embedded in the economy, making it harder to bring inflation back to the 2pc target.
summary: Government borrowing costs have surged to multi-decade highs, driven by a bond market sell-off triggered by rising oil prices amid conflicts in the Middle East. The resulting spike in interest rates threatens public finances, increases mortgage costs, and pressures central banks globally to tackle renewed inflation. The European Central Bank has already raised interest rates, while the Bank of England faces mounting pressure to follow suit despite Governor Andrew Bailey's previous resistance.
key_points: UK 20-year borrowing costs rose above 5.8pc, reaching their highest level since 1998.
Oil prices climbed over 6pc to trade above $107 per barrel following advances by Houthi rebels in the Red Sea.
The European Central Bank raised interest rates from 2.25pc to 2.5pc in response to persistent inflation pressures from the Middle East conflict.
Financial market traders now expect the Bank of England to implement four interest rate increases over the next year, taking rates to 4.75pc.
The surge in borrowing costs threatens to reduce John Healey's fiscal headroom by around £10bn ahead of his upcoming Budget.

title: One resignation turned the embers of AI fear into a wildfire
author: Nathan Lambert
content:
As AI became more powerful, it was inevitable that a different, growing group would start to take AI safety more seriously – what we did not know ahead of time, is which set of views they latched onto. We have seen that some of the most extreme views of risk, i.e. moderate probabilities of mass extinction, were the ones that reached the masses. A lot in the AI world is about to change due to this.
How did we get here? Why did this quitting announcement reach so far? In many ways, the rest of the world’s views around AI in the past was a dampening factor. You can think about this like the damp ground around a fire. Many people were striking matches for years about AI risk – they’d smolder in their community and largely burn out, going unnoticed. As the stakes of AI have risen this year, from the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident and breakthroughs like the Navier-Stokes result (also from OpenAI), the ground has dried out and the latent energy around the AI discourse has increased. More people not in the industry have thought, “huh, maybe I should care about this AI thing.” The ambient temperature and stakes have been obviously rising.
Then, some basic factors of human nature apply, with the most crucial being that fear sells. Fear is the simplest story, the one people cannot look away from. Jacob Coxon was the one who stumbled into this new powder keg, totally unaware of what was going to come. What looked like a fairly innocuous event – another AI researcher quitting citing safety risks – landed into a very different environment and it caught like wildfire. The discussion of existential risk, mass extinction, and the trajectory of AI has traveled further than even the most seasoned AI commentariat would ever predict.
There are a set of facts we need to get clear, which paint the picture of the situation. The key Tweets to reference are from Jacob Coxon, the resignation thread, and Evan Hubinger, the source of the >10% extinction risk figure .
- There are plenty of AI risks which are likely to cause harm, even if estimating annihilation is useless. It is important to weigh these with respect to the benefits. The entire discourse around existential risk is on very poor footing. At least Evan was clear in his post, with “kill all humans,” but a major problem in the AI Safety discourse is that people talk about existential risks, when they mean very different things (much like how AGI is a vaguely meaningless term). I put the probability of complete extinction as being so low it isn’t worth discussing, but the probabilities of AI caused disasters – e.g. cyber attacks on critical infrastructure or bio-risks – as being worth debating. Throwing this whole discussion out because there are not these disasters yet is a harmful reaction.
- Jacob Coxon is acting genuinely and with good intentions. The outpouring of support from more well-established AI researchers who know of him and his intentions of resignation is useful. Many factions of AI turned to scapegoating him individually, based on account metadata, personal factors, etc. These are not useful. Many frontier lab employees genuinely have similar views to him. I’m not sure it’s a majority, but there is a substantial group.
- Many frontier lab employees, especially at Anthropic, are out of touch and this will impact their forecasting and/or descriptions of current AI events. I say this without blaming individuals, but it’s a common agreement among my friends not at OpenAI/Anthropic (Ant especially) that people at the labs operate with a religious energy. It’s very common to go through very out of touch interactions with them. I do not blame most of the individuals who get distorted views being part of these companies, but the interactions are wild and spill over into a lot of wack discussions in the AI media ecosystem. Living in this environment that normalizes such out of touch behavior will inevitably distort any human’s understanding of technical progress.
- This was not a mass political campaign, but rather an opportunistic media coordination. For context, the Wall Street Journal had an exclusive story that Jacob coordinated before posting. I suspect that Jacob shared his plan of quitting in groupchats with AI safety advocacy groups ahead of time, e.g. the morning of posting, asking for amplification. This is normal practice, and could have included some prominent politicians. From there, I think it’s more likely that other politicians are bandwagoning on a rising issue. When you combine this with other factors, like Daniel Kokotajlo’s appearance on Joe Rogan coming out the same day – it definitely looks like a very well-executed, coordinated media campaign. This doesn’t mean it’s a conspiracy or a regulatory capture tactic within Democratic political structures. The determining factor seems to be that no one – including Jacob and those posting about X-risk today – knew that it would go so viral.
- We do not have proof that RSI causes the risks these researchers forecast. The general argument for RSI follows as: The current pace of progress is very high, the current progress is heavily dependent on AI tools, the current AI tools are superhuman in some domains (e.g. math) – so, all together, AI is going to work more on itself and become superhuman in all relevant areas over time to autonomy and intellect. This view dramatically undersells human bottlenecks in building models and allocating resources at organizations, and draws conclusions on future AI capabilities more broadly. 
 I called my alternative view to this, Lossy self-improvement. AI has always been very jagged, and we are making models which are superhuman goal-seekers at math and software engineering, but they have massive limitations on intuitions, creativity, and other types of reasoning that humans are strong at. With AI agents assisting research, we will rapidly find the areas where AI is superhuman – and I expect there to be well more than just research mathematics – but it won’t be a panacea for the current limitations of our approaches to LLMs.
 There is another understandable social dynamic at play here, causing many deep AI insiders to overstate the returns from RSI. Many of these researchers were the earliest people to bet on AI’s progress, and the extent to which they were visionaries should not be downplayed (see Ilya’s comments on deep learning as early as 2015). They have been right again and again, forecasting AI’s capabilities better than I certainly could have guessed. This does not, though, mean that their forecast of what will come next will be right. The core idea of RSI is a way to spend more compute on the process of developing a model recipe, rather than just spending more compute on the training run itself. We’re seeing benefits from it, but I argue the expected return on that input is far less than they believe.
Their argument is that RSI will make AI progress go exponential, make it so we cannot monitor the technology, and enable rogue models and new forms of risk. This scenario is often called “Fast Takeoff”. We have not seen the stacking efficiency gains that massively reduce model size and cost, that would lead to an explosion in progress by allowing consistent speedups in experimentation.
- The biggest short-term risk could be from the AI labs not taking safety seriously enough – they haven’t hardened their own infrastructure, enabling AI misuse to proliferate. From my earlier post on the HuggingFace-OpenAI incident, Lessons from the hacks: 
  - Frontier labs do not seem like they’re watching the models closely enough, due to a general frenetic competitive environment & current SF culture
 From OpenAI’s own retrospective, the misaligned model behavior was unfolding over months, and in some cases OpenAI did not know about the hacks for ~weeks. The time to response is too long and I do not think this is an OpenAI only characteristic – rather it is that the frontier labs continually seem underwater in the amount of work they feel like they should do. I am not optimistic in the long-term that the labs change a sufficient amount here to meaningfully mitigate this type of oversight risk in the future. Yes, it is very likely that OpenAI is putting a ton into understanding this – and delayed their latest models to make sure they get it right – but the financial pressure to grow revenue or risk the companies’ long-term balance sheets makes me think it will not be a sustained pattern of caution.
Overall, I think this episode is very bad for the AI ecosystem. It’s pushed the acceptable views in the AI community closer to the extremes. More accelerationists will discount the need for any form of safety, citing mass delusion of the “doomers.” It feels like a very narrow path to believe in AI risks, but to not worry about extinction from the technology.
For example, it is a horrible temporary period for cybersecurity, where AI models going a bit off script and poking around unintended pieces of the web seems like a new normal. This is accelerated by the labs competing veraciously towards their views of AGI, and a slow uptake in the necessary hardening of our cyber infrastructure around the world. This doesn’t mean that it’s an existential risk and something we cannot solve. Each risk will have its own set of solutions and paths forward.
I feel particularly exposed in the current environment as a supporter of open models. If an open model were to be used by a third party organization to intentionally hack another company — similar to how the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident went down, but intentional — my expected outcome would be a severe restriction on the development of stronger open models going forward. Open models are needed for many organizations to perform this cyber hardening, and to maintain the ability to adapt to new forms of AI risks in the future.
Through all of this, we need to stay grounded on what is actually unfolding. Yes, monitoring AI’s behavior is heavily reliant on other AI models, which adds in new types of monitoring risks. These are not inherently insolvable. A recurring read of mine on the emerging agent swarms is that they’re attempting to do a task given to them, and they’re using skills we didn’t know they yet had to circumvent the intended path to success. This is a huge win, as when you squint, the AIs are doing what we told them to do. The models are certainly very odd, and we should accelerate our progress on understanding them, but these swarms are far from being novel independent entities. The models are trained to coordinate on tasks, to write down their progress, and to be extremely persistent. There will be new oddities we find in the future, but prescribing current uncertainty on how AI works to future certainty that we cannot understand AI is a form of giving up.
In this world, we need to rely on the rule of law and science. If the AI labs are not able to do enough safety research themselves to understand the models, they should be more transparent on what is happening so more scientists can make progress on the problem. If an AI lab commits crimes unintentionally, they should be punished, so they have clear incentives to prevent it in the future.
It is a natural reaction to things changing very fast to feel more uncertain about how to create good outcomes — that is actually the correct mental update. We need to use this humility to motivate ambitious solutions.
summary: A researcher's resignation citing AI safety risks unexpectedly went viral, turning niche discussions of existential threat into widespread public fear. The author argues that while extreme predictions like human extinction are exaggerated and unproven, real risks such as cyber vulnerabilities and inadequate lab infrastructure demand serious attention. Ultimately, this hyper-focused panic harms the broader AI ecosystem by polarizing the debate and pushing views toward unhelpful extremes.
key_points: Jacob Coxon's resignation announcement unexpectedly went viral, fueled by human nature where fear sells and a supportive media coordination.
Discussions around existential risk and recursive self-improvement often rely on poor footing and exaggerate future capabilities while ignoring human bottlenecks.
Frontier AI labs face significant short-term risks, such as inadequate infrastructure hardening and slow response times to security incidents, driven by intense competitive pressures.
The recent viral panic pushes the AI community toward unhelpful extremes, alienating nuance and making it harder to address tangible issues like cybersecurity and AI misuse.

title: Lawmakers blast AI companies after researcher warns of human extinction by 2030
author: Dara Kerr
content:
Just a day after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, lawmakers have begun lashing out about the risks of the burgeoning technology.
Ted Cruz, a republican senator from Texas, said in an interview on ABC’s The View, that AI poses a “catastrophic risk” and that he “read that whole tweet thread that that developer put out. It was highly concerning.
“It reminded me, last year I had Elon Musk on my podcast … and one of the questions I asked him, I said, ‘OK, what are the odds that AI destroys humanity?’ And he looked at me and said, ‘10-20%.’ And I’m like, ‘holy crap,’” Cruz added.
On the polar end of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont, said: “A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.”
The outrage began after Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon announced on social media on Tuesday that he was resigning from the company, saying AI will soon be “superhuman systems” that could cause human extinction by 2030.
“I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly,” Coxon wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
After Coxon’s post, at least two other Anthropic employees responded to back up these predictions. One said: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”
Both Cruz and Sanders have been working on legislation that would put guardrails on AI, and echoed this sentiment on Wednesday. Other lawmakers also called on Congress to act. Ted Lieu, a Democrat congressman from California, said Coxon’s post was “exhibit number 739 for why we need to pass the bipartisan AI Kill Switch Bill asap”.
Lori Trahan, a Democrat congresswoman from Massachusetts, said it was “past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job”.
“Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway,” Trahan added.
Even musician Sheryl Crow weighed in, posting on Instagram about Coxon’s warning and saying that AI has the capacity to “eliminate us in order to continue”.
“I am begging and pleading that we wake up to this moment and demand our leaders put aside their greed and prevent this from going forward,” Crow wrote. Singer-songwriter Maggie Rogers reposted Crow, writing: “what she said”.
The outrage comes after both OpenAI and Anthropic revealed that some of their AI agents went rogue in hacking sprees over the past couple of months. Executives at the companies have touted the power of their technology and warned of its potential, but have stopped short of prognostications like Coxon’s.
On Wednesday, Anthropic published a lengthy cybersecurity incident report about its occurrences. The company said it scanned hundreds of millions of transcripts to look for further incidents and that it “found no other cases of similar or worse severity”. Anthropic insisted that while the agent’s actions were “misaligned, they remained within a narrow scope”.
“We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks,” an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian. “To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.” The spokesperson added that the industry should work together “to pace how we release powerful models”.
OpenAI did not return a request for comment.
summary: Lawmakers have reacted with alarm after an Anthropic researcher resigned and warned that advanced artificial intelligence could lead to human extinction by 2030. Senators Ted Cruz and Bernie Sanders, along with other members of Congress, called for immediate legislation and safety guardrails to regulate the rapidly developing technology. The warnings follow recent incidents where AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic engaged in rogue hacking sprees, prompting heightened scrutiny from politicians and public figures.
key_points: An Anthropic researcher resigned and warned on social media that AI could cause human extinction by 2030.
Senators Ted Cruz and Bernie Sanders expressed deep concern over AI risks and are working on legislation to establish safety guardrails.
Lawmakers including Ted Lieu and Lori Trahan urged Congress to take immediate action and pass AI regulatory bills.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic recently revealed that some of their AI agents went rogue in hacking sprees.

title: Heathrow live: Passengers ‘unlikely to get compensation’ as 2,000 UK flights affected
author: Natalie Wilson; Sophie Dickinson; Amelia Neath
content:
Tens of thousands of passengers plunged into travel chaos this week are unlikely to get compensation, the regulator has warned.
The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA), which is conducting an independent review, has told those impacted that the “disruption caused by the Nats outage is likely to be considered the result of ‘extraordinary circumstances’ under passenger rights rules”.
This means passengers are “unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident,” it said.
More than 2,000 flights to and from the UK were cancelled or delayed on Tuesday and Wednesday due to a “technical issue”.
London Heathrow, London Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted airports were among the most disrupted aviation hubs on Wednesday.
National Air Traffic Control Service (Nats) chief Martin Rolfe was summoned at lunchtime on Wednesday to see Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, after reporting a problem with the organisation’s flight data processing system.
Asked whether Ms Alexander and the prime minister still have confidence in Rolfe, a spokesperson said: “We have confidence in him and he’s been tasked with an investigation.”
Have you been affected by airport delays? Get in touch by emailing sophie.dickinson@independent.co.uk
Editorial: Britain’s crumbling vital infrastructure cannot be allowed to fail
The latest ‘technical glitch’ to cause widespread chaos at Britain’s airports must not be allowed to happen yet again. But preventing it will mean confronting the awesome challenge – and cost – of modernising air traffic control.
Read more:
2,163 flights were affected on Tuesday and Wednesday
Across two days of travel chaos, 2,163 flights were affected, according to Cirium, the aviation analytics company, in its final update at 11.59pm on Wednesday.
Yesterday, 417 flights were cancelled or did not fly: 184 departures and 233 arrivals.
In pictures: Heathrow airport on Wednesday

London airport delays latest
As of midday Thursday, flight tracking service Flightradar24 shows 219 delayed flights at London Heathrow, with an average delay of 15 minutes.
At London Gatwick, 160 flights are delayed by an average of 14 minutes, with 79 flights delayed by an average of just 10 minutes at London Stansted.
Airline passengers face more delays as Gatwick strikes planned next week
Flight passengers at Gatwick airport could face further disruption next week as more than 220 assisted travel workers plan to strike over pay.
The walkout was announced by trade union Unite on Wednesday, the day after around 1,300 UK flights were grounded following a technical issue with air traffic control systems.
The industrial action will take place from 17 September to 21 September, then 23 September to 26 September.

Heathrow airport making some schedule changes
Following Tuesday's technical issue, Heathrow has said that there “may still be some changes to schedules”.
The airport said on X: “We know the knock-on effects of Tuesday's disruption have been frustrating, and we thank those affected for their patience.
“We advise passengers to check with their airline for the latest flight information before travelling to Heathrow.”
Ryanair boss Michael O’Leary compares other airlines to rapists in bizarre rant
Ryanair chief executive Michael O’Leary has said it is “absolutely” appropriate to compare other airlines to “rapists”.
The billionaire businessman made the remarks ahead of his airline’s annual general meeting in Dublin on Thursday.
Mr O’Leary told reporters at the company’s headquarters: “You might find some people will choose not to fly with Ryanair – but you know they’ll be overrun with the people abandoning Aer Lingus, Lufthansa, BA, and others desperate to get to Ryanair’s low fares because they can’t afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe.”
Asked whether this was appropriate language, Mr O’Leary told reporters: “Absolutely.”

British Airways operated 80 per cent of flights on Wednesday
British Airways said it operated almost 80 per cent of its flight schedule on Wednesday, with flights rebooked for “the vast majority of our customers”.
Virgin Atlantic customers told to 'come on time' to airport
Airlines have advised passengers to arrive at the airport on time as the aviation industry recovers.
Virgin Atlantic said: “Following the widespread disruption from the technical issue affecting the Nats air traffic control system, we expect to operate our planned flying programme on Thursday 10 September, and ask that customers come to the airport on time for their departure.”

What counts as ‘extraordinary circumstances’ – and why can they prevent refunds?
The Civil Aviation Authority has said that “disruption caused by the Nats outage is likely to be considered the result of ‘extraordinary circumstances’.”
This means passengers are “unlikely to be entitled to compensation.”
But what counts as extraordinary circumstances?
Typically, the phrase is understood to mean “political instability, meteorological conditions incompatible with the operation of the flight concerned, security risks, unexpected flight safety shortcomings and strikes”.
Court cases have gradually refined the concept of “extraordinary circumstances” to exclude mechanical problems. A judge ruled such issues are “inherent in the normal exercise of the activity of the air carrier”.
Ryanair says: “Only a small number of claims will be eligible for compensation. Most delays/cancellations are out of Ryanair’s control.”

summary: Tens of thousands of passengers affected by recent travel chaos and flight cancellations across UK airports are unlikely to receive compensation. The Civil Aviation Authority stated that the National Air Traffic Control Service (Nats) technical outage likely qualifies as 'extraordinary circumstances'. Meanwhile, passengers face potential further disruption due to upcoming strikes by assisted travel workers at Gatwick airport.
key_points: Over 2,000 UK flights were canceled or delayed due to a Nats technical issue on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The Civil Aviation Authority stated that affected passengers are unlikely to be entitled to compensation because the outage is considered 'extraordinary circumstances'.
Gatwick airport faces upcoming strikes by more than 220 assisted travel workers scheduled for late September.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander summoned Nats chief Martin Rolfe following the flight data processing system failure.

title: Passengers caught in flight chaos unlikely to get compensation, regulator says - live
author: Natalie Wilson; Sophie Dickinson; Harriette Boucher
content:
Tens of thousands of passengers plunged into travel chaos this week are unlikely to get compensation, the regulator has warned.
The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA), which is conducting an independent review, has told those impacted that the “disruption caused by the Nats outage is likely to be considered the result of ‘extraordinary circumstances’ under passenger rights rules”.
This means passengers are “unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident,” it said.
Airports have warned of further disruption on Wednesday after more than 2,000 flights to and from the UK were cancelled or delayed due to a “technical issue”.
National Air Traffic Control Service (Nats) chief Martin Rolfe was summoned at lunchtime to see Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, after reporting a problem with the organisation’s flight data processing system.
Asked whether Ms Alexander and the prime minister still have confidence in Rolfe, a spokesperson said: “We have confidence in him and he’s been tasked with an investigation.”
Around 1,300 flights to and from UK airports were cancelled on Tuesday, according to Flightradar24, with a further 417 cancellations recorded on Wednesday.
Have you been affected by airport delays? Get in touch by emailing sophie.dickinson@independent.co.uk
Delays ‘very distressing for elderly people’, says Independent reader
An reader from Australia, Jill Parkes, has shared her experience of the disruption.
“We are two women in our seventies,” she writes. After her flight from Zurich was cancelled on Tuesday, she says there were “no BA support staff in the airport. Dnata staff told us to take our luggage and find accommodation at our own expense, with no assurance of new flights.
“Very distressing for elderly people with no experience in booking online, or without access to surplus funds to cover these unexpected costs. So far it has cost more than CHF600 (£545).
“We have had to pay for two nights’ accommodation, plus taxis and food bought at Aldi.
“At midnight on the first night, we were offered new flights with Thai from Zurich, via Bangkok. We readily accepted, but the flights are not until today, 10 September.
“So we’re still in Zurich.”
Travel disruption expected to wind down on Thursday
There is little disruption expected on Thursday after 400 flights were cancelled yesterday, aviation analytics firm Cirium said.
Its data last night showed that cancellations were continuing to slow and there were none scheduled for today.
Some 399 flights in and out of the UK were cancelled on Wednesday, including 209 flights meant to and from Heathrow.
Overall, thousands of flights have been cancelled or delayed due to the “technical issue” that caused chaos at airports across the country.
'Fraudsters tried to sell me fake BA flights', stranded passengers say
Holidaymakers Geoff and Janina McBride are warning people about a scam that NatWest fortunately rescued them from.
The McBrides, from Hampshire, were trying to travel to Lisbon and then on to the Azores to celebrate their 30th wedding anniversary – but their flight was cancelled.
Former government nanotechnology scientist Mr McBride, 63, told PA they called a phone number on what they thought was the official BA website.
A fraudster pretending to work for the airline tried to offer them alternative flights from London City, Gatwick or Heathrow airports and via Munich.
The false flights were about £600 each, but the payments to him were not going through.
His wife, 64, called NatWest to ask why and they told her “get off the phone to them immediately”, Mr McBride said.
His card was blocked and the payments cancelled, he added, telling PA: “What do you do when you’re in a drama?
“I’m very well-versed in cybersecurity, but it’s that one click, isn’t it?
“And it looked legitimate, proper, he sounded proper, he was going through all the different flights, had all the details, so he can pull that off the internet and speak to me down the phone, credit card details – so I was lucky, very lucky.”
Mr McBride added: “We were in a panic – that’s when they get you.”
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/09/17/01M23EC5F7S2718KEGGRPCC3GT.jpg)
In depth: Inside the IT ‘glitch’ that triggered UK flight chaos – and the warnings issued three years ago
As airport passengers began seeing flights delayed on departure boards at Heathrow and Gatwick, National Air Traffic Services (Nats), the UK’s air traffic control provider, issued an alert over a “technical issue” causing disruption.
An hour and a half later, amid heightened chaos that had spread to other major airports across the country, the public-private partnership body sent out an update, explaining that the issue in “our flight processing system” had been identified. Some 75 minutes later it said had been fixed and systems were recovering – but with a warning that the disruption could last days.
Such a recovery took longer than hoped, conceded Nats in a further statement at 7.30pm, as the increasingly under-fire body offered an unreserved apology to the growing thousands of passengers stranded at airports, including Bristol, Birmingham and Manchester.
To the hardened airline traveller, it brought, perhaps, a sense of déjà vu.
Ryanair repeats calls for 'overpaid failing' air traffic boss to be sacked
Ryanair has taken another jab at the ‘overpaid failing” boss of Nats, repeating calls for him to sacked after yesterday’s technical glitch.
Chief operating officer Neal McMahon said: “The last thing UK passengers and airlines need after yet another NATS system collapse is another ‘review’ or ‘report’.
“Asking failed CEO Martin Rolfe to conduct this report is similar to asking a failed student to mark his own exam paper!”
He added: “Martin Rolfe, after the Aug 2023 NATS system collapse promised Parliament that this wouldn’t happen again, and that an effective back-up system would be introduced. UK passengers learned yesterday that these assurances were worthless. The NATS ATC system collapsed again, and yet again, there was no back-up system.
“Martin Rolfe, the overpaid failing CEO cannot be trusted to report on his own failings. He should be sacked and replaced with someone competent to run the UK ATC system and to prevent repeated collapses of UK ATC and it’s non-existent back-up systems.”
In pictures: Hundreds of flights cancelled on Wednesday as disruption continued across UK
400 UK flights cancelled on Wednesday
Some 399 flights in and out of the UK were cancelled on Wednesday, the latest data has shown.
According to aviation analytics firm Cirium, 7 per cent of all flights failed to take off today.
There were 209 flights arriving or departing Heathrow that were cancelled, 23 to Manchester, and 18 to Gatwick.
The worst affected airlines were British Airways, which had 88 flights cancelled, and easyJet which had 31.
Cirium said interruption was slowing down on Wednesday evening, with no cancellations currently expected tomorrow.
Everything that happened yesterday after technical issued sparked travel chaos
Another 400 flights were cancelled yesterday after Nats’ “technical issue” sparked chaos at airports across the country.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers who have been affected by the air traffic control problems have now been told by the regulator that they are “unlikely to be entitled to compensation”.
Calls are continuing to grow for air traffic boss Martin Rolfe to resign after he was summoned by transport secretary Heidi Alexander at lunchtime yesterday.
Ms Alexander said she did not believe the air traffic control issue was “unavoidable”, and asked Mr Rolfe to carry out a full investigation and report back in one week's time.
The transport secretary said that along with the prime minister, she still had confidence in Mr Rolfe.
She also ordered the Civil Aviation Authority to conduct an independent review.
Disruption is due to wind down on Thursday, with no cancelled flights currently expected.
Editorial: Britain’s crumbling vital infrastructure cannot be allowed to fail
The latest ‘technical glitch’ to cause widespread chaos at Britain’s airports must not be allowed to happen yet again. But preventing it will mean confronting the awesome challenge – and cost – of modernising air traffic control
In the UK and Europe, what can I expect if my flight is delayed?
For delays of under two hours, you have no rights (unless a short delay in the UK triggers a missed connection and much later arrival at your final ticketed destination – see below).
For longer delays, the airline should provide refreshments as appropriate after a specified length of time. This applies regardless of the cause of the delay.
The time at which the duty of care kicks in depends on the distance you are flying:
- Short flights (up to 1,500km): refreshments after two hours
- Mid-haul journeys (1,500 to 3,500km): three hours
- Longer trips: four hours
Note that if the airline believes providing the care would further delay the flight, it need not deliver.
If the delay extends overnight, the airline is obliged to find and pay for a hotel room. In practice, carriers often say, “too difficult”, and invite the passenger to book their own and reclaim later.
While this attitude does not comply fully with the rules, aviation authorities tend to turn a blind eye to it.
The duty of care applies regardless of the cause of a delay or cancellation.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/07/24/10/47/iStock-1196391579.jpeg?trim=0,0,0,0&width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
summary: A technical issue in the National Air Traffic Control Service's flight data processing system caused thousands of flight cancellations and delays across the UK. The Civil Aviation Authority warned that affected passengers are unlikely to receive compensation because the disruption falls under extraordinary circumstances. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander summoned Nats chief Martin Rolfe and tasked him with an investigation, while travel disruption is expected to wind down.
key_points: Over 2,000 flights to and from the UK were cancelled or delayed due to a Nats technical issue.
The Civil Aviation Authority stated that passengers are unlikely to receive compensation due to extraordinary circumstances.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander met with Nats chief Martin Rolfe and ordered an investigation into the outage.
Travel disruption is expected to ease with no cancellations scheduled for Thursday.
Stranded passengers faced additional challenges, including an attempted booking scam and costly unexpected accommodation expenses.

title: Brent crude surpasses $100 a barrel as Iran, US escalate attacks
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![A street sign for Wall Street is seen outside the New York Stock Exchange \[FILE:Andrew Kelly/Reuters\]](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/2026-09-09T100020Z_1739521985_RC2MFNAIDEUH_RTRMADP_3_USA-STOCKS-MIDTERM-1788953549.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Global stocks have come under pressure and Brent crude oil surpassed $100 a barrel as escalating fighting across the Middle East stokes fears of energy-driven inflation.
The benchmark crude contract rose to $100.19 on Wednesday, its highest level since July 24, when a memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran was in place, and its price was on the downswing.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Yemen’s war is back: A new battle for Sanaa and the Red Sea
- list 2 of 3US, Iran engaged in tanker war: Where is the months-long conflict headed?
- list 3 of 3Saudi-Houthi fighting in Yemen escalates: What happened, and what’s next?
The US military attacked five Iranian crude oil carriers overnight, with Iran retaliating with missile attacks on US forces in Jordan and attacks on shipping.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would keep hitting Iranian oil tankers in response to attempted attacks on US warships.
Wall Street’s three main stock indexes – the S&P, Dow and Nasdaq – each saw small losses. European stocks dropped to one-week lows, with industrial and banking stocks hit the worst. Canada’s blue-chip stock futures also inched down.
Asian markets fluctuated, although technology shares continued to climb back from a July low, driven by the artificial intelligence boom.
Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at Swissquote, told Reuters that risk appetite remained weak due to rising oil prices from the war.
“Summer was full of hope that a peace agreement could be achieved,” he said. “This optimism is fading as we enter September.”
Manish Kabra, a multi-asset strategist at Societe Generale, said $100 was a “psychological threshold” rather than an economic one.
“We think crude needs to hit $150 to create a major drawback in demand cycle,” he said. Rising diesel prices could feed into inflation and services, he added.
The surge in oil prices has added to concerns that higher inflation will lead central banks to adopt more restrained monetary policies.
The European Central Bank is expected to hike interest rates on Thursday, and next week the US Federal Reserve will meet to determine whether they will do the same.
Bond markets are feeling the strain as well. Inflation concerns have raised yields in recent weeks as traders anticipate central bank tightening.
Since the US and Iran resumed attacks on each other at the end of August, benchmark bonds in the US, Japan and some European countries have seen multidecade-high yields, raising concerns over government borrowing costs and the health of global financial institutions.
summary: Global stock markets have declined and Brent crude oil prices have surpassed $100 a barrel following escalating military conflict between the United States and Iran. The surge in oil prices has raised concerns about energy-driven inflation and potential interest rate hikes by central banks. Bond markets are also under pressure, with benchmark bond yields in several countries reaching multidecade highs.
key_points: Brent crude oil rose to $100.19 a barrel on Wednesday amid escalating Middle East fighting.
The US military attacked five Iranian crude oil carriers, prompting Iranian retaliatory missile and shipping attacks.
Wall Street indexes saw small losses, and European stocks dropped to one-week lows.
Rising oil prices and inflation concerns have increased expectations of central bank interest rate hikes.
Benchmark bond yields in the US, Japan, and parts of Europe reached multidecade highs.

title: Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030
author: Richard Luscombe
content:
Artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, according to three researchers with the industry giant Anthropic, one of whom has quit his job in protest.
The latest doom-laden predictions came in posts on social media on Tuesday by a researcher who said he resigned because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or, at best, mishandling their response to the threat.
“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” wrote Jacob Coxon.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.”
The post garnered responses from at least two other Anthropic employees who backed up Coxon’s dire predictions.
In the first, Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said his former colleague was “correct”, and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential.
“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”
Hubinger’s comments mark a surprising affirmation of Coxon’s unflattering, apocalyptic predictions from a person still on Anthropic’s payroll. A second response came from Samuel Marks, Anthropic’s “scalable oversight lead”, who posted a lengthy analysis he stressed was in his personal capacity, and not the views of his employer. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Marks. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.”
Their musings on the possibility of human extinction follow more concrete warnings about AI’s cybersecurity capabilities by Sam Altman, chief executive of Anthropic’s rival OpenAI. OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, has conceded previously that “we underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models”.
Altman said last year that certain aspects of AI, including what he called the “silent surrender” of human decision-making, terrified him.
AI executives have shared some concerns about the direction of AI and its growing ability to manipulate, seize and control human functions and actions. A sharp rise was reported this summer in incidents of AIs escaping users’ control to lie, ignore instructions and pursue goals in harmful ways.
after newsletter promotion
In one of the most publicized examples, staff at OpenAI recorded rogue behavior among its leading AI agents that escaped a closed training environment in July to access the open web and launch an unprecedented hacking attack on the software repository Hugging Face.
OpenAI, the San Francisco-based startup behind the publicly available AI bot ChatGPT, later admitted that it should have responded earlier to warning signals of the days-long attack, which is widely considered to be the first autonomous agent cyber-attack.
Those executives, however, have stopped short of agreeing with the full doomsday warnings like Coxon’s and have bristled at any attempts to regulate the AI industry.
Some politicians have urged the industry to slow down, or in some cases, halt development on AI altogether.
Bernie Sanders, the independent Vermont senator, reposted Coxon’s resignation on Wednesday with his own note: “Mr. Coxon is right. The very people building this technology admit that it could threaten the future of humanity.” Sanders said he would soon introduce legislation to “ban superintelligence” and pause AI development.
summary: Three researchers from the AI giant Anthropic have stated that artificial intelligence could cause human extinction within the decade, prompting one of them to resign in protest. The departing researcher and his colleagues criticized the industry for racing toward self-improving superintelligence without adequate safety plans. While industry executives have previously expressed various concerns about AI capabilities, some politicians are now calling for legislation to pause development and ban superintelligence.
key_points: An Anthropic researcher resigned in protest, claiming Anthropic and OpenAI are ignoring the existential threat of AI.
Two other Anthropic employees backed the predictions, with one estimating a greater than 10% chance of AI killing all humans within the next decade.
Researchers noted that senior AI executives privately fear human extinction outcomes, though public phrasing is often more restrained.
Senator Bernie Sanders responded to the resignation by announcing plans to introduce legislation to pause AI development and ban superintelligence.

title: 'It's been a nightmare': Passengers face airport chaos after UK air traffic issue
author: Alex Boyd; BBC Your Voice reporters
content:
'Horrendous experience': Passengers react to travel chaos
- Published
Passengers left stranded by an hours-long air traffic control issue at UK airports have told the BBC of nightmare delays, chaotic scenes and waylaid holiday plans.
Hundreds of thousands of people are thought to have been hit with flight cancellations and delays throughout Tuesday and Wednesday after a technical problem caused the air traffic outage.
That included newlyweds Sasha and James, who told BBC Your Voice they spent three hours stranded in Wetherspoons at Gatwick after their flight to their honeymoon was cancelled.
Some also described sleeping on airport floors and chaos at baggage reclaim as thousands looked to reorganise their plans, while others have been stranded abroad while trying to get back to the UK.
Nats, the UK's air traffic control provider, has said flight operations are now stable but airlines have warned of continued knock-on disruption. Passengers have been advised to check their flight status before travelling to airports.
The boss of Nats Martin Rolfe apologised for the disruption and also met with Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday, who asked for a full investigation.
Most of the UK's main airports were hit by the problem including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.
Speaking to the BBC earlier on Wednesday, newly married couple Sasha and James Graham said they were boarding their flight from Gatwick to Funchal on the island of Madeira when they were "turned right back around".
![James (left) and Sasha (right) smile at the camera while sat at a table in the airport Wetherspoons](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/542/cpsprodpb/2c68/live/f2cee0a0-ac63-11f1-be57-03729df1d736.png)
The newlyweds spent three hours at a Wetherspoons in Gatwick after a flight to their honeymoon was cancelled
Sasha said: "We spent three hours stranded in Wetherspoons, making the best of it.
"It's certainly not the experience we planned, but I think starting your marriage with a national disruption is certainly very memorable!"
They weren't able to reclaim their luggage but have since booked onto a new flight.
"It feels like we will spend our honeymoon at Gatwick," Sasha added.
![Phil White smiles at the camera as he sits on an EasyJet plane](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1552/cpsprodpb/569d/live/c0857750-ac66-11f1-80f0-9795d1a5edbc.jpg)
Phil White said tempers frayed at Gatwick as people tried to reclaim their luggage on Tuesday
Phil White also spoke of incredibly busy scenes in the airport's baggage reclaim hall, describing it as "carnage" as an influx of disrupted passengers tried to find their luggage.
"All the bags from every cancelled flight were sent to one reclaim carousel. So there were a thousand or so people trying to get close enough to get their cases," he said.
"The baggage hall was the worst and they're very lucky that there wasn't any sort of incident as tempers frayed and the concourse was getting hotter."
Elsewhere, people spoke of spending the night on the floors of airports and hotels across the globe when flights back into the UK were cancelled.
Sukie Perera, from Cardiff, describing her experience of being stuck in Turkey said "it has been a nightmare" and communication at the airport was poor.
She won't be able to fly home until Thursday but joked that at least "the view is beautiful".
Paul Willows, currently in Rhodes, Greece, with his family said they had to sleep on the floor of a hotel's conference room on Tuesday night.
He said: "They stripped all the cushions off the sunbeds and laid them in the conference room. I dare say there were about 80 of us on the floor."
Despite it having "not been a comfortable night at all", Paul said there was a "good element of pulling together" from those impacted.
Alan Jones and Kelly Fewery also said their family was "absolutely exhausted" after sleeping on the floor of Dalaman Airport in Turkey without blankets or pillows.
More than 340 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.
Airlines are still obliged to get passengers to their destinations - even if that is via another carrier - when their flight is cancelled, or give a refund.
Those delayed may have the right to food, or a hotel stay, depending on the length of the wait. But no extra compensation payments should be expected as the air traffic control issue was not the fault of any airline.
summary: An hours-long technical problem with the UK air traffic control provider, Nats, caused widespread flight cancellations and delays across major UK airports on Tuesday and Wednesday. Hundreds of thousands of passengers faced severe disruption, including stranded holidaymakers sleeping on airport floors, chaotic baggage claims, and postponed honeymoons. Although Nats reported that flight operations are now stable, airlines have warned of continued knock-on effects, prompting the transport secretary to request a full investigation.
key_points: A technical issue at Nats, the UK's air traffic control provider, caused widespread flight cancellations and delays across major UK airports on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Passengers reported chaotic scenes, including crowded baggage claims and sleeping on the floors of airports and hotels both in the UK and abroad.
More than 340 flights were cancelled on Wednesday alone, and airlines have warned of continued knock-on disruption.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander met with Nats boss Martin Rolfe and requested a full investigation into the incident.

title: JP Morgan boss Jamie Dimon warns UK chancellor against bank tax hike
author: Lauren Almeida
content:
Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of the largest US bank, JP Morgan, is understood to have warned the UK chancellor, John Healey, against raising taxes on banks in his inaugural budget in October.
