The Wall Street billionaire met the new chancellor on Wednesday and cautioned him that higher taxes could put investment and employment in the UK at risk, it is understood.
The meeting came amid speculation that Healey is considering a windfall tax on banks and oil companies in his budget on 28 October.
Dimon has a long track record of lobbying against Britain’s additional bank taxes, which were imposed after the government bailed out big UK lenders in the 2008 financial crisis.
Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, as well as a separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets.
The JP Morgan chief executive has previously warned that raising these taxes further could have “adverse consequences”. In August, he told Healey in a telephone conversation that higher levies could hit jobs, citing a fall in finance roles in New York that he blamed on the city’s tax regime.
Dimon was among a group of bank bosses who successfully lobbied against higher taxes before Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves’s budget last year – with Dimon hosting Varun Chandra, who remains in his post as the prime minister’s business envoy, at a birthday celebration for King Charles at the bank’s Manhattan headquarters.
Days afterwards, Dimon announced plans to build a 3m sq ft tower in London’s Canary Wharf district, although he added that a “continuing positive business environment in the UK” was required.
However, in May this year, he said he could scrap plans for the £3bn tower – which is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters and house more than half its 23,000-strong UK workforce – if Keir Starmer were replaced by a new Labour prime minister who was hostile to banks.
after newsletter promotion
Andy Burnham has not made any specific comments about a bank tax so far. However, he has faced calls to introduce higher levies from the TUC and the campaign group Positive Money, which argue a tax increase could help cover rising household bills as part of his drive to tackle the cost of living.
The UK’s four biggest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds Banking Group – have generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years, largely off the back of rising interest rates.
UK banks together paid an estimated £43.3bn in tax for the financial year that ended in March 2025, according to a report commissioned by the industry body UK Finance.
summary: JP Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon has warned UK Chancellor John Healey against raising taxes on banks in the upcoming October budget. Dimon cautioned that higher levies could jeopardize investment and employment in the UK. UK lenders currently pay a 28% corporation tax rate along with a separate balance sheet surcharge.
key_points: JP Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon met with UK Chancellor John Healey to warn against increasing bank taxes.
Dimon cautioned that higher taxes could risk UK investment and employment.
UK lenders currently face a 28% corporation tax rate and an additional balance sheet surcharge.
Groups like the TUC and Positive Money have called for higher levies to help cover rising household bills.

title: UK flight cancellations pass 1,900 as pressure grows on air traffic control boss on second day of travel chaos – business live
author: Julia Kollewe
content:
UK flight cancellations pass 1,900 as pressure grows on air traffic control boss on second day of travel chaos – business live
Technical issue at Nats resolved but flights to and from UK airports still disrupted; oil prices hit $100 a barrel for first time since July and gas prices also jump
Passengers at Heathrow Airport in west London, during disruption after a system issue hit Nats, which provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. Further cancellations and delays are expected today. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA
Passengers at Heathrow Airport in west London, during disruption after a system issue hit Nats, which provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. Further cancellations and delays are expected today. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA
More than 1,900 flights cancelled over two days, according to Cirium
In total, more 1,900 flights had been cancelled by 5am today, according to the aviation analytics company Cirium, since yesterday’s system issue at National Air Traffic Services.
Nats provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. While the technical problem has been resolved, the flight chaos has continued into a second day. Other flights have been delayed, causing chaos for tens of thousands of passenggers travelling to and from the UK.
Cirium says:
8 September: More than 1,750 flights arriving into and departing from UK airports were cancelled — 902 departures and 860 arrivals, out of 5,800 scheduled. A normal day is under 1–2%.
9 September: So far, 153 flights are cancelled — 55 departures and 98 arrivals. Just over 3%.
European stock markets slide while energy stocks are higher
Energy companies BP, Shell and British Gas parent Centrica are among the main risers on the FTSE 100 index today, as the oil price surged through $100 a barrel, for the first time since 24 July.
Centrica shares are up 2.1%, BP has gained 1.5% and Shell is 0.9% ahead.
The wider FTSE 100 index is trading lower, down 0.6% or 66 points at 10,745. The German, French, Italian and Spanish indices have fallen even more, between 1.1% and 1.9%.
Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at the trading platform capital.com, said:
Markets remain on the defensive as the latest escalation in the Middle East pushes Brent to $100 a barrel. US forces have struck Iranian oil tankers following attempted attacks on US naval vessels, while Iran retaliated against a US-used base in Jordan and says it targeted vessels attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities have widened the threat further, raising concerns that disruption could spread beyond Iranian supply to the infrastructure and alternative routes that have helped keep Gulf crude flowing.
That has brought the inflationary consequences of the conflict firmly back into focus. Wall Street fell on Tuesday as higher crude revived concerns that the energy shock could stall disinflation and force central banks to remain restrictive. US rate expectations have shifted accordingly, while upcoming inflation data will be particularly important in determining whether $100 oil is beginning to feed more materially into the Fed[eral Reserve] outlook.
Europe faces an even more immediate policy test with the European Central Bank meeting on Thursday. Markets are widely positioned for a 25 basis point hike, after the ECB explicitly warned in July that the full inflationary impact of the energy shock had yet to emerge. The latest surge in oil, and European gas prices, makes that concern harder to dismiss. Focus will be on Christine Lagarde’s guidance on whether this is sufficient insurance against the energy shock or whether further tightening remains likely.
UK and European gas prices surge to multi-year highs
UK and European gas prices have risen to a multi-year highs, while the oil price jumped above $100 a barrel.
The escalating Middle East conflict, cooler weather and rising Asian gas prices has led to aggressive gas buying ahead of the winter.
The benchmark Dutch gas contract leapt nearly 4% to €78.73 per megawatt hour, the highest since January 2023.
The British contract rose 7.77 pence 196.57p per therm, the highest since late December 2022.
In oil markets, Brent crude surged through $100 a barrel for the first time since July, rising 2.7% to $100.68 a barrel.
European gas stores are only 67% full, compared to 79.5% a year ago, according to data from Gas Infrastructure Europe.
Analysts at HSBC are forecasting that European stock levels will reach 73% by 1 November, the lowest since data collection began in 2009, and do not expect Qatari liquefied natural gas exports, excluding damaged facilities, to return to normal until early next year at the earliest.
More than 1,900 flights cancelled over two days, according to Cirium
In total, more 1,900 flights had been cancelled by 5am today, according to the aviation analytics company Cirium, since yesterday’s system issue at National Air Traffic Services.
Nats provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. While the technical problem has been resolved, the flight chaos has continued into a second day. Other flights have been delayed, causing chaos for tens of thousands of passenggers travelling to and from the UK.
Cirium says:
8 September: More than 1,750 flights arriving into and departing from UK airports were cancelled — 902 departures and 860 arrivals, out of 5,800 scheduled. A normal day is under 1–2%.
9 September: So far, 153 flights are cancelled — 55 departures and 98 arrivals. Just over 3%.
UK boss of Wizz Air urges Nats CEO to consider resigning
The UK boss of Wizz Air has urged Martin Rolfe to consider resigning over the repeated technical failures at National Air Traffic Services.
Yvonne Moynihan, the managing director of Wizz Air UK, said Wizz Air had 24 cancellations on Tuesday and more than 21 flights had long delays, so over 10,000 passengers coming in and out of London were disrupted at the Hungarian budget carrier alone.
“It’s completely unacceptable that the travelling public has to pay for this,” told BBC radio 4’s Today programme.
This is now the third time that we have had an ATC [air traffic control] failure, and during the peak period as well. So major questions need to be asked. At the moment, of course, the immediate priority is getting passengers to their destinations. But the longer term question really is understanding what exactly has happened and how has this happened on three different occasions? There are serious questions about the resilience of the system.
Asked whether the Nats boss should resign, she said:
In any industry when you’ve had three failures you need to consider three strikes and you’re out. It’s certainly something that he needs to look at.
A third time and a third excuse is not enough any more. What we need to see from leadership is accountability. There are serious questions about the resilience of the system.
I think Nats and the leadership need to look deep inside themselves.
What we need to see from the leadership is accountability and reassurance that we won’t face these repeated failures.
Oil price hits $100 a barrel for first time since July
Brent crude has just hit $100 a barrel for the first time since 24 July, as military strikes in the Middle East escalate.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, jumped to $100.19 a barrel, up more than $2, and a 2.2% increase. The oil price has risen by a quarter since early last month as hopes vanish for a deal between the US and Iran to end the six-month war that began with air strikes by the US and Israel on Tehran on 28 February.
This week, attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels from Yemen have set Saudi oil facilities ablaze, in an escalation of the conflict. The attacks could threaten oil shipments via the Red Sea, an alernative route to the strait of Hormuz which has been effectively closed for months.
The boss of National Air Traffic Services, which is half-owned by the government, has insisted that the organisation has invested enough in its systems.
Martin Rolfe told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme:
Nats was actually a partial privatisation, 25 years ago, and since that point has had access to funding, we’ve invested way more than a billion [pounds], in technology over that time. Our service has consistently improved. Our safety has consistently improved from a very good base. But all of those things don’t detract from the fact that when these things happen, it is disappointing and upsetting, for which I apologise.
We are in a critical national infrastructure business where safety is our priority and it runs 24/7. It runs, you know, every single day of the year, every minute of the day, every minute of the night. It is never quiet in UK skies. Inevitably, things do go wrong in complex systems. We never want them to. We always hope they won’t, but we absolutely plan for them to and make sure we handle them properly.
When asked if they “go as wrong in other countries”, Rolfe replied:
Absolutely. In fact, I would say the UK has one of the best reputations in the world for its air traffic control service, both from a safety perspective and from a resilience perspective.
We do have one of the best systems and one of the best services in the world. and that’s consistently recognised globally.
The UK cannot have a repeat of the travel disruption seen at airports, the foreign secretary has said.
Asked about the flight chaos, Ed Miliband told BBC Breakfast:
First of all, I want to apologise to all of the passengers who have faced disruption.
This is frankly unacceptable. It was a problem at the National Air Traffic Service, but we can’t have this happen again.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, is calling in the head of the National Air Traffic Service this morning to get answers to this. Miliband added:
Frankly, we’ve got to have our airports running smoothly and properly, without those problems, and that is what the transport secretary will be asking for from the head of the National Air Traffic Service.
Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband speaks at the House of Commons in London, Britain, 8 September. Photograph: House Of Commons/Reuters
Nats boss rules out cyber attack as he apologises to passengers
The boss of National Air Traffic Services, Martin Rolfe, has ruled out a cyber attack as a cause of the flight chaos, and apologised to passengers caught up in the flight chaos caused by a system issue on Tuesday, and said he understands their frustration –- but stressed that safety comes first.
Speaking to BBC radio 4’s Today programme, he said:
I’d like to start, as you might expect, by apologising to everyone who’s been impacted by the issue that we had yesterday.
In terms of the recovery, I absolutely understand the frustration. There is nothing we hate more than delaying people, and not allowing them to get to their destination. It disrupts airports and disrupts airlines. And we absolutely take accountability and responsibility for that. That is our job. But our job is also to make sure that people stay safe. We never do this lightly.
He ruled out a cyber attack.
We will be doing a very, very thorough and full investigation. We have at this point ruled out cyber. We don’t believe it was a cyber attack.
Obviously my focus and that of the team has been on both getting our system operating back up normally, which it is now. But there’s obviously a huge tail to the disruption. And we’ll be working on that through the course of today.
And then obviously our attention will turn to exactly what’s happened, this particular incident. What I will say is I don’t believe we’ve ever seen an incident happen more than once. So this will be something different that we’ve never seen in 50 years of operation.
Rolfe insisted that Nats dealt with the issue as quickly as it could:
We had everybody on site. Everybody was in the right place. We had all the engineers in place. We had our various partners from software industries and so on, all on hand. So this was resolved as quickly as it could be, but within the limits of making sure that it all stayed safe.
In the markets, oil prices are rising towards the $100 a barrel level for the first time since July.
Brent crude has jumped 1.5% to $99.36 a barrel, as escalating attacks across the Middle East are fuelling fears over supply disruptions.
Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen launched strikes on several Saudi cities while US forces hit several Iranian oil tankers and Iran targeted a US base in Jordan and attacked ships.
There is some confusion over the situation at Heathrow airport.
Heathrow said on X this morning:
Following yesterday’s NATS technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew. Please check your flight status with your airline before travelling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be operating.
We apologise to those affected and have extra colleagues across our terminals to support passengers while we work with NATS and airline partners to restore normal operations as quickly as possible.
However, the flight tracking website Flightradar24 says 177 flights have been cancelled so far on Wednesday, nearly all at London-Heathrow.
Air traffic control boss to meet UK transport secretary as second day of flight chaos takes cancellations past 1,300
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
The boss of the air traffic control provider Nats has been summoned by the UK transport secretary, as flight chaos carried on into a second day after a system issue, with after more than 1,300 flights cancelled to and from UK airports.
National Air Traffic Services provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. Its chief executive Martin Rolfe is due to speak to Heidi Alexander, before she addresses MPs in the Commons for the second reading of the Civil Aviation Bill.
Tens of thousands of passengers have been caught up in the chaos, with more cancellations and delays expected as airlines deal with the knock-on effects at airports including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted.
According to FlightRadar, 246 flights had been cancelled at Heathrow Airport by 6am on Wednesday, while Gatwick passengers faced 33 cancellations.
Rolfe said he “always accept(s) full responsibility” when asked if he was considering his position after the incident.
He told Sky News:
I am the CEO of a piece of critical infrastructure, so it is my job to take responsibility for that.
What I absolutely take responsibility for is keeping people safe and delivering the best service we possibly can on a day like today.
You will understand my focus is entirely about how we actually resolve this issue, get things back to normal, help our airlines, our airport customers and the travelling public.
The “technical issue” at the air traffic control services provider Nats caused Britain’s third major stoppage in just over three years. Nats said on Tuesday evening:
This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.
The breakdown started at about 1pm on Tuesday and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted. By the time Nats said it had fixed its flight processing system almost four hours later, most flights scheduled to depart were yet to take off. The disruption spread to include incoming flights to much of southern England.
summary: More than 1,900 flights have been cancelled over two days following a technical system issue at National Air Traffic Services (Nats), causing widespread travel disruption across the UK. While the technical problem has been resolved, pressure is mounting on Nats boss Martin Rolfe, with the UK boss of Wizz Air suggesting he consider resigning and government officials demanding answers. Simultaneously, global oil prices surpassed $100 a barrel for the first time since July due to escalating Middle East conflicts, contributing to surging UK and European gas prices and sliding European stock markets.
key_points: Over 1,900 flights have been cancelled over two days due to an air traffic control system issue at Nats.
The UK boss of Wizz Air urged Nats CEO Martin Rolfe to consider resigning following repeated technical failures.
Brent crude oil prices surged past $100 a barrel for the first time since July amid escalating Middle East tensions.
UK and European gas prices reached multi-year highs as aggressive buying occurred ahead of winter.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander summoned the head of Nats for answers regarding the unacceptable travel disruption.

title: Oil prices rise above $100 a barrel for first time since July as Iran war escalates
author: Lauren Almeida; Mark Sweney
content:
The price of oil has risen above $100 a barrel for the first time since July as the escalating conflict in the Middle East threatens further disruption to global supplies.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose 2.1% past the milestone after tensions increased in the Gulf amid the latest tit-for-tat exchange of fire between the US and Iran.
The US military said it had “destroyed” multiple Iranian tankers, after Tehran attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles. The exchange came after Iran-backed Houthis attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia the previous night, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze.
On Tuesday the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, said the latest rise in oil prices was putting pressure on inflation and interest rates.
“The risks, I’m afraid, are on the upside,” he told MPs. “And that’s really the risks coming from energy prices.”
The oil price has jumped by a quarter since early August as hopes for a permanent resolution to the six-month-old war faded and as fighting flared again.
The climb in costs has hit UK motorists, with petrol at the pump reaching an average of 166.2p a litre on Tuesday, the highest level in four years, according to the motoring body the AA.
The AA said diesel hit an average of 187.7p, a price it last reached in May. Prices per litre of petrol have risen 4.4p since the August bank holiday, with diesel up 4.1p.
Brent is up more than 60% this year, and has risen above the $100 mark for three periods so far in 2026.
China, the world’s largest importer of crude, has increased purchases in recent days, after a hiatus that had been a factor keeping oil prices somewhat in check in the early part of the conflict.
“For the direction of crude prices, we are also monitoring Chinese crude imports as a key indicator,” said Giovanni Staunovo, a commodity analyst at UBS Global Wealth Management, in a note.
“Chinese crude imports recovered to nearly 9m barrels per day in August, up from the June low of 7.15m, but still lower compared to the [pre-conflict] February imports of 12.6m. It looks like the recovery trend could continue.”
after newsletter promotion
Oil prices have fluctuated in the six months since the start of Tehran’s block on the strait of Hormuz prompted what many feared would be the greatest energy supply disruption in history.
In the first weeks after the first US-Israeli attacks on Iran in late February, oil prices soared past $100 a barrel and analysts predicted that prices could rise to as high as $150 as flows through Hormuz came to a halt.
The oil price peaked at $126 in April during the conflict but later fell back amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price then began to climb again after a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and hostilities restarted.
Gas prices have also risen on the back of the conflict. UK natural gas prices hit the highest level in three and a half years this month.
The rise in energy prices has stoked fears around inflation and the prospect of higher interest rates this year. In the US, economists are expecting at least one interest rate rise from the Federal Reserve by the end of the year.
summary: Oil prices have risen above $100 a barrel for the first time since July due to escalating conflict between the US and Iran in the Middle East. The surging energy costs are increasing pressure on inflation and interest rates, while also driving up fuel prices for UK motorists and natural gas prices. The conflict follows Iran's block on the strait of Hormuz and recent attacks involving Iranian forces, the US military, and Iran-backed Houthis in Saudi Arabia.
key_points: Brent crude prices rose 2.1% to surpass $100 a barrel amid escalating US-Iran tensions.
Iran-backed Houthi attacks on four Saudi Arabian cities wounded over 70 people and set oil installations ablaze.
The Bank of England warned that rising energy prices are putting upward pressure on inflation and interest rates.
UK petrol prices reached a four-year high of 166.2p a litre, while diesel hit 187.7p a litre.
China has increased its crude oil purchases, with imports recovering to nearly 9 million barrels per day in August.

title: UK airport disruption: what are your rights if you have been affected?
author: Zoe Wood; Rupert Jones
content:
Airports across the UK including Manchester, Birmingham and all those in London were hit by problems at air traffic control on Tuesday.
The technical issue was announced shortly before 2pm and was resolved about three hours later. By that time, hundreds of flights had been cancelled, with knock-on disruption across Britain and at destination airports abroad likely to continue into the evening and possibly Wednesday.
Here we explain what you can expect if you have been affected.
Is your flight delayed or cancelled?
The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) website explains how long the delay has to be before you are entitled to care and assistance from your airline while you wait. The timeframe differs by flight distance. This assistance should cover food and drink and the ability to make phone calls or send emails, plus accommodation and the necessary transfers if the flight is delayed until the next day.
Many airlines will provide vouchers for you to buy food and drink, and overnight accommodation will typically take the form of a nearby hotel (unless you live nearby, in which case your airline may reimburse your costs for getting to and from home).
Sometimes airline staff are unable to arrange care and assistance for all passengers, in which case you can sort yourself out and claim the cost back later.
But don’t splash the cash – and keep receipts. The CAA says airlines may have guidelines on this, adding: “Airlines are unlikely to consider alcoholic drinks, luxury hotels or luxury meals to be reasonable.”
If your flight has been cancelled and is covered by UK law – that means one departing from an airport in the UK on any airline, or arriving at an airport in the UK on an EU or UK airline, or arriving at an airport in the EU on a UK airline – your airline must offer you the choice of another flight or a refund.
If you select an alternative flight, it is up to you whether you fly as soon as possible or at a later date.
If the delay is more than five hours you can choose not to travel and receive a refund.
I am due to fly imminently – should I still go to the airport?
If you are due to travel on Tuesday evening or Wednesday, check the latest advice from your airport or tour operator, or airline apps and airport social media feeds, for the most up-to-date information.
The air traffic control service provider Nats had advised that it would “take some time” to rectify the problem but at about 5pm it posted on social media that it had “implemented a fix and our flight system is starting to recover”. The knock on impact on flight schedules could take some time to be resolved.
Will I be entitled to compensation from the airline?
If your flight was cancelled or delayed as a result of Tuesday’s issue, you are unlikely to be owed compensation by the airline. This is because the technical issue affecting flights will be considered an extraordinary circumstance and out of the airline’s control.
Causes of disruption classed as outside an airline’s control also include severe weather and security alerts.
Anna-Marie Duthie, a travel insurance expert at the financial ratings company Defaqto, says: “Travel insurance may cover you if you cannot claim costs back from the airline, operator, or credit card but that will all depend on whether your policy includes cover for delay, travel disruption, missed connection or abandonment.”
summary: A technical issue at UK air traffic control on Tuesday caused widespread cancellations and delays across major airports like Manchester, Birmingham, and London. Although the system issue was resolved within three hours, knock-on disruptions are expected to continue. Passengers facing significant delays are entitled to care and assistance from airlines, while cancelled flights qualify for a refund or alternative travel.
key_points: A technical issue at UK air traffic control on Tuesday led to hundreds of flight cancellations and ongoing disruptions.
Airlines must provide care and assistance, such as food, drink, and accommodation, for qualifying delays, though passengers can arrange their own and claim reasonable costs back with receipts.
Passengers with cancelled flights under UK law are entitled to a refund or an alternative flight of their choice.
Passengers are unlikely to receive compensation from airlines because air traffic control technical issues are considered extraordinary circumstances outside the airline's control.

title: Warnings of more airport disruption as air traffic control recovery taking 'longer than hoped'
author: Live Reporting Edited by Caitlin Doherty
content:
![](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/128/cpsprodpb//vivo/live/images/2023/12/7/a93e9c68-70e5-4dc5-954b-2e9c6e8b0857.jpg.webp) Tara Mewawalla
Live reporter
There are warnings of further disruption at airports after hundreds of flights were cancelled and delayed due to an issue with air traffic control.
Nats - the air traffic control provider - has fixed the issue this evening, but said earlier that recovery is taking "longer than we had hoped".
Europe's busiest airline, Ryanair, earlier reported that more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed by up to eight hours, and British Airways warned of "significant knock-on" impacts.
Chief executive of Nats Martin Rolfe defends the body as "fit for purpose," but says there is a "huge backlog" of flights and passengers.
Bristol Airport said flights are now arriving and departing and London Heathrow said arrivals had been suspended for the rest of the day "to ensure safety", but departures had resumed. Both said disruption was expected to continue
Manchester Airport and East Midlands Airport both issued statements saying they expect a "full flight schedule" to operate tomorrow, though - again - disruption is expected for the rest of the day
We are pausing our live coverage - but you can read more in our news story
![Passengers at Heathrow Airport](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/9/8/b19f5ded-57fc-436b-ad3d-a5aac00d48ec.jpg.webp) Image source, PA Media
summary: Airports are facing continued disruption following a technical issue with air traffic control provider Nats. Although the technical fault has been fixed, Nats stated that the recovery is taking longer than hoped, resulting in a huge backlog of flights and passengers. Major airlines like Ryanair and British Airways reported significant delays and cancellations affecting tens of thousands of travelers.
key_points: Nats fixed the air traffic control issue, but recovery is taking longer than expected.
Ryanair reported that over 65,000 passengers faced delays of up to eight hours.
London Heathrow suspended arrivals for the rest of the day to ensure safety, while departures resumed.
Manchester and East Midlands airports expect full flight schedules the following day despite ongoing daily disruptions.
Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe defended the body as fit for purpose despite the backlog.

title: Bank of England: Mortgages rising at fastest known rate in the G7
author: Tim Wallace
content:
![Andrew Bailey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/08/TELEMMGLPICT000500127511_17888882022530_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Andrew Bailey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/08/TELEMMGLPICT000500127511_17888882022530_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Britain’s homeowners have suffered what is thought to be the biggest increase in mortgage rates in the rich world since the war in Iran began.
Andrew Bailey, the Governor of the Bank of England, said borrowing costs had risen rapidly even as officials kept the base rate of interest on hold.
“UK mortgage rates typically are about 75 basis points, 0.75 percentage points, higher than they were at the point the conflict broke out,” Mr Bailey said.
“I think with the possible exception of Japan, though that is a little hard to map, that is the largest increase in mortgage rates in the G7. We have seen a tightening of financial conditions.
“Obviously that will affect individual families.”
A typical five-year fixed-rate mortgage now costs 5.7pc, according to Moneyfacts, up from 4.95pc before the war began.
It means a household with a £250,000 mortgage during a 25-year term faces paying around £1,565 a month if they fix today. That is £110 a month more than if they had locked in the cheaper rates available in February.
Mr Bailey said higher borrowing costs reflected the risks that the war in Iran spreads inflation throughout the economy and forced the Bank to raise interest rates. As financial markets worry about this possibility, mortgage borrowers are paying the cost.
“The risks [to inflation] are on the upside,” the Governor conceded, leading to an expensive “risk premium” in the cost of borrowing.
“The conflict is still going on. It is also causing a high level of energy prices and also quite a bit of volatility in energy prices. That volatility is feeding through to financial markets, and nearly all of that volatility you can trace back to events in the Gulf,” Mr Bailey told the Treasury select committee.
“We have got higher energy prices. They could be higher still. The Strait [of Hormuz] remains closed.”
Inflation currently stands at 2.9pc, above the Bank’s 2pc target. The nine-strong Monetary Policy Committee, chaired by Mr Bailey, meets next week to vote on interest rates.
At July’s meeting, six officials voted to hold rates at 3.75pc, while three backed a rise to 4pc.
Traders in financial markets expect another hold next week, but are pricing one increase to 4pc by the end of the year.
They are then betting as many as two more rate rises next year to take borrowing costs as high as 4.5pc by September of 2027.
summary: Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey reported that UK mortgage rates have risen at the fastest rate in the G7 since the conflict in Iran began. Borrowing costs have increased rapidly despite interest rates being held, driven by financial market fears of inflation and energy price volatility. A typical five-year fixed-rate mortgage has climbed from 4.95pc to 5.7pc, adding approximately £110 a month for a household with a £250,000 mortgage.
key_points: UK mortgage rates experienced the largest increase in the G7 since the war in Iran started, according to Andrew Bailey.
A typical five-year fixed-rate mortgage has risen to 5.7pc from 4.95pc before the conflict.
The rise in borrowing costs reflects a risk premium driven by market worries over inflation and energy price volatility linked to the Gulf.
Inflation currently stands at 2.9pc, remaining above the Bank of England's 2pc target as the Monetary Policy Committee prepares to meet.

title: All flights into Heathrow and Gatwick airport halted - live updates
author: Ruby Cline; Tom Jeffreys; Gareth Corfield; Neil Johnston
content:
![A miserable passenger at Heathrow](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/08/TELEMMGLPICT000501682435_17888877016240_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqlnoKbsnqupgsmdP1L78oDclaDlfF5Xha6GNIFIMmbLw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![A miserable passenger at Heathrow](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/09/08/TELEMMGLPICT000501682435_17888877016240_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqlnoKbsnqupgsmdP1L78oDclaDlfF5Xha6GNIFIMmbLw.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Flights have been grounded throughout Britain after an air traffic control technical failure.
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled across the country, with all arrivals into London Heathrow and Gatwick halted.
Airports including London City, Manchester, Stansted, East Midlands, Birmingham and Belfast City are also experiencing disruption.
The Telegraph understands that equipment at the headquarters of Nats, the air traffic control company, at Swanwick, near Southampton, has failed. Controllers based at the HQ are responsible for safely guiding flights across all UK airspace.
The “data processing” failure happened just after 1pm, multiple sources said.
Nats acknowledged a “technical issue” had occurred but gave no details of what had broken or why it had happened.
Later on Tuesday, Nats said its flight system was “starting to recover” after a fix was implemented.
Air traffic control: Outage recovery taking ‘longer than hoped’
National Air Traffic Services (Nats) have said recovery from today’s outage has taken “longer than hoped”.
In a post on X, the service said: “Recovery from today’s system issue has taken longer than we had hoped.
“Our system issue is now resolved, we are operating normally and working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights.”
It added: “We are truly sorry for the ongoing flight disruption. We know this is hugely frustrating and apologise unreservedly. Passengers should continue to check with their airline.”
Wheelchair-bound passenger offered no assistance
A woman assisting her wheelchair bound uncle home to Belfast said they’d been offered no assistance by Gatwick Airport.
Charlene Farrell, 39, was scheduled for the 19.00 EasyJet flight to Belfast but has been given no update beyond an updated time of 01.05 tomorrow.
She told The Telegraph: “He’s only just out of hospital so it’s awkward, not great.
“It’s inconvenient, he’s in a wheelchair and would usually be in bed at this time. We have not had very much information because our flight is not cancelled, it just says keep checking.
“I don’t think there’s much they can do. We need airport assistance but they just said stay here before security just in case you have to come back. There’s been nothing [for him], but surely they have to do something? And we’ve heard nothing about compensation.
“You have to stay positive but it’s not great. He’s stiff and sore, he’s tired.”
Gatwick pubs packed with delayed passengers
Gatwick’s South terminal Wetherspoons pub is packed with travellers consoling themselves over a pint. The neighbouring Giraffe Restaurant has a queue outside.
Catrina Sutton, 68, has had two flights returning home to Dublin cancelled at 18.20 and 21.25.
She said a fellow punter had been in a plane for Greece, and was on the tarmac for four hours before finally being sent back through customs without the offer of food or a hotel.
Ms Sutton told The Telegraph: “No one’s telling me anything. Ryanair just goes straight to voicemail, it’s scandalous.
“I’m consoling myself by having a pint, what can you do? The really bad thing about this, the really big annoyance – they will compensate you but you have to organise a hotel, organise a taxi, and keep receipts, but when you go to put them in you only get half back, no apology, no nothing, just shut up and put up with it.”
She added: “There’s two Ryanair girls at bag drop but they haven’t a clue, I rang my husband and he told me everything, rebooked my flight – there was no help from anybody here.
“Where am I going to get a hotel? Here’s going to be packed. This is the s--- people have to put up with, it’s scandalous.”
Night flight restrictions lifted to clear backlog
Flights from the major London airports will be allowed to take off and land all night long to help clear the backlog, The Telegraph understands.
A government source confirmed that usual restrictions on night-time flights at Heathrow, Gatwick and Stansted has been lifted after the Nats meltdown.
Normally, flights at Heathrow and Stansted all but cease after 11.30pm, while Gatwick has a tight quota for the noisiest aeroplanes during the hours of darkness.
Lifting the curfew is a sign of how seriously the government is taking the prospect of tens of thousands of people being stranded at British airports.
Transport Secretary: ‘Lessons will be learned’ from air traffic chaos
The Transport Secretary has thanked workers involved in solving the air traffic control outage – but has said “lessons will be learned” from the chaos.
In a post on X, the MP for Swindon South said: “Pleased Nats have fixed the issue, and huge thanks to those working to get people moving.
“It will take time to fully resume flights, so continue to check with airlines. I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job.”
London airports will not accept arrivals until 11pm
Major London airports will not start accepting new arrivals until at least 11pm.
Eurocontrol, which runs European air traffic control services, issued an update to controllers saying that Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Stansted will not be available for arriving flights until late tonight.
This raises the prospect of tens of thousands of passengers being stranded overnight at airports.
All other UK airports will be operating at a reduced rate until 1am because of the Nats outage, the air traffic control organisation added.
summary: An air traffic control technical failure at Nats caused widespread flight cancellations and disruptions across British airports, including Heathrow and Gatwick. Although the system issue has been resolved and is recovering, the outage left thousands of passengers stranded and prompted the government to temporarily lift night-flight restrictions to help clear the backlog. Transport officials have acknowledged the severe disruption and stated that lessons will be learned from the incident.
key_points: A data processing equipment failure at the Nats headquarters in Swanwick caused widespread flight groundings and disruptions across the UK.
Arrivals into London Heathrow and Gatwick were halted, with multiple other airports experiencing delays.
Nats confirmed the system issue has been resolved, though recovery has taken longer than hoped.
The government lifted night-time flight restrictions at Heathrow, Gatwick, and Stansted to help clear the massive backlog of flights.
Passengers faced long delays, communication difficulties with airlines, and a lack of airport assistance.

title: Heathrow and Gatwick among airports hit by air traffic control problems
author: Theo Leggett
content:
![Aerial view of Heathrow Airport](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/09a1/live/58e34b40-ab8f-11f1-aa04-efbf6a882854.jpg)
- Published
Flights from airports in the UK and Ireland are being heavily disrupted by a technical problem affecting the air traffic control provider Nats.
Heathrow, Gatwick, Stansted, East Midlands and Dublin are among those to warn of potential delays.
At Heathrow, departures were initially paused around lunchtime. Traffic then resumed, before facing further disruption in the afternoon. It is understood that very few flights are currently taking off.
British Airways has already cancelled a number short-haul services. The airline is prioritising long-haul departures.
Gatwick said it was currently being affected by the issue, along with other airports. Easyjet, the airport's largest carrier, confirmed it was being affected, and while the situation was fluid cancellations were to be expected.
With few aircraft able to take off, it is understood landings are being restricted, leading to some flights being prevented from departing from overseas airports.
Passengers have been advised to contact their airlines to check the status of their flights.
East Midlands has also been affected by the issue, while Manchester Airport warned that some departing flights could be delayed. Passengers have been advised to contact their airlines to check the status of their flights.
Belfast's two airports have both advised passengers to check flight information.
In a statement, Nats said it was investigating an issue in its flight processing system, which it said was causing some disruption to flight departures.
Engineers were on site, it said, and it was "working urgently to resume normal operations as quickly as possible".
The organisation apologised for the delays caused and advised passengers to check the status of their flight with their airline. Nats said it would provide updates on www.nats.aero and X.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said she was aware of the situation., and realised it would be frustrating for passengers.
Edinburgh Airport said in a post on X that the issue might affect its operations, while Dublin and Cork airports in Ireland are also experiencing delays.
British Airways said in a statement on its website that passengers should travel to the airport as normal if they have not been contacted by the airline directly. It added that the situation was "entirely out of our control".
Ryanair said affected passengers would be notified.
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple banner image.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/4080/live/7480f040-ab95-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.png)
summary: Airports across the UK and Ireland, including Heathrow and Gatwick, have experienced heavy flight disruptions due to a technical problem with the air traffic control provider Nats. Nats stated it was investigating an issue within its flight processing system and working urgently to resume normal operations. Airlines such as British Airways and Easyjet warned of delays and cancellations, with passengers advised to check their flight status before traveling.
key_points: A technical issue at air traffic control provider Nats caused widespread flight disruptions across the UK and Ireland.
Major airports including Heathrow, Gatwick, Stansted, Manchester, and Dublin warned of delays and cancellations.
Nats deployed engineers to investigate and resolve the flight processing system issue.
Airlines advised passengers to check their flight status with them before heading to the airport.

title: Investors dump British stocks amid Budget speculation
author: Tom Saunders
content:
![John Healey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501511748_17887927906530_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqA7N2CxnJWnYI3tCbVBgu9T0aesusvN1TE7a0ddd_esI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![John Healey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/07/TELEMMGLPICT000501511748_17887927906530_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqA7N2CxnJWnYI3tCbVBgu9T0aesusvN1TE7a0ddd_esI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
British investors sold £600m from UK stock funds last month amid speculation about John Healey’s first Budget.
Share funds suffered overall net outflows of £315m during August, according to data from Calastone, the global fund network, marking the fourth consecutive month of net selling.
The worst affected were UK equity funds, which experienced outflows of £601m. European funds were sold down by £145m. Investors instead turned to cash and bonds.
Bond funds attracted £407m of new capital in August, and money market funds saw net inflows of £364m.
Since June last year, investors have withdrawn more than £15bn from equity funds, according to Calastone, while money has instead flowed into money market and bond funds, which are considered less risky.
Edward Glyn, the head of global markets at Calastone, said caution about rumoured changes to tax breaks could be a factor in the selling.
Mr Glyn said: “Continuous Budget speculation is adding to that caution. If investors believe capital gains and pension tax breaks are in the firing line, some of them have a reason to act now rather than risk delay.”
The stock sell-off comes as one of the biggest pension bosses in the UK has warned about speculation before Mr Healey’s first Budget, which is scheduled for Oct 28.
Andy Briggs, the chief executive of Standard Life, said that he was concerned that rumours about changes to the rules around pensions were encouraging people to save less.
He said: “I really worry when there’s speculation on pensions every year in the Budget cycle. Pensions is a long-term business, and it needs consistency of policy and approach over multiple decades.
“People aren’t saving enough as it is, and if people think that the rules might change and the goalposts might move, that risks them saving less than they otherwise would.”
Rumours of a change to the amount of money people can take from their pensions as a tax-free lump sum contributed to roughly £10bn of pension withdrawals in last year’s Budget in November, according to data from AJ Bell. The rumoured change never materialised.
Mr Glyn, of Calastone, said another factor driving the stock market sell-off is that markets are close to record highs.
“When investors can earn a decent return without taking equity risk, there is much less pressure to chase the market,” Mr Glyn said. “They can afford to sit on the sidelines and wait for a better reason to buy.”
summary: British investors withdrew £600m from UK equity funds in August amid ongoing speculation surrounding the upcoming Budget and potential tax changes. This marked the fourth consecutive month of net outflows from share funds as investors shifted their money into safer assets like bonds and cash. Industry experts noted that the uncertainty and rumors regarding pensions and tax breaks are causing caution and potentially discouraging long-term savings.
key_points: UK equity funds experienced outflows of £601m in August, contributing to overall share fund net outflows of £315m.
Investors redirected their capital into less risky assets, with bond funds attracting £407m and money market funds seeing £364m in net inflows.
Analysts suggest that rumors regarding potential changes to capital gains and pension tax breaks in the upcoming Budget are driving the sell-off.
Standard Life chief executive Andy Briggs warned that annual Budget speculation and shifting pension rules risk discouraging people from saving enough for the long term.

title: 'JLR job cuts a cause for uncertainty and worry'
author: Andy Giddings
content:
![A large white building with the letters JLR in black writing on the side](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/dc2d/live/47e15190-aad9-11f1-aa35-df10e5ff32f4.png)
Jaguar Land Rover has been facing a number of pressures as it attempts to make strides in the electric market
- Published
News that Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) was to cut 4,000 jobs was a cause for uncertainty and stress for company workers and those in the wider supply chain, experts have said.
Prof David Bailey from the Birmingham Business School said he worried it could limit the company's ability to innovate in the future while David Roberts, chairman of Coventry-based Evtec Group, said up to 200,000 jobs could be tied to JLR.
The cuts will happen over the next two years and will mostly affect the head office in Whitley, Coventry.
But there are concerns about the impact the job cuts will have on the West Midlands' skill base.
"The danger there is, in part, if they cut for example too many workers in research and development that could affect their future ability to develop new cars," Bailey said.
"So it's a really critical phase for the company and there's going to be real concern at the firm about what's happening."
He said he understood JLR was facing a range of issues, but cutting the workforce was risky.
"When margins are squeezed, companies cut costs and investment; when investment is delayed, the UK becomes less competitive; and when competitiveness falls, future investment increasingly goes elsewhere," he said.
Bailey said the British motor industry needed government help to compete in the electric car market and it was crucial to more than jobs on the factory floor.
He said: "It anchors research and development, engineering capability, component suppliers and regional economies.
"Once those capabilities disappear, they are extremely difficult to recreate."
![A man with blonde hair and a blonde moustache smiles into the camera. He is wearing a grey pullover with a shirt underneath and a bright green lanyard. There is a green wall behind him](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/770/cpsprodpb/54d9/live/98d2ced0-aade-11f1-aa35-df10e5ff32f4.jpg)
David Roberts, the chairman of Evtec which supplies parts to Jaguar Land Rover, said it was a worrying time
Evtec supplies parts to JLR and chairman David Roberts said it was a "worrying time".
"A lot of the jobs here, if they go, they go, they leave the sector," he said.
"And these are jobs with real skills that take years to build and it's easier to lose them."
JLR has been dealing with falling sales, the consequences of a devastating cyber-attack that paralysed production last year, competition from China and rising energy prices.
At the same time, it has invested billions in an effort to reinvent itself for an electric future.
Dr Steve McCabe, a political economist from Birmingham City University, said he believed the job cuts were a strategic move.
"What JLR are trying to do is clean themselves up and make themselves more efficient in the hope that alowes them to survive," he said.
"The hope is of course that its a temporary thing," he added.
The company's reinvention is due to take another step forward when it unveils a new electric car on 6 October.
Kevin Moreley, a former managing director of the Rover Group believes it could be a pivotal moment.
He said: "I always thought that only 300 redundancies for JLR was a little optimistic given the new Jaguar launch is still unpredictable, and VW are making 100,000 workers redundant.
"4,000 will not be the end of it if the new Jaguar doesn't sell the numbers they hope."
![Rows of black and silver Land Rover cars](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/7a3e/live/10af6a80-aada-11f1-aa35-df10e5ff32f4.png)
American tariffs and a cyber attack have affected JLR sales in the last two years
There are concerns about the impact the job cuts will have on the region's skill base.
Emily Stubbs, head of policy at Greater Birmingham Chambers of Commerce, said: "We've got deep advanced manufacturing skills base here in the West Midlands.
"The government, employers, training providers, need to work together to retain that within the regional economy."
Richard Parker, Mayor of the West Midlands, said: "These are highly skilled people and I want those skills to stay here in the West Midlands."
The Combined Authority had put together a Â£500,000 support package for JLR workers who take voluntary redundancy, he said.
He said more support may become available in the future and described JLR as "hugely important to our region".
summary: Jaguar Land Rover's announced plan to cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years has caused uncertainty and stress for workers and the wider supply chain in the West Midlands. Experts warn that the cuts, particularly in research and development, could limit the company's future innovation and risk regional manufacturing skills. JLR has faced pressures including falling sales, a cyber-attack, Chinese competition, rising energy costs, and the expensive transition to the electric vehicle market.
key_points: JLR plans to cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years, mostly affecting its head office in Whitley, Coventry.
Experts warn that reducing research and development staff could hinder the company's ability to innovate and develop new cars.
Up to 200,000 jobs in the wider supply chain and regional economy could be tied to JLR.
JLR has been dealing with falling sales, the impact of a cyber-attack, competition from China, and rising energy prices while investing in electric vehicles.
Local leaders and the West Midlands Combined Authority are working to retain skilled workers and provide support packages for those affected.

title: JLR announces 4,000 job cuts as EV blitz begins | Auto Express
author: Tom Jervis
content:
JLR announces 4,000 job cuts as EV blitz begins
After a tough couple of years, JLR has announced thousands of job cuts – mainly at its head office
![Range Rover Electric - front action](https://media.autoexpress.co.uk/image/private/s--GRtu8YUH--/f_auto,t_primary-image-mobile@1/v1752500322/autoexpress/2025/07/Range%20Rover%20Electric%202025-10.jpg)
The Government is set to meet with the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover this week as the British automotive giant has announced a voluntary redundancy programme as part of what’s confirmed to be around 4,000 job cuts.
In a statement, JLR’s chief executive, PB Balaji, said: “The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty.
“As part of this transformation, we will reduce our global workforce by around 4,000 roles over the next two years. We recognise this will be difficult news for colleagues affected, and are committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect.”
It’s understood that the vast majority of the redundancies will be for ‘white collar’ positions at the firm’s head office in Whitley, Coventry. Aiming to save around £1.7billion in business costs over the next two years, JLR says it’s launched a voluntary redundancy scheme “offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business” until early October.
Business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, told the BBC over the weekend that he plans to meet with JLR bosses to discuss means to “mitigate any job losses”, and although future Government investment in the brand is potentially on the table, he ruled out “bailing people out”.
“A company the size of JLR, which is a huge British success story, at various times in its business cycle, the number of, directly, people it employs will change,” Reynolds explained. “If this is about making sure over time that the workforce is right to make the business as competitive as possible, that's the conversation we need to have.”
It’s been an incredibly tough period for Jaguar Land Rover, which posted a £244million loss for the 2025/26 financial year, down from a £1.8billion post-tax profit the year prior. The firm has cited several reasons for this, including hefty tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump that made exporting to the firm’s biggest market significantly more expensive.
As well as the controversial relaunch of the Jaguar brand and rising operational costs, JLR has also had to contend with a huge cyber attack. This time last year, the firm was hit by a ransomware demand which saw the firm’s production lines grind to a halt for five weeks at a cost to the UK economy of £1.9billion.
JLR is far from the only automotive giant making job cuts in recent months and years. Earlier in September, Volkswagen announced that it would shed 100,000 positions globally by 2030 in a company-wide restructuring that could also see the phase-out of the SEAT brand. This time last year, Lotus announced that it would cut almost half of its 1,300-strong workforce in Hethel, Norfolk, while in 2024, Ford also announced it would axe 4,000 jobs – 800 in the UK – by 2027.
This could well be a case of it always being darkest before the dawn, however, because JLR has just begun its own electric car blitz, beginning with the new Range Rover Electric. This will be followed by the smaller Range Rover Sport Electric, swoopy Range Rover GT and, of course, the Jaguar Type 01 which will finally be fully unveiled later this year.
Get the latest car news in your inbox, for FREE! Sign up to the Auto Express email newsletter...
summary: Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has announced plans to cut around 4,000 jobs globally over the next two years, primarily affecting white-collar positions at its head office. The restructuring aims to save £1.7 billion amid financial challenges, including a £244 million loss for the 2025/26 financial year. Despite these difficulties and a recent cyber attack, JLR is launching its electric vehicle blitz, starting with the new Range Rover Electric.
key_points: JLR is reducing its global workforce by approximately 4,000 roles over the next two years, mainly at its Whitley head office.
The company launched a voluntary redundancy scheme running until early October to help save £1.7 billion in business costs.
JLR reported a £244 million loss for the 2025/26 financial year following previous profits, impacted by US tariffs, operational costs, and a major cyber attack.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds plans to meet with JLR bosses to discuss mitigating job losses without a bailout.
The job cuts coincide with JLR's new electric vehicle blitz, which includes the Range Rover Electric and upcoming models.

title: Flight recorders recovered from 'devastating' Amazon cargo plane crash
author: Jessica Rawnsley
content:
Homendy: 'In the van were seven persons'
- Published
Investigators have recovered the flight recorders from the Amazon cargo plane that crashed at Miami International Airport, but the priority remains the recovery of victims, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has said.
Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air, overshot the runway shortly before 14:00 local time (19:00 BST) on Sunday.
The plane hit two vehicles, including a white van carrying seven people within the airport perimeter, and a Toyota with three passengers.
NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said it was too early to draw conclusions about what caused the crash, with investigators still in the "fact finding stage".
Speaking at a press conference at Miami International Airport on Monday, Homendy said the aircraft had two crew members on board and was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on its third flight of the day.
The plane struck navigational aids and equipment after overrunning the runway, before hitting a white Ford van owned by a contract cleaning company.
![Tesla cars parked in a lot next to where a crashed Amazon Prime Air cargo plane came to rest](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/c84c/live/fc526aa0-ab02-11f1-93bd-5b304745dac3.jpg)
It then travelled through a perimeter fence and collided with a Toyota Corolla, coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.
Homendy described the crash scene as "devastating", with debris from the aircraft, vehicles and airport fencing scattered across the area.
"It's hard to see, and I'm sure very difficult for the first responders as well," she said.
She said recovering victims' bodies was the current priority, adding: "The investigation and access to the aircraft, as well as evidence, can wait."
The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered and are being sent to NTSB headquarters for evaluation.
Homendy said investigators could not yet say anything substantive about the cause of the crash as they were still collecting evidence at the scene.
Investigators will examine the flight history, crew experience and training, radar data, and aircraft performance. Separate teams will look at the plane's systems and engines, while a meteorologist will assess the weather conditions at the time of landing.
The NTSB will also examine whether the runway should have had an engineered materials arresting system (EMAS), which is designed to slow and stop aircraft that overrun a runway. Homendy said this would be a "key" part of the investigation.
Earlier analysis by BBC Verify found there was an active thunderstorm near the airport shortly before the crash, with winds gusting up to 26 knots.
The NTSB has appealed for members of the public to share photographs or videos that could aid the investigation.
Homendy said the agency would make safety recommendations at the end of its investigation. "That's why we're here - to prevent the next tragedy," she said.
"Our recommendations must be implemented, or we'll be here again."
Two of the four runways at the airport remained closed following the crash. Passengers have been warned to expect further disruption after Sunday's cancellations affected the arrival of aircraft and flight crews.
The crash happened during the Labor Day holiday weekend, one of the busiest travel periods in the US.
Amazon said it was "heartbroken" by the loss of life and that it was working closely with authorities.
21 Air, the company operating the aircraft, expressed its condolences and said it was co-operating with the investigation.
summary: Investigators have recovered the flight recorders from an Amazon cargo plane that crashed after overrunning the runway at Miami International Airport, resulting in five deaths and five serious injuries. The Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air and arriving from San Juan, struck two vehicles, including a van and a Toyota, within the airport perimeter. The National Transportation Safety Board stated that the current priority is recovering victims and that it is too early to determine the cause of the crash.
key_points: Five people were killed and five others seriously injured in the crash.
The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered for evaluation.
The aircraft overshot the runway and collided with two vehicles inside the airport perimeter.
The NTSB is investigating various factors, including weather conditions, crew experience, and whether an engineered materials arresting system should have been present.

title: Next overturns equal pay ruling that raised basic wages for shop staff
author: Julia Kollewe
content:
The UK retailer Next has overturned a 2024 court ruling forcing it to pay its shop staff the same higher basic pay rates as its warehouse workers under equal pay rules.
The chain, led by the Conservative peer Simon Wolfson, said it had “won a landmark victory in its ongoing equal pay litigation”. It has succeeded in its appeal to the employment appeal tribunal “on the key issue of basic pay”, it said.
It comes two years after 3,540 claimants won a six-year legal fight for equal pay, which the fashion and homeware retailer then appealed against. Shop workers accused Next of paying its retail sales staff – who are predominantly female – lower hourly wages than its warehouse workers, the majority of whom are male.
Since that employment tribunal ruling in Leeds, several thousand more Next staff have brought equal pay claims, bringing the total number of claimants involved in the litigation to more than 6,400. Next employs more than 20,000 store staff across 458 stores in the UK and Ireland.
Next said the appeal judgment endorsed its position that it “should not have to pay shop assistants and warehouse operatives the same amount of basic pay, in circumstances where the market and working conditions are very different”.
The retailer argued that it had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse staff because of recruitment and retention pressures, which it said did not apply to the workforce in its stores. It added: “Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense.”
The retailer said the judgment affirmed: “Employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so.”
The law firm Leigh Day, which represents Next store workers, described it as a “mixed ruling” as it rejected Next’s challenge to the tribunal’s findings that it had failed to justify lower rates of night-time pay, overtime pay and the failure to provide paid rest breaks to store workers.
Next also failed to persuade the employment appeal tribunal that lower Sunday premium payments to store workers were justified. The appeal tribunal held that the issue remains to be determined and should return to the employment tribunal.
The Next case, which covered the period from 2012 and 2023, explained women made up almost 78% of retail sales jobs, while men made up about 53% of warehouse staff. During that time, some warehouse staff were able to earn between 38p and £3.13 more an hour than retail sales workers, according to Leigh Day.
Elizabeth George, a partner at Leigh Day representing the claimants, said: “I am pleased that the employment appeal tribunal rejected Next’s arguments that its pay practices do not disadvantage women. They plainly do and the appeal tribunal firmly recognised that. I am also pleased that the tribunal upheld the findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.
“The appeal tribunal’s conclusion on basic pay is disappointing. Next pays market rates in both its stores and its warehouses in order to recruit and retain staff. The market rate is higher in the predominantly male warehouse labour market, even though the work carried out in stores has already been found to be equal work.
after newsletter promotion
“While the store staff and their legal team welcome many aspects of this appeal judgment, we respectfully disagree with this approach to justification. We remain confident in our clients’ position and intend to appeal.”
Next had argued that the equal pay ruling created a threat to the viability of many of its stores, and that it put retailers operating their own warehouses at a “material disadvantage” to rivals that contract out their warehouse operations.
The original employment tribunal and the appeal tribunal found that there was no direct discrimination. The employment tribunal found: “It was all about cost. Gender did not enter into the equation” when Next set pay rates.
Next said it had won the vast majority of the terms challenged in the equal pay litigation, including bonus pay to warehouse staff previously, and now basic pay. It intends to seek permission to appeal in relation to other terms.
“This judgment has come at the right time, the UK economy desperately needs jobs and the loss of this appeal would have represented a hammer blow to retail employment in the UK,” the company said.
summary: UK retailer Next successfully overturned a 2024 employment tribunal ruling that required the company to pay its predominantly female shop staff the same basic pay rates as its predominantly male warehouse workers. The employment appeal tribunal agreed with Next that differing market rates and working conditions justify the pay differences. However, the ruling was described as mixed, as the tribunal upheld findings against Next regarding lower night-time pay, overtime pay, and paid rest breaks for store workers.
key_points: Next won an appeal at the employment appeal tribunal regarding the key issue of basic pay.
The original 2024 ruling had favored thousands of claimants arguing that retail sales staff were paid lower hourly wages than warehouse workers.
Next argued that higher warehouse pay was necessary due to market recruitment and retention pressures.
Law firm Leigh Day, representing the workers, called it a mixed ruling and stated they intend to appeal the basic pay decision.
The appeal tribunal rejected Next's challenge regarding lower night-time pay, overtime pay, and paid rest breaks for store workers.

title: Jaguar Land Rover: Why the carmaker has decided change is needed
author: Theo Leggett
content:
![A line of Range Rovers](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/2bb7/live/3ca652b0-aabd-11f1-b960-379ca4827622.jpg)
- Published
Jaguar Land Rover's decision to shed 4,000 jobs comes after the carmaker has travelled down a very rough road.
The company has seen sales fall in all of its major markets and has been dealing with the consequences of a devastating cyber-attack that paralysed production last year.
At the same time, it has invested billions in an effort to reinvent itself for an electric future, in which it is likely to face intense competition from aggressively expanding Chinese brands.
Executives have now decided a major overhaul is needed.
One of the main concerns for JLR is China. Not so long ago, it was seen as a land of opportunity for western carmakers, where the rapidly expanding middle classes seemed to have an inexhaustible appetite for upmarket foreign-badged vehicles.
JLR, along with other European brands such as BMW, Audi and Mercedes Benz, was all too willing to meet that demand, at a time when the European market was extremely crowded and growth hard to find.
Today, things are very different. The past decade has seen rapid growth among domestic Chinese carmakers, firmly backed by their government, which has been determined to make the country a leading player in electric vehicles.
This has created an environment of intense competition, in which local manufacturers have rapidly raised the bar in terms of technology and development speed.
That, combined with a slowdown in the Chinese economy and a reduction in sales overall, has made China a much more difficult market for European brands.
JLR's Chinese sales fell from a high water mark of 146,000 cars in 2017 to just 62,400 in the last financial year. At the same time, competition and a new luxury car tax have hit profit margins.
All of this has resulted in a sharp fall in revenues from the region. JLR is not alone in this; the Volkswagen Group, for example, has also seen its earnings in China pummelled â a major factor in its decision to axe 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade.
The state of the Chinese market has had another consequence for European carmakers, including JLR. Faced with cut-throat competition at home, Chinese firms such as BYD and Chery have been flexing their muscles abroad.
They have been rapidly gaining market share in the UK and Europe â with Chery's Jaecoo 7, nicknamed the 'Temu Range Rover' the third best-selling car in this country over the first half of the year.
Analysts say traditional brands will face an uphill struggle to compete with new rivals, who can sell cars more cheaply and develop them more quickly.
The US is also a major market for JLR. In the year to the end of March 2025 it sold more than 120,000 cars there. The following year, that figure had fallen to just under 100,000.
Part of that could be attributed to the impact of the cyber attack, which heavily disrupted production in late 2025. It affected JLR worldwide and cost the company Â£1.9bn.
But sales and profits were also hit by the introduction of import tariffs by the US, and subsequent uncertainty over the levels of those tariffs. As automotive analyst Matthias Schmidt puts it, the company is "seeing a head-on hit each time a Land Rover rolls off a ship onto US soil".
JLR is now planning a partnership with Stellantis to build new Defender-badged vehicles in the US. These cars, which would be developed specifically for the US market, would not attract tariffs.
Then, there are energy costs, which affect JLR and its rivals. Carmakers and their suppliers are industrial businesses that use copious amounts of energy, and prices in the UK are among the highest in Europe.
According to Prof David Bailey of Birmingham Business School, "electricity is a fundamental input into modern industrial production".
"If producing a car in Britain is structurally more expensive because the energy required to manufacture it is substantially more expensive, Britain is effectively imposing a competitiveness tax on its own industry."
All of these challenges have come at a time when JLR has been ploughing money into the development of a new generation of electric vehicles. The first fruits of the Â£15bn programme were seen last week, with the official unveiling of the first electric Range Rover.
That was relatively uncontroversial â but so far the relaunch of Jaguar as an all-electric brand has been anything but. In late 2024 the company drove straight into the heart of the culture wars with a polarising advertising campaign that some saw as excessively "woke". The first actual car is due to make its public bow on 6 October â and it will be a pivotal moment for the company.
It is easy to see why JLR's chief executive PJ Balaji feels action is necessary to trim costs and make the company leaner. That is bad news for employees, with thousands of jobs to go and compulsory redundancies not being ruled out.
But the carmaker's network of suppliers are also being squeezed.
"JLR has been pushing hard for cost savings", one leading supplier told the BBC. "But those suppliers are also facing high energy costs and high employment costsâ¦there's huge anxiety right now."
summary: Jaguar Land Rover is undergoing a major overhaul, including the shedding of 4,000 jobs, following falling sales across major markets, a debilitating cyber-attack, and heavy investments in electric vehicles. The carmaker has faced intense competition from rapidly expanding domestic Chinese brands, declining revenues in China and the US, and high domestic energy costs in the UK. Executives are implementing cost-saving measures and seeking partnerships, such as building US-specific vehicles with Stellantis, to navigate these severe financial challenges.
key_points: JLR is planning to cut 4,000 jobs amidst a broader company overhaul to reduce costs and trim operations.
Sales in China dropped from 146,000 cars in 2017 to 62,400 in the last financial year due to intense local competition, a slowing economy, and a new luxury car tax.
US sales fell from over 120,000 cars to just under 100,000, impacted by import tariffs, tariff uncertainty, and a £1.9bn cyber-attack that disrupted production.
UK energy prices remain among the highest in Europe, creating structural cost disadvantages for industrial manufacturers like JLR.
JLR has invested heavily in an electric vehicle transition, marked by a £15bn programme that recently introduced the first electric Range Rover and an upcoming electric Jaguar relaunch.

title: UK house prices fall for first time since 2023, led by London and south-east
author: Lauren Almeida
content:
UK house prices have fallen for the first time in almost three years, as prospective buyers were squeezed by higher mortgage rates, geopolitical uncertainty and stretched affordability.
Prices have dropped by 0.4% compared with a year ago, the first year-on-year decrease since November 2023, according to the lender Lloyds. That came in below expectations of a 0.2% annual rise, according to a poll of economists by Reuters.
The average property cost £298,468 in August, falling 0.2% or £685 compared with July, the bank’s monthly index found.
Andrew Asaam, a director at Lloyds, said the UK’s housing market was “subdued” in the face of higher inflation, borrowing costs and geopolitical tensions.
“What we’re not seeing is a rush of homeowners cutting prices,” he said. “But more are choosing to sit tight, with sellers reluctant to accept offers they feel are too low, while some buyers are waiting to see how conditions develop.”
He added that the market is forecast to “remain fairly subdued in the months ahead, but this will likely only have a limited impact on house prices”.
Tensions in the Middle East have stoked fears around inflation this year, feeding expectations of further interest rate rises.
Property buyers looking for a mortgage deal have faced months of heightened volatility, with the average rate for a two-year fixed residential mortgage at 5.6% on Friday, according to the market tracker Moneyfacts, while the average five-year deal was 5.66%. Both were below 5% at the start of the year.
Mortgage approvals were at their lowest level since the start of 2024, Lloyds said.
Jeremy Leaf, an estate agent in north London, said the slowdown in the market reflected a “standoff” between nervous buyers and sellers who believe they have already reduced their prices by as much as they can.
“There is more movement when sellers set realistic asking prices from the outset and appreciate after a period of marketing that even a cheeky offer is worth considering,” he said.
“Activity is picking up now that the main holiday season is over, which is helping to improve confidence a little.”
after newsletter promotion
