summary: Increasingly unstable weather systems and rising temperatures driven by climate change threaten to cause more flight disruptions, delays, and cancellations for airlines and passengers. While summer storms in June already caused significant chaos at London airports, experts warn that future severe weather could lead to widespread groundings, heavier fuel costs, and risks from phenomena like clear-air turbulence and rising sea levels. However, industry insiders hold differing views on the severity of these worst-case scenarios, noting that new technologies and mitigation strategies could help manage future risks.
key_points: Climate change is increasing atmospheric moisture and instability, which can lead to more impactful and violent thunderstorms.
Severe weather shrinks available airspace, forcing air traffic controllers to reroute flights and manage potential airport gridlocks.
Experts warn that intense storms could eventually force simultaneous diversions across multiple London airports, raising serious fuel and safety concerns.
Clear-air turbulence, which is invisible and harder to avoid, has increased significantly on busy routes like the North Atlantic due to a warming climate.
Rising sea levels pose a severe long-term threat to coastal airports, heightening the risk of runway flooding similar to past incidents in New York and Dubai.

title: Thousands of jobs to be cut at Jaguar Land Rover after slump in profits
author: Angus Thomson
content:
Thousands of workers at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) will be offered redundancies after Britain’s largest car manufacturer had its revenues slashed by falling sales, a cyber-attack and Donald Trump’s tariffs.
JLR informed workers and their union on Saturday that the company would be opening a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management team members, the BBC and Sunday Times reported.
As many as 4,000 jobs would be cut over two years, the Times reported. JLR told the BBC it was yet to confirm the number but the company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata Motors, needed to save about £1.7bn over the next two years.
Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, told the BBC she and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would meet JLR’s chief executive, PB Balaji, next week, after a weekend of intensive talks to mitigate job losses.
About 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK. Most of them work at 14 plants across the West Midlands, where the company is one of the region’s largest employers.
The job cuts will be unwelcome news for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who has pledged to “safeguard sovereign manufacturing” and reindustrialise Britain.
Under his predecessor, Keir Starmer, Labour said it would underwrite a £1.5bn loan guarantee to JLR after it halted production for several weeks last year in response to a cyber-attack.
The attack led to a 27% drop in overall production and cost the company about £200m. It was one of several factors contributing to JLR posting a profit before tax of just £14m – down from £2.5bn the year before.
Tariffs on vehicles imported into the US – which Trump raised to 25% before agreeing a deal for 10% for the UK – also caused turmoil for the carmaker, which is attempting to push more luxury cars to the US market. This contributed to the company’s retail and wholesale volumes – sales via dealerships – falling by about 70,000 and 90,000 respectively.
“These challenges arrived with the global automotive industry already under continued pressure from cost inflation, slower-than-expected uptake of electric vehicles, and the deterioration of market conditions in China,” Balaji said in the company’s annual report published in May.
The carmaker this week launched its first electric Range Rover in an effort to appeal to climate-conscious fans of the luxury SUV – at a starting price of £154,070.
summary: Jaguar Land Rover is opening a voluntary redundancy programme that could cut up to 4,000 jobs over two years as the company attempts to save £1.7bn. The job cuts follow a severe slump in profits down to £14m, caused by falling sales, a cyber-attack, and US tariffs. Union leaders and government officials are scheduled to meet with JLR's chief executive to discuss mitigating the job losses.
key_points: JLR is offering voluntary redundancies to salaried and management team members.
The cuts aim to save about £1.7bn over the next two years following a profit drop to £14m.
Challenges include a cyber-attack, US vehicle tariffs, cost inflation, and slower electric vehicle uptake.
Union officials and the business secretary are set to meet JLR's chief executive to discuss the job losses.

title: London Paddington fire causes rail chaos as Heathrow trains cancelled
author: Guardian staff reporter
content:
Hundreds of passengers were evacuated from trains and services to Heathrow airport were cancelled after a fire near tracks in the London Paddington area caused major disruptions to London’s rail network.
The fire caused an electricity supply failure which left all lines between Paddington and the airport blocked, National Rail said on Saturday afternoon.
Photos on social media showed large plumes of smoke rising from the Paddington area.
London fire brigade was called to the grass fire near Scrubs Lane, North Kensington, just after 4pm on Saturday, with six fire engines and 40 crew tackling the blaze.
Fire crews were also called upon to help evacuate 380 passengers left stranded on an Elizabeth line train.
The Elizabeth line was suspended between Paddington and Heathrow Terminals 4 and 5, and between Paddington and Reading, while the line to Abbey Wood also experienced severe delays.
Passengers travelling to the airport were advised to use the Piccadilly line, although that line also experienced severe delays between Heathrow and Acton Town. There were minor delays along the rest of the line due to an earlier trespasser at Hammersmith, TfL said.
Heathrow airport advised passengers to leave extra time for their journeys.
Great Western Railway (GWR) services to Reading were cancelled, and disruptions were expected until the end of the day.
summary: A grass fire near tracks in the London Paddington area caused a major rail disruption and electricity supply failure on Saturday afternoon. Hundreds of passengers were evacuated from stranded trains, and services to Heathrow Airport were cancelled or heavily delayed. Fire crews responded with six engines and 40 personnel to tackle the blaze near Scrubs Lane.
key_points: A grass fire near Scrubs Lane in North Kensington prompted the evacuation of 380 passengers from an Elizabeth line train.
The fire caused an electricity supply failure that blocked all lines between London Paddington and Heathrow Airport.
Elizabeth line, Great Western Railway, and Piccadilly line services experienced major cancellations and severe delays.
Heathrow Airport advised passengers to allow extra time for their journeys due to the disruptions.

title: Major disruption as grass fire hits Heathrow train links
author: Ewan Somerville
content:
![Crowds fill the concourse of London Paddington station with the departure boards blank showing no services.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/de80/live/5ff9eda0-a962-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Departure boards appeared to have gone blank at Paddington as train services were cut into Saturday evening
- Published
Trains to and from Heathrow Airport have been halted after a trackside grass fire caused delays and cancellations.
National Rail said "major disruption" was expected until the end of Saturday following the incident which began shortly after 16:00 BST.
A statement said all lines were blocked between London Paddington station and Heathrow's terminals, as well as Reading, due to "a failure of the electricity supply caused by a fire next to the track".
It comes hours after a separate grass fire on Heathrow's airfield shut a runway earlier on Saturday.
Pictures on social media showed crowds of stranded passengers at Paddington, one of London's main rail hubs.
London Fire Brigade said six fire engines and around 40 crew members were tackling the blaze near Scrubs Lane, North Kensington.
Great Western Railway, external cancelled its services to Reading and no Elizabeth line or Heathrow Express services were running between Paddington and Heathrow on Saturday night.
The airport advised passengers to leave extra time for their journeys, adding that the Piccadilly line, which runs services to the airport, also has delays.
Earlier on Saturday, Heathrow's southern runway was closed while crews tackled a grass fire on the airfield.
It caused some disruption with at least two flights diverted elsewhere. Heathrow apologised for any disruption and said the fire was extinguished quickly.
That comes weeks after another grass fire near Heathrow's southern runway which forced 18 flights to divert and destroyed a large area of grassland.
While weather has cooled across much of the UK in recent days following record-breaking heat over the summer, fire crews have still been warning of wildfire risks.
The Met Office's Fire Severity Index, external shows that if a wildfire was to occur, it would have a "high" fire severity in most of south-east England and some of the Midlands.
The fire severity is "exceptional", the highest level on the index, in some parts of London including Heathrow, as well as on the Essex and Suffolk coasts.
- ![Part suspended service information board at station](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/f886/live/d55e47c0-94a0-11f1-b485-c780285c5cc1.jpg)
  - Published31 July
 ![A composite of a Heathrow fire and rescue truck on a runway and Edward Killiwick](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a427/live/adfea090-8cde-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
- ![Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/f13c/live/382364b0-679f-11f0-8979-21e9e3d3b0da.png)
- ![A woman uses an umbrella to shelter from the sun, surrounded by several other people, in a sun-drenched Trafalgar Square in London](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/84de/live/4bd31cb0-a51c-11f1-89d5-dd5482a9fcc2.jpg)
summary: A trackside grass fire near Scrubs Lane caused major disruptions and electricity supply failures, halting train services between London Paddington, Heathrow Airport, and Reading. National Rail warned that the disruptions would last until the end of Saturday, leaving crowds of passengers stranded. This incident followed an earlier grass fire on Heathrow's airfield that temporarily closed a runway and forced flight diversions.
key_points: Trains between London Paddington, Heathrow Airport, and Reading were halted due to an electricity supply failure caused by a trackside grass fire.
Major disruption was expected to continue through the end of Saturday, affecting Great Western Railway, Elizabeth line, and Heathrow Express services.
London Fire Brigade deployed six fire engines and about 40 crew members to tackle the blaze near Scrubs Lane in North Kensington.
A separate grass fire earlier on Saturday closed Heathrow's southern runway and led to flight diversions.
The Met Office's Fire Severity Index rated wildfire risk as exceptional in parts of London, including Heathrow.

title: ‘The chancellor is in a bind’: is No 11 at odds with Burnham’s big vision?
author: Pippa Crerar; Heather Stewart; Jessica Elgot
content:
Until now, Andy Burnham has been a lucky prime minister. In office for just over six weeks, no major domestic crisis derailed his plans over the summer, Reform has been on the back foot, and he arrived back at Westminster with his personal approval ratings soaring and optimism undampened.
But underneath the sense of relief that many Labour MPs are feeling that their high-stakes gamble of ousting Keir Starmer appears – for now – to have paid off, there is an unease that Burnham’s premiership is yet to make contact with economic reality.
In their early weeks in office, his team were able to point to some inherited green shoots: below-forecast inflation figures, sustained growth, signs that sluggish productivity could be starting to turn around. All despite the economic turmoil unleashed by the Iran conflict.
This week, all that changed. With the end of summer recess came a global bond sell-off amid anxiety over oil prices, sticky inflation and pressure to ramp up defence spending, which pushed government borrowing costs to their highest since the 2008 financial crash.
It makes the backdrop to John Healey’s first budget as chancellor a difficult one. Economists reckon about half of the £24bn fiscal breathing space his predecessor Rachel Reeves had built up at her spring forecast has since been wiped out by higher inflation and interest rates, severely limiting Healey’s room for manoeuvre.
Among the more experienced hands in government, there is a firm view that the new administration cannot return to the days of slim headroom given Reeves’s experience last year, which led to more brutal proposed welfare cuts and ultimately a backbench rebellion last summer.
Healey has just returned from the G20 finance ministers’ meeting in North Carolina and is acutely conscious of factors beyond his control that will hit the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, including the rising cost of oil after bombing resumed in Iran.
![Andy Burnham and John Healey in July.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ec8f1fe5942071c9288c63ad712f8a6d4f58be38/1446_0_3924_3139/master/3924.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
It is little surprise, then, that he has repeatedly stressed that fiscal responsibility is the “bedrock” of his approach and he will stick to Reeves’s fiscal rules.
But his cautious tone jars uncomfortably with the prime minister’s large – and costly – policy vision: more public control of utilities, reform of the broken social care system and a mass social home building programme.
“[Healey] is in a bind,” one Treasury source said. “His instinct is to keep things steady, especially while the OBR does its snapshot, but that’s not Andy’s gameplan for his first week back.”
Indeed, Downing Street has been eager to ensure Burnham’s vision stays front and centre. In a mammoth three-and-a-half-hour Commons session on Tuesday, he repeatedly promised to deliver the “much more substantial change” the country was crying out for.
Among Burnham’s closest allies, there have been some mutterings that Healey could, like chancellors before him, be in danger of being “captured” by the Treasury and its more orthodox arguments. “John did not exactly show in the Ministry of Defence that he was good at questioning internal departmental wisdom and pressures,” one government aide said.
The friction between the two operations burst into the open last week when Healey suggested in a television interview that Burnham was running a “continuity” government.
No 10 insiders pushed back hard. “Nobody listening to Andy and his plans for growth could think he is just about continuity,” said one senior figure. “He’s going to change things.”
A timely report that suggests Manchester’s economic success – one of Burnham’s biggest legacies – could be replicated across England to unlock untapped growth potential of up to £80bn is released this weekend.
Mandala Partners, a global economic research consultancy that was led by Nick Williams – a former Downing Street economic adviser who is now working for the first secretary, Louise Haigh – found that housing, transport and health devolution would be crucial to achieving the prime minister’s aim of “growth in every postcode”.
Of these, the impact of following Manchester’s housing investment model is most striking. The report found that an £8.5bn programme of revolving public risk capital across mayoral strategic authorities could unlock almost 100,000 additional homes, crowd in more than £20bn of private investment and support more than 70,000 jobs.
after newsletter promotion
While not commissioned by No 10, Mandala’s study nevertheless bolsters Burnham’s central growth argument that learning from the success of Manchester’s devolution model could deliver far-reaching economic benefits and release the country from its low-growth chokehold.
The chancellor has privately acknowledged there is room for modest additional borrowing to fund investment given Reeves’s rule change in 2024, which allowed the Treasury to offset financial assets against government debt.
However, there is little sense of a radical new perspective emerging from the new regime at No 11. On Monday, Healey will give a speech on the government’s mission for growth, which is expected to stress the importance of devolution and public investment – both themes Reeves repeatedly returned to.
The chancellor will emphasise the need to give the private sector the confidence to invest – raising doubts about whether he is likely to go ahead with one of the big revenue raisers that progressive economists and the TUC have called for: a windfall tax on banks.
Treasury sources have declined to say whether Healey will stick to Reeves’s intention of holding only one major “fiscal event” each year, with the spring forecast a much more low-key affair. That would leave open the possibility of using his 28 October statement to fund the gaps in the defence investment plan and make more progress on tax devolution, while leaving the weightier tax and spending decisions until the spring.
Labour MPs are anxious for change as quickly as the government can deliver it. They applaud Burnham’s ambition and the sense of hope he fosters but worry that the economic realities will drag him down.
Tan Dhesi, the Labour chair of the Commons defence committee, summed up the mood when he suggested at PMQs that “vibes alone just will not be enough”. While he was referring to military spending, the sentiment is shared across the backbenches.
Burnham has repeatedly said he will be relentless in fulfilling his priorities. But some of his MPs are already worried that his promise to repair the crumbling state and offer “breathing space” on the cost of living could be hard to reconcile with promises of fiscal responsibility.
Downing Street sources argue, however, that it is only by improving infrastructure and devolving power that the British economy can grow as fast as Manchester’s. They cite Burnham’s visit to Cornwall this summer, where businesses told him it was taking them a year to connect to the grid.
Healey’s economic instincts are less clear. When asked what would be the main difference between him and his instinctively prudent predecessor, one adviser said: “To be honest, I think he will actually be more cautious.”
Despite his apparent wariness, government aides insist the chancellor is fully onboard with Burnham’s vision. One said: “There will always be tensions between the different parts of government, but John is aligned with Andy’s agenda. And he knows who is boss.”
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has returned to Westminster with high approval ratings and an ambitious agenda for public control and social housing. However, Chancellor John Healey faces a tightening fiscal environment due to rising global bond yields, oil prices, and inflation, which has halved the government's previous fiscal breathing space. This tension has sparked friction between Downing Street and No 11 over how to balance fiscal caution with the prime minister's costly growth vision.
key_points: Prime Minister Andy Burnham's high approval ratings and ambitious reform agenda contrast with a deteriorating economic backdrop for the new administration.
Chancellor John Healey faces shrinking fiscal headroom following a global bond sell-off and rising oil prices stemming from the conflict in Iran.
Healey's cautious, fiscally responsible approach has sparked friction with Downing Street's desire for rapid, substantial change.
A new report suggests that replicating Manchester's devolution model for housing, transport, and health could unlock significant economic growth.
Labour MPs and government insiders remain concerned that economic realities and Treasury caution may hinder Burnham's wide-ranging policy promises.

title: Jaguar Land Rover confirms plans for voluntary job cuts
author: Richard Price
content:
![The silver leaping Jaguar emblem is on a grey pillar sign outside one of its factories with the green, oval Land Rover badge below.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/ee01/live/b5506920-8c0f-11f1-b2ab-0dd01740f9f6.jpg)
JLR has its worldwide headquarters in Coventry
- Published
Car manufacturer Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.
The firm said it needed to save about Â£1.7bn over the next two years as it seeks to adapt to "evolving global market conditions".
It was reported by The Times on Saturday that as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.
The firm told the BBC it had not confirmed the numbers. It said the decision to cut jobs was to help "simplify" the organisation as well as "improve efficiency and build greater resilience".
"Today, we informed our colleagues, and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business," a spokesperson said.
"We will share further information with our colleagues first."
Unite general secretary. Sharon Graham. said the union had been warning about a "perfect storm" hanging over the automotive industry for some time.
"Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said.
She added there had been "intensive" discussions over the weekend about mitigating jobs losses adding that she and Business Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would be meeting JLR's chief executive, PB Balaji, next week.
"This is an incredibly worrying and stressful time for JLR workers," said Unite national officer, Des Quinn. "Unite is working round the clock to deliver the best possible outcome."
![The exterior of Jaguar Land Rover's Wolverhampton factory. It is pictured at night, with a silhouetted person walking in front of the illuminated frontage of the building.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/70f8/live/37261730-8c0e-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
The firm said it needed to save about Â£1.7bn over the next two years
Meanwhile a government spokesperson said significant action had been taken to support the UK automotive industry by lowering electricity bills for manufacturers as well as financial support for the manufacture and sale of zero emission vehicles.
Reynolds was also understood to have spoken with West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, about supporting the business and its staff.
JLR said over the past three years, it had strengthened its brands and had prepared for production of its next generation of vehicles.
In July, the company said it expected fewer than 300 people would leave the firm under cost savings plans announced at the time.
The company has its global headquarters at Whitley, Coventry, and manufacturing sites in Solihull and Wolverhampton as well as Halewood on Merseyside.
It employs about 30,000 people in its UK operations, with approximately 10,000 people employed at plants overseas.
The cyber attack in September 2025 led to the shut down of all manufacturing at JLR for several weeks, meaning not a single vehicle rolled off its production lines.
That led to a 27% drop in overall production at the company, which is one of the West Midlands' biggest employers.
The overall cost of the cyber-attack and the subsequent loss of manufacturing was estimated to be Â£1.9bn.
In June, the firm announced it planned to cut about Â£1.7bn in costs over the coming years to help towards its recovery from the attack.
JLR had indicated at the time that it would make the savings through cuts in areas such as materials, warranty and fixed costs.
summary: Car manufacturer Jaguar Land Rover has confirmed it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management team members to save about £1.7bn over the next two years. The cuts aim to simplify the organization, improve efficiency, and build resilience in response to evolving global market conditions, tariffs, and a drop in sales. While media reports suggested up to 4,000 jobs might be lost, the firm has not confirmed this figure. Union officials and government representatives are engaging in discussions with JLR leadership to mitigate job losses and support workers.
key_points: Jaguar Land Rover confirmed the opening of a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management team members.
The firm aims to save approximately £1.7bn over the next two years to adapt to market conditions and improve efficiency.
While reports estimated up to 4,000 potential job losses, JLR has not confirmed the specific number of cuts.
Unite union officials and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds are scheduled to meet with JLR's chief executive to discuss mitigating job losses.

title: Labour tax raids make US gas cheaper than North Sea supplies
author: Matt Oliver
content:
![Offshore gas rig](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/04/TELEMMGLPICT000471699926_17885281303200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Offshore gas rig](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/04/TELEMMGLPICT000471699926_17885281303200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Labour’s tax raids have made producing North Sea gas more expensive than importing gas from the US, energy experts have warned.
The cost of drilling and delivering new gas from the UK Continental Shelf is now about 50pc higher than the cost of sending US liquefied natural gas (LNG) to Europe, according to analysis by Thunder Said Energy.
This is despite the fact the American figure includes extraction, the cost of liquefaction and shipping the gas thousands of miles across the Atlantic.
Analysts at Thunder blamed the “totally crazy” oil and gas windfall tax first imposed by the Conservatives, and then expanded under Labour, for driving up the cost of production.
This was discouraging investment and leaving the UK more dependent on imports at a time of rising geopolitical turmoil, they said.
The analysts added that if the tax burden were eased and political uncertainty reduced, the cost of North Sea production could be cut in half.
The figures will raise further questions about Labour’s approach to oil and gas at a time when Andy Burnham is under pressure to approve domestic fields including Jackdaw, which could provide significant domestic supplies and reduce the country’s reliance on imports.
According to Thunder, the long-term gas price needed to break even from North Sea developments currently stands at about $13.50 (£9.99) per thousand cubic feet (MCF) – up from $7 per thousand cubic feet previously.
By comparison, the break-even figure for producing US LNG and delivering it to Europe is about $8-$9 per MCF. This typically includes up to $3.5 for the gas itself.
It means it is currently more economical for the UK to source gas from the US than to use domestically produced supplies from the North Sea.
Seb Kennedy, the chief executive of market analysis firm Energy Flux, said the situation was “a damning indictment of UK tax policy”.
Oil and gas companies currently face a 78pc levy on their UK profits after Labour increased the windfall tax on the industry when it came to power.
The Government has also extended the levy by two years, from 2028-2030, and banned new oil and gas exploration.
Ministers have defended what they say is a “pragmatic approach” and claim the North Sea will play an important role “for decades to come”.
But Mr Kennedy said the windfall tax’s current level “only makes sense if the Government doesn’t want to produce these resources”.
He added: “Clearly there would be a much stronger investment flow if the fiscal burden was reduced.”
Only a substantial tax cut ‘would move the needle’
Norbert Ruecker, the head of economics at Julius Baer, agreed that the numbers reflected political choices.
He said Britain’s approach stood in stark contrast to Norway, where a “more stable and predictable policy environment” had helped to keep gas production “competitive on a global scale, including against US LNG”.
In the past year, oil and gas companies have blamed Labour’s tax policies for their decision to scale back investment in the North Sea.
However, the Government also faces opposition from climate campaigners who have argued that relaxing constraints on drilling will make little difference to prices and send the wrong message internationally.
Mr Kennedy said he believed there might be “some policy movement” under Mr Burnham but added: “Whether Labour has the stomach for the backlash this would generate among climate-aligned Left-leaning voters is an open question.
“It would take a substantial tax cut to move the needle on the North Sea investment calculus, and would be framed by opponents as a bung to investors while households are feeling the pinch.”
A Treasury spokesman said: “We are making sure the North Sea has a prosperous and sustained future through record investment that helps deliver the next generation of skilled jobs while growing the clean energy industries of the future.”
The windfall tax, known officially as the energy profits levy, has raised £13bn for the public purse since its introduction in 2022, the spokesman added.
The Office for Budget Responsibility has forecast that total tax paid by oil and gas firms will reach £8.3bn in the next five years.
summary: Labour's expanded windfall taxes on the oil and gas industry have made producing North Sea gas significantly more expensive than importing liquefied natural gas from the US. Analysis by Thunder Said Energy indicates that the break-even cost for new UK Continental Shelf gas is about 50 percent higher than delivering US LNG to Europe. While the Government defends its pragmatic tax approach and notes the levy has raised billions for the public purse, industry experts warn the fiscal burden discourages investment and increases import dependence.
key_points: Producing new North Sea gas is now about 50pc more expensive than importing US LNG to Europe.
Analysts blame oil and gas windfall taxes, expanded by Labour to a 78pc levy on profits, for driving up production costs.
The long-term break-even price for North Sea gas is roughly $13.50 per thousand cubic feet, compared to $8-$9 for US LNG.
Industry experts warn that high taxes discourage domestic investment and increase the UK's reliance on energy imports.
The Government defends the energy profits levy, stating it ensures a prosperous future and has raised £13bn since 2022.

title: Meccano relaunched in attempt to become ‘Britain’s Lego’
author: Jonathan Prynn
content:
![Meccano Aston Martin set](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/04/TELEMMGLPICT000500705924_17885266582670_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqxx4ofqeRdaCxMF1N6jM5x1HwtdpQwyNje2OyIL7x97s.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Meccano Aston Martin set](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/04/TELEMMGLPICT000500705924_17885266582670_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqxx4ofqeRdaCxMF1N6jM5x1HwtdpQwyNje2OyIL7x97s.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
It was high on the Christmas wish list of millions of British children growing up in the 1960s and 1970s.
But in recent years, Meccano, the classic construction kit made up of metal strips and plates held together by nuts and bolts, has almost disappeared to toy heaven in the computer-game era.
The venerable 125-year-old brand is being dusted down and revived for a new generation with the aspiration to create a “British Lego”.
Meccano’s new British rights owner, The Entertainer, believes it is a “sleeping giant” that can recover from its commercial near-death experience to once again take its place on the world stage.
Andrew Murphy, the chief executive of Teal Group, The Entertainer’s parent company, said: “From a consumer perspective in the UK, Meccano has barely existed for 10 years.
“There may have been some dusty boxes on shelves somewhere but as a major consumer product in the UK it just wasn’t there.”
Global sales dwindled to just £7m under the ownership of the Canadian giant Spin Master, the world’s fourth-biggest toy company, which bought Meccano in 2018.
But the Toronto-based multinational signed a long-term licensing agreement with Teal in January 2025 in an effort to reverse its fortunes.
Mr Murphy said he was convinced the brand has the potential to grow sales “easily into the hundreds of millions of pounds” by tapping into a renewed interest in engineering.
The chief executive added: “We get people all the time asking for something that’s ‘like Lego but not Lego’. That is the role Meccano has played in the past and can again.”
![Meccano](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/04/TELEMMGLPICT000500702777_17885264842813_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqA7N2CxnJWnYI3tCbVBgu9T0aesusvN1TE7a0ddd_esI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Meccano’s relaunch will be marked by the release of two new limited-edition collective sets: Meccano Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Race Car, with 1,203 pieces and priced at £200, and a Meccano Ducati Monster Motorbike priced at £40.
There will also be four new product ranges: Makers, Builders, Masters and Pro for different age groups starting from three-plus.
Packaging and the once notoriously complex building instructions have been overhauled for a modern audience.
Meccano was patented in Liverpool in 1901 by Frank Hornby, an English inventor and businessman, whose train sets also became world famous. It was originally known as Mechanics Made Easy, before adopting the Meccano name in 1907.
It has been sold in more than 100 countries, with the strongest markets outside the UK including France, Australia and the United States. Meccano is now made in Hungary, India and China.
summary: The 125-year-old construction toy brand Meccano is being revived by its new British rights owner, The Entertainer, with the goal of becoming a "British Lego". Under previous ownership by Spin Master, global sales fell to £7m, but a long-term licensing agreement signed in January 2025 aims to rebuild the brand. The relaunch features new product ranges, overhauled packaging, simplified instructions, and limited-edition sets like an Aston Martin Formula One Race Car and a Ducati Monster Motorbike.
key_points: Meccano is being relaunched in the UK by its new rights owner, The Entertainer, after nearly disappearing from the consumer market.
Global sales previously dwindled to £7m under Canadian owner Spin Master before a licensing agreement was signed with Teal Group in January 2025.
The relaunch introduces four new product ranges and two limited-edition sets: an Aston Martin Formula One Race Car and a Ducati Monster Motorbike.
Packaging and complex building instructions have been updated to appeal to a modern audience.
Originally patented in Liverpool in 1901 by Frank Hornby, the brand aims to tap into a renewed interest in engineering and fill a demand for alternatives to Lego.

title: Trump calls for interest rate cut after jobs figures raise hike bets
author: Michael Race
content:
![US President Donald Trump sitting down in the Oval Office at the White House. He is wearing a dark blue suit, white shirt and a red tie with a blue pattern on it.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/966/cpsprodpb/be4c/live/c74b2990-a883-11f1-824a-0fc4c5d895ae.jpg)
- Published
Donald Trump has called for interest rates to be cut later this month, claiming higher rates put the US at a "very unfair disadvantage".
The president's remarks came as stronger-than-expected jobs figures in the US added to growing expectations that rates could be increased, with inflation still running high and American households feeling the pinch of rising prices.
The number of roles added to the economy increased by 162,000 in August, almost triple the 56,000 forecast by analysts, driven by a boost in hospitality and education hiring.
Trump said the US should have the "LOWEST RATE of any country in the World".
"The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart - BE PATRIOTS for a change. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won't allow that to happen!", the president said in a post on social media, external.
Last week, Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US central bank, signalled that rates could be hiked if policymakers were not confident price rises were easing for Americans.
Inflation, which measures price increases over time, remains above the Fed's 2% annual target, with prices up 3.4% in the past 12 months, according to the latest data.
The next interest rate decision will be made on 15-16 September. Rates were left unchanged between 3.5% and 3.75% in July for the fifth time in a row, but concerns over inflation remain due to the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which has caused as surge in global oil prices.
On Friday, US diesel prices hit an all-time high of $5.85 a gallon on average, compared to $3.71 a year ago.
But despite the cost of living rising, wages also appear to be increasing. In August, average hourly earnings for all employees were $37.75 on average, having increased 3.1%.
"Even the most committed dove would struggle to find anything in the August employment report to justify keeping interest rates unchanged," said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics.
He added that the strength in the jobs market meant that the latest inflation figures released next week would only need to be moderately above the Fed's target to fuel expectations of a September hike.
"A hike in rates just became a bit more likely," said Neil Birrell, chief investment office of investment firm Premier Miton.
Almost 60% of traders were betting on an interest rate hike in September, according to CME Group's "FedWatch" data.
An increase in employment during the final month of the summer in restaurants and bars, as well as in local government education ahead of the new school year, was behind August's labour market rebound.
Weaker job figures released earlier in the summer were revised up by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, revealing a stronger labour market than previously thought. Instead of the economy being deemed to have shed 23,000 jobs in July, some 44,000 were found to have been created in subsequent estimates.
While many more jobs were added, the US unemployment rate remained unchanged at 4.1% last month, with seven million out of work. Both measures have changed little over the year.
In response to the stronger jobs figures raising expectations of a interest rate hike, US stock market indexes were trading down on Friday.
Trump called the response "crazy". "We just got GREAT Numbers on Jobs, the Market should go UP, because our Credit and Economy are better but, as always, for the past 25 years, the Stock Market goes DOWN, because we're living under False Reality that if things are good, you've got to "KILL IT" because of a "fear" of Inflation," he said.
summary: President Donald Trump has demanded that the Federal Reserve cut interest rates later this month, arguing that high rates place the US at an unfair disadvantage. His comments follow stronger-than-expected August jobs figures that increased market expectations for a potential rate hike due to ongoing inflation. The US economy added 162,000 jobs in August, driven by growth in hospitality and education hiring, while the unemployment rate remained at 4.1%.
key_points: Donald Trump publicly called for interest rates to be cut and urged the Federal Reserve to lower rates.
The US economy added 162,000 jobs in August, significantly higher than the 56,000 forecast by analysts.
Inflation remains above the Fed's 2% target, with prices up 3.4% over the past 12 months.
Stronger jobs data raised expectations among traders that the central bank might increase interest rates in September.
US stock market indexes traded down following the release of the employment report, which Trump criticized.

title: Bank of England chief: Defence spending fears fuelling bond turmoil
author: Emma Taggart; Chris Price
content:
![Andrew Bailey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/04/TELEMMGLPICT000500704782_17885259737680_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Andrew Bailey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/04/TELEMMGLPICT000500704782_17885259737680_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
The Governor of the Bank of England has warned that concerns about defence spending are fuelling turmoil in global bond markets.
Andrew Bailey said worldwide uncertainty about how to pay for defence was one of several “very substantial” challenges pushing up government borrowing costs.
Mr Bailey warned that military spending was one of the factors behind the sharp rise in government borrowing costs seen this week, alongside an ageing population and slow growth.
Speaking at an event at the London School of Economics on Friday, he said: “There are very, very substantial challenges at the moment, structural challenges, there’s the challenge of slow growth, there’s the challenge of these supply shocks.
“Then there’s these underlying, even deeper structural challenges around things like ageing, defence and so on that is [sic] relevant to thinking about the pressures on bond markets.”
The Governor also listed financing climate change as a significant pressure on public debt.
Borrowing costs around the world rose sharply at the start of the week and Britain suffered the G7’s biggest increase in bond yields on Tuesday. Interest rates on 10-year gilts, as UK bonds are known, reached 5.28pc at one point on Wednesday, their highest level since 2007.
The sell-off in bond markets reignited on Friday after the US added far more jobs than expected last month, triggering bets that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates.
The yield on two-year US Treasury bonds jumped to its highest level since 2024 in response. Borrowing costs in the UK rose in tandem, given the close ties between the British and US debt markets.
Official data showed non-farm payrolls grew by 162,000 in August, triple the forecasted 55,000. Donald Trump hailed the surprise increase, but called for the Fed to lower rates.
The warning from Mr Bailey comes as questions grow about how Britain will fund a rise in defence spending.
John Healey, the Chancellor, will use next month’s Budget to detail plans to fill a near £5bn gap in the Defence Investment Plan signed off by Sir Keir Starmer.
Mr Healey warned this week that “difficult decisions” would need to be taken to address the gap.
However, he is not expected to commit to spending 3pc of GDP on defence by 2030, despite resigning as Defence Secretary over the issue from Sir Keir’s government.
Filling the existing funding gap marks a far cry from Nato’s target for countries to boost defence spending to 3.5pc of GDP by 2035.
Growing fears about gaps in Britain’s defence spending come after the Army has suspended live-fire drills and major war games in an attempt to save money.
Interest rate policies under fire
The Resolution Foundation, a think tank with close links to Labour, warned that it was “unrealistic” to promise an increase in military spending without broad-based tax increases, including on middle-earners.
Economists at the think tank said in a report published this week that it was “becoming increasingly pressing” to determine who will pay for higher defence spending while Britain grapples with soaring costs from government borrowing.
Mr Bailey also warned that the Bank was facing a challenge from “populist political movements” as interest rate policies come under fire.
The Governor said that economic prosperity was at stake if the independence of central banks were called into question but added that the Bank should “demonstrate how our actions serve the public good”.
Mr Bailey’s comments come at a time of growing scrutiny of interest rate policies.
The Bank has come under scrutiny in recent years over how it reacted to soaring inflation after the pandemic. Meanwhile, Donald Trump called Jerome Powell, the former Federal Reserve chairman, a “numbskull” and a “moron” for refusing to cut interest rates quickly.
summary: Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey has warned that global uncertainty surrounding how to fund defence is contributing to turmoil in bond markets and rising borrowing costs. Speaking at the London School of Economics, he cited military spending, an ageing population, slow growth, and climate change financing as deep structural pressures on public debt. The remarks coincide with surging bond yields in the UK and US, as well as mounting questions over how the British government will fund a nearly £5bn gap in its Defence Investment Plan.
key_points: Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey stated that concerns over how to pay for defence are driving turmoil in global bond markets.
Rising borrowing costs have also been attributed to structural challenges including an ageing population, slow growth, and the financing of climate change.
UK government borrowing costs surged this week, with 10-year gilt interest rates reaching their highest level since 2007.
Chancellor John Healey faces difficult decisions to address a near £5bn gap in the Defence Investment Plan in the upcoming Budget.
The Resolution Foundation warned that funding increases in military spending would require broad-based tax increases, including on middle-earners.

title: Full list of stores closing in September - including restaurant chain, Poundland and more - AOL
author: Andrea Blazquez
content:
![Express UK](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/logos/light/express-uk.png?v=1784568534)
![View up the High Street in Stroud, a market town in Gloucestershire. Situated in the Cotswolds at the meeting point of the Five Valleys, England, Unit](https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/09/04/6d810ad8-3d85-35ff-af55-e20b8570608b/8f321408-f99a-45ba-8fcb-8d083e3a77e2.jpg)
Poundland
Poundland is set to close two branches this autumn after the company could not agree on ongoing leases. The retailer shut nearly 150 shops last year but explained that "any future closures will be a consequence of standard business-as-usual lease events expected at a retailer with a large store network".
Poundland stores closing:
- The Brewery, Romford - closing on September 14
- Courtenay Street, Newton Abbot - closing on October 10
TG Jones
Retailer TG Jones, which replaced WHSmith, confirmed the closure of 19 branches in September after announcing a restructure earlier this summer, with around 150 stores at risk.
Closing-down sales have been launched, with shoppers able to get up to 30% off.

Beefeater and Brewers Fayre
A total of 106 Beefeater restaurants and 89 Brewers Fayre pubs are set to close in September after Whitbread, which also owns hotel chain Premier Inn, announced a five-year strategy to save £250million.
Dominic Paul, Whitbread's chief executive, said: "We plan to convert all our remaining branded restaurants to an integrated food and beverage offer that is preferred by our hotel guests and will unlock the addition of more highly profitable extension rooms. Our continued efforts to drive our commercial plan and efficiencies will extend our market-leading position and allow us to take share from our competitors, many of which are struggling to grow."

summary: Multiple retail and restaurant chains are closing numerous locations this September due to restructuring, lease expirations, and cost-saving strategies. Poundland is closing two branches, TG Jones is shutting 19 stores following a restructure, and Whitbread is closing 106 Beefeater restaurants and 89 Brewers Fayre pubs as part of a plan to save £250 million.
key_points: Poundland is closing branches in Romford and Newton Abbot due to lease agreements.
TG Jones has confirmed 19 branch closures in September alongside closing-down sales.
Whitbread is closing 106 Beefeater restaurants and 89 Brewers Fayre pubs as part of a five-year strategy to save £250 million.
The restaurant and pub closures are intended to convert remaining branded locations to integrated food and beverage offers for hotel guests.
